> English edition of `docs/区域模式端到端验收测试用例.md`; the Chinese file remains the source of record until both are maintained together.

# Regional-Mode End-to-End Acceptance Test Cases

> **Maintenance contract:** case ids and the `GF-REGIONAL-*` heading anchors stay stable, but the body must be
> revised to match the current implementation; mutually conflicting steps must not be kept side by side in an "append-only history corrections" style.
> The `procedure` entries in `testcases/fault-scenarios.yaml` reference these heading anchors directly;
> headings must not be renamed casually. Whenever the body, risk or order is changed, the catalog must be updated
> in the same change and `tests/test_fault_scenario_catalog.py` plus the regional case index generator must be run.

## 1. Goals and scope

This manual covers exactly one deployment form: **a CPU-cluster control plane and a GPU-cluster data plane, separated**
(`GPU_FAULT_DEPLOYMENT_MODE=regional`). The system under test is:

- one regional CPU control plane: `gpu-fault-api-ha` with three replicas + a shared Aurora PostgreSQL,
  running in a dedicated HyperPod CPU instance group, which **holds no kubeconfig of any GPU cluster**
  and does not use its own in-cluster Kubernetes client to operate GPU clusters;
- one data plane per GPU HyperPod cluster: Collector, Node Agent,
  CompletionWatcher, `gpu-fault-cluster-executor`;
- a single outbound TLS channel between the two sides; actions use the pull/claim/lease/result protocol.

These cases are meant for an approved staging or isolated HyperPod environment. The deterministic software-level assertions are
covered by `tests/regional/test_regional_control_plane.py` and `tests/hyperpod/test_cluster_executor.py`;
the cases in this manual **do not replace** them. Instead they verify the process boundary, identity boundary,
network boundary and blast radius in a real environment -- exactly the parts a single-process pytest structure cannot prove.

### 1.1 Region and cluster identity pre-gate

Normal administrator acceptance uses `site.yaml` as the source of truth; `regional-env.sh` and
`regional-release.json` are for low-level break-glass only. Before running any regional case, the AWS Region, cluster ARNs
and the current Runtime Profile must be read from `site.yaml`; they must not be inferred from the current shell,
the kubectl context, the historical `hyperpod-v1` or sample values. The acceptance baseline includes:

- the EKS ARNs that the CPU/GPU kubeconfigs actually point to must each equal the configured ARN;
- every EKS ARN, ACM certificate and GPU cluster `region` must belong to the top-level
  `aws_region`;
- HyperPod `Orchestrator.Eks.ClusterArn` must equal the corresponding EKS ARN;
- `NodeRecovery` of every managed GPU HyperPod must be `None`;
- any placeholder, cross-Region ARN, wrong context or managed node-recovery configuration must fail before the first
  Kubernetes apply.

The offline contract is covered by `tests/regional/test_regional_release_orchestrator.py`,
`tests/regional/test_regional_release_commands.py` and
`tests/regional/test_production_safety_config.py`; they also pin the deployment's
"no change, no wait" behaviour: when the CNAME already matches the expectation exactly, no Route53 UPSERT is submitted; when any of value/TTL/absence
differs, the full submit and INSYNC wait still runs; and the role-split script composes the ConfigMaps of the selected roles into
one multi-document apply. A real environment must still run
CPU-1, REG-1 and the regional acceptance of this manual separately; synthetic-ARN unit tests are no substitute.

Division of labour between the two public documents:

| Document | Answers | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| This manual | **what to run and how to judge** | Preconditions / Steps / Verdict / Cleanup. A specification; contains no historical results |
| [`regional-case-index.md`](regional-case-index.md) | **in what order to run** | Generated artifact; its sources are two YAML files |
| [`change-impact-and-test-selection.md`](change-impact-and-test-selection.md) | **which cases this change affects** | Reverse-selects pytest and regional cases from code paths |

An ordinary code change does not re-run all the cases in this manual by default. Day-to-day development runs
`make test-impact BASE=origin/main`; a PR or release candidate runs
`make regional-impact-plan BASE=origin/main` and reviews the non-destructive and approval-required cases.
Only a formal first go-live, a major architecture change or a fail-closed escalation of the impact selector
runs the complete order of this manual. destructive/live cases always require a corresponding implementation change, a maintenance window and explicit approval.

Real execution results, on-site resource identifiers and per-round defect records are kept in a non-public internal evidence store, keyed by case id,
and do not enter this public specification. The redacted historical narrative and coverage audit kept to explain how the cases evolved is at
[`docs/evidence/regional-history/区域模式验收历史与覆盖审计.md`](../evidence/regional-history/区域模式验收历史与覆盖审计.md);
that file is not PASS evidence for the current steps or the current release.

Case numbering rule: `GF-REGIONAL-<domain>-<sequence>`, where the domains mean:

| Domain | Coverage | Gate mapping (`docs/en/high-level-design.md` §10) |
|---|---|---|
| `BOOT` | fail-closed startup guards on both the control-plane and executor sides, and whether the deployment manifests themselves come up | control-plane EKS is not modified |
| `AUTH` | per-cluster credentials, header/payload anti-forgery, endpoint authorization inventory, TLS | cluster A credentials cannot operate cluster B |
| `ISO` | cross-cluster state isolation; one cluster going offline does not spread | identical node/job/attempt IDs isolated; one cluster offline does not block |
| `CMD` | remote command protocol and all boundary values | lease expiry, duplicate results, stale fencing rejected |
| `HA` | replica/node/Aurora failover | replica and CPU node exit; Aurora failover does not repeat destructive steps |
| `PREEMPT` | higher-tier workflow preempts lower-tier, DAG branch/join, cross-fault-domain action dominance | no corresponding §10 entry |
| `NET` | network outage and catch-up submission on recovery | events cached during network outage, submitted late by idempotency key |
| `CAP` | queue and Store I/O capacity admission | one cluster offline/overloaded does not block other clusters |
| `BLAST` | blast radius and least privilege | control-plane EKS is not tainted/drained/Job-modified |
| `WORKLOAD` | submission path of managed training jobs and attempt observation baseline | no corresponding §10 entry (`RESTART_WORKLOAD` only appears in the notification gate, which belongs to `NOTIFY`) |
| `DESTR` | tiered acceptance of destructive actions | reset/reboot/replace verified inside a maintenance window |
| `NOTIFY` | SES mail and de-duplication | notification `SENT` + non-empty MessageId |
| `COLLECT` | live acceptance of the collection layer: kmsg/DCGM/EFA collection and XID/SXID verdict coverage | Collector side of the per-cluster E2E gate |
| `E2E` | per-cluster Collector → control plane → local executor | every GPU cluster completes E2E separately |

The two "no corresponding §10 entry" marks in the table are honest annotations, not omissions: `docs/en/high-level-design.md` §10 explicitly
states that "the content and order of the entries in this chapter are an external reference contract", so this manual does not unilaterally add entries to that chapter.
`PREEMPT` and `WORKLOAD` are preconditions for the `DESTR` gate to be trustworthy, so they still stand as separate sections
and are scheduled separately in the execution order (see §17).

### 1.2 Runner and evidence contract

- Formal cases must pass one by one in machine order before proceeding. A `manual` case that was not executed, a read-only analysis PASS,
  or a local proxy pytest PASS can never be promoted to a live execution PASS; when the formal summary is missing results, has duplicate case IDs,
  unknown states, a failed independent re-check, or still has required cases at NOT_RUN, complete acceptance success must not be returned.
- Live plan schema 3 binds the actual CLI arguments, source contents, preflight results, site profile and
  execution scope. An old schema, a failed precheck or target drift requires a fresh plan; changing only the confirmation is not enough.
  The bare protocol fragments in this document explain the assertions; real execution must go through the corresponding audited runner.
- The plain entry points of CMD-017, CMD-018 and NET-006 likewise require a real read-only identity and prechecks.
  `--cpu-kubeconfig`, `--gpu-kubeconfig`, `--gpu-context`, `--namespace`,
  `--cluster-id`, `--region` may be supplied by the same site profile and must match the existing perf
  environment / import-time targets. The top-level `cluster_id` binds the physical cluster and must not be `perf-cap-000`;
  the synthetic execution identity is recorded separately as `synthetic_cluster_id`. Re-read and compare the approved identity before executing;
  old canonical results are archived first, and a failed or partial result cannot be promoted to a formal PASS by back-filling fields.
- Evidence of a run in progress does not keep an old PASS. Failures and cleanup errors must be written to disk; prechecks accept only complete, current,
  same-identity passing evidence. When subprocess supervision is lost, write
  `command-supervision-lost.json` and block further retries in this round until the process and resources have been independently verified.
- CPU probes use `/opt/gpu-fault/control-plane/bin/python`, GPU Pod probes use
  `/opt/gpu-fault/executor/bin/python`; the system Python does not contain the business packages. Node host probes use
  `/opt/gpu-fault/current/venv/bin/python`. The full local source environment is never taken as proof of the deployed image.
- HostProbe binds the nonce, Pod/ConfigMap UID, Node UID and script SHA in a private log;
  a resource with the same name but a different UID must not be reused or deleted. A lost create response must be reconciled by ownership, not recorded as "not created";
  when host file cleanup has not been proven successful, keep the cleanup channel and logs; do not delete the Pod early and then claim there is no residue.
- CPU/Executor environment-window records carry the full target identity, use UID/resourceVersion conditional updates,
  and restore only the variables controlled in this run; `closed_at` is written only after the new Pod total and every container's Ready are all satisfied.
  Window records left by another release identity: those already CLOSED are archived directly; those still OPEN/OPENING
  are retired and archived (`retired_by: release change`) only when the online Deployment has been re-rendered (UID or generation changed) and every window variable
  is no longer in effect; otherwise opening and closing keep
  refusing, and a window still held by another identity is never silently taken over. When the window is still in effect (target UID unchanged, every
  assignment still online), opening refuses and names the exit: only when the operator explicitly runs
  `--close --close-foreign-release --confirm CLOSE_…` is the baseline in the record restored verbatim and
  `closed_under_release` written; a case's own cleanup never carries this switch.
  Permission errors, empty output and an incomplete replica list do not mean "absent" or "healthy".
- The old PASS bindings of the 43 manual and 3 live command cases modified in this round have been withdrawn to NOT_RUN,
  and NOTIFY-006 also had its old binding withdrawn because the selected assertion set changed; old records are history only;
  unit tests and code review cannot issue a new live PASS. The four newly added cases likewise await an approved real run.

## 2. Destructiveness levels

### 2.0 Deployment modes (fix the mode first, then talk about levels)

**System-level hard constraints (not configurable; three items):**

1. HyperPod `NodeRecovery` of a managed GPU cluster must be `None` (automatic node recovery disabled);
2. this system never calls `BatchReplaceClusterNodes` under any circumstances;
3. **HyperPod's automatic job recovery must be disabled; automatic recovery of training jobs is taken over entirely by this system**
   (managed jobs must not carry `enable-job-auto-resume=true`, Slurm must not carry
   `--auto-resume=1`). Job-level ownership is covered in §2.0.1.
4. **Only HyperPod EKS orchestration is supported; HyperPod Slurm orchestration is not supported for now.**
   All cases run on HyperPod EKS clusters only; a cluster whose `DescribeCluster.Orchestrator`
   is not EKS is out of acceptance scope.
   The Slurm assertions that appear in this manual (`scontrol` isolation evidence, the `--auto-resume=1` check)
   **are not executed at present**; they are kept so that nothing has to be rewritten when that orchestration is opened up later.

The argument is in `docs/en/high-level-design.md` §2.1 and §2.3; in summary: GPU scarcity makes a same-spec allocation on the provider side
quite likely to fail -- after a failed managed replacement the node is removed and capacity shrinks, which is worse than not replacing at all;
and managed replacement is a second lifecycle writer outside this system. Node replacement can only go through a warm spare.
The reason for constraint 3 is implementation simplicity: the control loop of managed job recovery lives on the AWS-managed side, and
this system cannot share the restart budget and checkpoint gate with it.

The rest of §2.0 below discusses only the **node-level** constraints 1 and 2; constraint 3 is covered in §2.0.1.

Hence only two forms remain, differing only in **whether there is a warm-spare pool**:

| | Mode B: with warm spare | Mode C: without warm spare |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HyperPod `NodeRecovery` | `None` (mandatory) | `None` (mandatory) |
| warm spare (`gpu-fault.io/spare=true`) | **required** | none |
| Role of this system | executor of the recovery | isolation + alerting only; replacement is manual |
| Does this system call `BatchReplaceClusterNodes` | **no** | **no** |
| How node replacement happens | migrate to the customer's own warm-spare node; the faulty instance is not destroyed | does not happen automatically; the `REPLACE_NODE` step is judged `FAILED` |

**The removed Mode A** (`NodeRecovery=Automatic`, this system as a pure observer)
is **no longer supported** under this constraint. The onboarding precheck must include
`DescribeCluster.NodeRecovery == "None"`, otherwise onboarding of that cluster is refused.

This yields several simplified acceptance invariants:

- **Any `BatchReplaceClusterNodes` appearing in CloudTrail is judged FAIL, regardless of who the caller is.**
  This is far simpler than the earlier "distinguish whether the caller is HyperPod or the executor",
  and harder to bypass -- every case that involves replace has the uniform assertion "must be `[]`".
- `GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_HYPERPOD_REPLACE` and
  `GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_WITH_AUTOMATIC_NODE_RECOVERY`
  **are always `false`; they are invariants, not defaults** --
  no case may switch them on temporarily "to get some path through".
  Step 1 of the original `DESTR-004` did exactly that and is now retired (see that case).
- The IAM permission for `BatchReplaceClusterNodes` **must not be granted** to the execution role.
  When the regional release orchestrator finds that permission, it must fail before any Deployment change.
- `GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_HYPERPOD_REBOOT` may still be `true` --
  a reboot does not destroy the instance and is not affected by this constraint.

The `destructive-provider-replace` level therefore **becomes a pure disproof level**:
the action it describes does not exist in this system, and any case observing it means the constraint has been broken.

**The current regional manifests enable the spare coordinator whether or not warm-spare nodes exist.**
Having no warm-spare pool does not mean `spare_coordinator=None`: `REPLACE_NODE` still uses
`HEALTHY_WARM_SPARE_ONLY`, fails explicitly when no node can be allocated, and is forbidden to fall back to the provider API.
In addition there are two independent invariants:

1. `GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_HYPERPOD_REPLACE=true` is rejected outright at configuration construction;
2. both the Executor IAM and the regional release orchestrator forbid `BatchReplaceClusterNodes`.

Hence the old Mode C procedure "temporarily disable the coordinator, then verify that only one switch remains" has left live acceptance
and is kept only as a defence-in-depth negative test in an isolated process (`DESTR-011`).

How the code implementation maps to the constraints above:

- **The mandatory nature of `NodeRecovery=None` is expressed by two guards together** (both fail-closed):
  - `src/gpu_fault/hyperpod.py::HyperPodLifecycleAdapter.preflight` -- when `NodeRecovery == "Automatic"` and
    `GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_WITH_AUTOMATIC_NODE_RECOVERY=true` is not set, preflight fails with the
    text `HyperPod automatic node recovery is enabled; direct batch mutation
    would create a second lifecycle trigger`.
  - `src/gpu_fault/adapters/` -- when `warm_spare_only` is true but
    `NodeRecovery == "Automatic"`, it fails with the text
    `healthy warm-spare replacement requires HyperPod NodeRecovery=None;
    provider replacement is disabled`.
    Note that it **does not cover Mode C** (the whole condition short-circuits when `warm_spare_only` is false).

  These two are the **backstop of the onboarding precheck**, not a runtime form: the constraint requires the cluster to be
  `NodeRecovery=None` from the start, and a cluster that fails the precheck should not be onboarded.
- Both runtime forms, with and without warm spare, use: the warm spare entry below + layer 3 of §2.1
  + the "no fallback to the provider API" in `src/gpu_fault/adapters/`.
- Independent guard rails for provider replace: configuration construction rejects true, IAM deny, pre-release permission audit.
- **Paths kept but never to be triggered**: `ManagedRecoveryObserverAdapter`
  (`src/gpu_fault/adapters/`) and `HyperPodManagedRecoveryObserver.observe()`
  (`managed_recovery.py:137-159`) were originally used for node-level observation in Mode A.
  Node-level observation should not be triggered under this constraint; the two classes are kept because
  the job-level hit path of the former is **equally non-compliant** under the hard constraint (see §2.0.1),
  and keeping it is only a fail-closed backstop;
  and the identity ledger of `HyperPodIdentityRegistry` is also used on the warm spare path
  (`hyperpod_spares.py:339-352`).
  This retained path has one known gap, see the last paragraph of `docs/en/high-level-design.md` §2.2
  (on a spontaneous replacement the old agent is not fenced, and the new agent may hit
  `another agent incarnation holds the node lease`) --
  it cannot happen under this constraint, but if managed replacement is ever reintroduced it must be fixed first.

### 2.0.1 Ownership of job restarts: exclusively this system under the hard constraint

**Hard constraint (the same one as in §2.0): HyperPod's automatic job recovery must be disabled;
automatic recovery of training jobs is taken over entirely by this system.**
Managed jobs **must not** carry `sagemaker.amazonaws.com/enable-job-auto-resume=true`,
and Slurm submission scripts **must not** carry `srun --auto-resume=1`.
The reason is implementation simplicity: the control loop of managed job recovery lives on the AWS-managed side; this system cannot see its retry count,
cannot share the restart budget and checkpoint gate with it, and the managed side may bring the job back up while the incident is still
`QUARANTINED`. The argument is in `docs/en/high-level-design.md` §2.1 constraint 3 and §2.3.

Job-level recovery (`workloadStop` / `workloadRestart`) is still **parametrically** independent of the node-level `NodeRecovery`
(it is decided by the workload annotation rather than a `DescribeCluster` field),
but **in terms of compliant forms it has been collapsed to a single one, just like the node level**:

| `sagemaker.amazonaws.com/enable-job-auto-resume` | Who restarts the training job | Role of this system | mode / owner expected in the profile | Compliance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `false` (or the key is absent) | **this system** | executor | `OWN` / `gpu-fault-kubernetes-adapter` | **the only compliant form** |
| `true` | HyperPod | observer + sends alert notifications, performs no restart action | `DELEGATE` / `hyperpod-managed-job-recovery` | **non-compliant**; the onboarding precheck should refuse it; if it slips through, that step is `FAILED` at runtime |
| annotations cannot be read | undetermined; nobody acts | observe only | `OBSERVE` / `unresolved-recovery-owner` | code is fail-closed; not a runtime form |

The Slurm side is analogous: `srun --auto-resume=1` is equivalent to `true` (**forbidden**),
and not passing it is equivalent to `false` (`src/gpu_fault/hyperpod.py::HyperPodWorkloadRecoveryEvidence.from_slurm_auto_resume`).

**The constraint turns what used to be an implementation gap into "the implementation happens to be compliant"**: the deployment script statically fills
`workloadStop` / `workloadRestart` with `OWN` (see the ⚠ paragraph below),
and `OWN` is precisely the only compliant form, so **no code change is needed on the profile side**.
The other half -- detecting at runtime that a customer has turned on auto-resume on their own -- has been closed:
`KubernetesWorkflowAdapter` re-reads the annotation before writing the workload and fails closed
(see the ⚠ paragraph below). The responsibility of `DESTR-012` changed accordingly (see that case).

The following chain **is reached only when the profile has been misconfigured as `DELEGATE`**;
it is recorded to show that the consequence of misconfiguration is "failing on the safe side", not "nobody handles it".
The "observe only, do not restart" chain for `true` is complete in the code, link by link:

1. `hyperpod.py:88-104` `from_eks_annotations` classifies the annotation as
   `ENABLED` / `DISABLED` / `UNKNOWN`.
2. `hyperpod.py:439-453` `_recovery_capability` sets the owner of
   `WORKLOAD_STOP` and `WORKLOAD_RESTART` accordingly: `ENABLED` →
   `hyperpod-managed-job-recovery` (`DELEGATE`), `DISABLED` →
   `gpu-fault-restart-controller` (`OWN`).
3. `src/gpu_fault/orchestration/` `_owner()` takes that capability's owner from the profile;
   **both** `DELEGATE` and `OWN` are taken and filled into
   `WorkflowStepSpec.execution_owner` (`:4333-4340`) --
   so with `DELEGATE` the step is still generated, only the owner differs.
4. `src/gpu_fault/app/` puts `hyperpod-managed-job-recovery` into the default value of
   `GPU_FAULT_MANAGED_RECOVERY_OWNERS`;
   `src/gpu_fault/app/` installs `ManagedRecoveryObserverAdapter` with this set of owners.
5. `src/gpu_fault/adapters/` -- the adapter's `supports()` matches on
   `execution_owner in owners and operation in OPERATIONS`, and
   `OPERATIONS` (`:3258-3263`) **includes `RESTART_WORKLOAD` and `STOP_WORKLOADS`**.
6. `src/gpu_fault/adapters/`: it calls neither Kubernetes nor the provider;
   it only returns `waiting`, with details
   `mutation_submitted_by_control_plane: False` +
   `requires_external_confirmation: True`;
   it turns `succeeded` only once the confirmation from the HyperPod side has entered
   `confirmed_adapter_operation_ids`.
   **This is the "observer + performs no action".**

The alerting link is carried by `context.advisory_notifications.send`, shared with `SupportEscalationAdapter` and others
(`src/gpu_fault/app/`, `:763-766`).

**⚠ Constraint 3 is enforced at two layers, which must be accepted separately (see `DESTR-012`).**

**First layer: onboarding precheck (deployment time, manual).** Confirm namespace by namespace that managed training jobs do not carry
`enable-job-auto-resume=true` and Slurm scripts do not carry `--auto-resume=1`.
This is the required first layer, because the runtime guard can only **refuse actions**; it cannot change the customer's configuration on their behalf --
every fault recovery of a violating job will stop at `FAILED`.

**Second layer: runtime fail-closed guard (code, wired in).**
After `KubernetesWorkflowAdapter._set_workloads()` fetches each
workload object with `_read_workload()`, it immediately calls `_managed_job_recovery_conflict()`,
which re-judges the annotation with `from_eks_annotations()` from link 1 above;
if any workload is judged `ENABLED`, it returns `WorkflowStepOutcome.failed(...)`,
with details containing `managed_job_recovery_workloads` (listing only the violators), `required_annotation`,
`required_annotation_value` (`absent or false`) and, one per workload,
`kubectl annotate <kind> <name> -n <ns> sagemaker.amazonaws.com/enable-job-auto-resume-`
as `remediation_commands`. The guard is ordered **before** `_mark_terminating_pods()` and every patch;
`STOP_WORKLOADS` and `RESTART_WORKLOAD` go through the same entry, so both are covered.
**There is no per-workload exemption annotation**: whoever can turn on auto-resume in violation could equally add an exemption annotation.

Link 2 (`resolve_recovery_ownership()` deciding the owner) **is still only called by the manual CLI**
(`src/gpu_fault/hyperpod_cli.py::main`, where `--workload-recovery` is a human-supplied argument),
for the pre-onboarding check; the runtime guard does not depend on it. The owner in the production profile is still written statically at deploy time:
`deploy/hyperpod/deploy.sh:1527-1530` pins `workloadRestart` to
`gpu-fault-kubernetes-adapter`, and `:1579-1586` fills this set of capabilities
**unconditionally with `"mode": "OWN"`**; only `nodeReboot` / `nodeReplace` are split into
`DELEGATE` / `OWN` / `OBSERVE` by `node_recovery` (`:1566-1577`).
Under the hard constraint this static `OWN` happens to be the only compliant form.

One more boundary of an existing line of defence: `service.py:459-466`
`_workflow_owns_workload_restart()` only prevents two of this system's **own** incidents from restarting the same workload twice;
"guarding against the HyperPod side" is the job of the second-layer guard above, and the two cannot substitute for each other.

About `UNKNOWN`: `from_eks_annotations(None)` (annotations cannot be read) returns
`UNKNOWN` → degraded to `OBSERVE`; it **does not** guess "disabled" and then let the in-house Controller take over
(see `docs/en/detailed-design.md` §2.14). But that is the **function-level** behaviour of `hyperpod.py`;
at the call site of the guard above, `_annotations()` returns `dict(value or {})` and
**never returns `None`**, so `UNKNOWN` is unreachable there --
an unreadable workload raises earlier in `_read_workload()`, before the guard has run.
"Cannot read" and "read, but the key is absent" are two different conclusions -- only the latter is `DISABLED`/`OWN`.

The phase division of §17 is therefore adjusted to the hard constraint:

- The **"Warm spare"** phase verifies Mode B and asserts that `BatchReplaceClusterNodes` is `[]`.
- The **"Failover and constraint disproof"** phase was originally "verify that provider replace succeeds";
  **that goal is now retired.**
  The action does not exist in this system, so there is no scenario that needs its "normal operation" verified.
  The phase becomes **constraint disproof**: assert that the switch is always `false`, that IAM lacks the permission,
  and that `BatchReplaceClusterNodes` is `[]` in CloudTrail throughout.
  The original `DESTR-004` (temporarily enabling `ALLOW_HYPERPOD_REPLACE` and really destroying an instance)
  **is retired in its entirety** and must not be executed.
- Mode C is covered by `DESTR-011`, placed first in the phase **"Destructive capability acceptance (including non-destructive fail-closed negative cases)"**
  (the tier that does not touch the provider):
  it is a pure disproof case, but what it verifies is the only single-point guard rail shared by both forms.
- The job recovery ownership of §2.0.1 (constraint 3) is covered by `DESTR-012`, in the same phase.
  Its group B is a **purely read-only** constraint disproof and should **run first** within that case:
  if auto-resume really is on for a managed job, the restart assertions of group A cannot be attributed.

`REPLACE_NODE` has two **structurally completely different** implementation paths.
This system takes only the first (warm spare); the second is listed to make explicit that it **does not belong to this system**,
and any case observing it is judged FAIL:

| Level | Action | Implementation path | Node source | Calls provider API |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `live-non-destructive` | read-only collection, diagnostics, evidence freeze | control plane + Collector | — | no |
| `live-workload-restart` | `STOP_WORKLOADS` / `RESTART_WORKLOAD` | executor's local Kubernetes | — | no |
| `live-service-action` | `FABRIC_MANAGER_RESTART`, `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES` | Node Agent | — | no |
| `destructive` | `RESET_GPU` | Node Agent | — | no |
| `destructive-provider-reboot` | `NODE_REBOOT` | `batch_reboot_cluster_nodes` | the original node is rebooted | **yes** |
| `destructive-warm-spare` | `REPLACE_NODE` (`replacement_strategy=HEALTHY_WARM_SPARE_ONLY`) | `HyperPodLifecycleStepAdapter` + `HyperPodSpareCoordinator`, `local_only=True` | **only warm-spare GPU nodes that the customer provisioned in advance and brought under monitoring** (label `gpu-fault.io/spare=true`) | **no; calling `BatchReplaceClusterNodes` is forbidden** |
| `destructive-provider-replace` **(this action does not exist in this system; observing it is judged FAIL)** | `REPLACE_NODE` via the provider API | `batch_replace_cluster_nodes` | a new instance allocated by the provider | **yes -- hence forbidden by the hard constraint** |

The key differences between the two paths, which are also the anchors of the acceptance assertions:

- **Warm spare approach**: the faulty node is isolated (cordon + `gpu-fault.io/quarantined` taint),
  the workload migrates to the customer's own warm-spare node; the faulty node's instance is **not destroyed**, cluster capacity is unchanged,
  and nothing changes on the provider side. When the warm-spare pool is insufficient it must **fail and alert**;
  silently degrading to provider replace is never allowed.
  Code constraint: `src/gpu_fault/adapters/` --
  when `warm_spare_only` is true it skips the provider preflight, requires the spare coordinator to exist,
  requires HyperPod `NodeRecovery=None`, and with `local_only=True` enumerates warm-spare nodes only from Kubernetes
  labels (`src/gpu_fault/hyperpod_spares.py::HyperPodSpareCoordinator.allocate`).
  At the same time the managed/provider recovery adapter **explicitly refuses** to take over this kind of step.
- **Provider replace (forbidden in this system)**: calls `batch_replace_cluster_nodes`
  (`src/gpu_fault/hyperpod.py::HyperPodLifecycleAdapter.submit`; `857` is the reboot branch, both share the same submission path),
  and the old instance is destroyed permanently. Gated by `GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_HYPERPOD_REPLACE`, which
  `deploy/dataplane/cluster-action-executor.yaml:164-165` sets to `false` --
  **in this system that value is an invariant, not a "default"**;
  no case or maintenance operation may change it to `true`.

### 2.1 Which switch implements "allow reboot, forbid replace" (three layers, keep them apart)

This is the easiest place to misconfigure and the easiest to misread when checking: **`GPU_FAULT_ENABLE_HYPERPOD_ADAPTER`
is not the reboot/replace switch**; it only decides whether the adapter is installed at all.
In `src/gpu_fault/hyperpod.py::HyperPodLifecycleAdapter.submit`, reboot and replace are one submission path
that forks on `action`, so turning this switch off means **turning both off together** --
it cannot satisfy the requirement "allow reboot, forbid replace".

The gate that really separates the actions is layer 2, `src/gpu_fault/hyperpod.py::HyperPodAdapterConfig.action_enabled`:

```python
def action_enabled(self, action: HyperPodAction) -> bool:
    override = (self.reboot_enabled if action is HyperPodAction.REBOOT
                else self.replace_enabled)
    return self.execution_enabled if override is None else override
```

| Layer | Mechanism | Variable / parameter | Granularity | Manifest default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | whether the adapter is installed | `GPU_FAULT_ENABLE_HYPERPOD_ADAPTER` (`executor_from_environment` in `gpu_fault.cluster_executor.bootstrap`) | **shared** by reboot/replace; off turns both off | `false` (`:146-147`) |
| 2 | per-action release (**fail-closed hard gate**) | `GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_HYPERPOD_REBOOT` / `GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_HYPERPOD_REPLACE` (`hyperpod.py:203-206`) | each action independently | `true` / `false` (`:162-165`); **the latter is an invariant, always `false`** |
| 3 | warm spare vs provider | step parameter `replacement_strategy=HEALTHY_WARM_SPARE_ONLY` | decides routing, not permission | decided by the workflow |

`GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_HYPERPOD_MUTATION` is the legacy reboot compatibility switch:
`from_environment` falls back to it only when the dedicated reboot switch is unset; the replace default is always false;
explicitly setting `GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_HYPERPOD_REPLACE=true` makes the process refuse to start.
The regional manifests must therefore leave the legacy variable unset and explicitly keep replace=false.

The error text when layer 2 is violated (`hyperpod.py:737-744`, the anchor of the acceptance assertion):

```
HyperPod preflight failed: HyperPod REPLACE mutation is disabled by configuration
```

**The two paths are not guarded by the same gate; that is why the "Warm spare" phase and the
"Failover and constraint disproof" phase are accepted separately
(the latter is now constraint disproof and no longer verifies that provider replace succeeds):**

- The provider replace path is protected by layer 2. When `replacement_strategy` is misspelled or missing,
  `warm_spare_only` is `False` and the provider preflight in `src/gpu_fault/adapters/`
  runs; there `ALLOW_HYPERPOD_REPLACE=false` yields
  `safe_to_submit=False`, and the step **fails** instead of destroying a node. This is fail-closed.
- The warm spare path **skips the preflight entirely** (the
  `if not warm_spare_only` in `src/gpu_fault/adapters/`), so the layer-2 gate **plays no part** in the warm-spare decision.
  It relies on two other guards: at `3536-3542`, "the spare coordinator exists but no spare was allocated, so fail immediately,
  **no fallback to the provider API**" (`warm-spare replacement is required; provider node
  replacement API fallback is disabled`), and at `3469-3475`,
  "require HyperPod `NodeRecovery=None`".

The correct way to check the configuration: **do not look only at `ENABLE_HYPERPOD_ADAPTER`**;
the two layer-2 variables must be read together from every running executor replica:

```
GPU_FAULT_ENABLE_HYPERPOD_ADAPTER=true     # layer 1: installed (needed for reboot)
GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_HYPERPOD_REBOOT=true       # layer 2: allow reboot
GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_HYPERPOD_REPLACE=false     # layer 2: forbid provider replace
GPU_FAULT_ENABLE_HYPERPOD_SPARE_FAILOVER=true
GPU_FAULT_ENABLE_NODE_ACTION_ADAPTER=true
```

That is, "allow `BatchRebootClusterNodes`, forbid `BatchReplaceClusterNodes`",
consistent with the experimental constraint. Note that these three `ENABLE_*` being `true` on the executor is **correct and required**
(the regional architecture delegates mutation to the data plane precisely);
do not confuse this with `BOOT-004`/`005` -- what those two guards forbid is the **control plane** turning them on,
and on the control-plane side they must all be `false` (see `BOOT-010`).

Cases at the `destructive*` levels may only run inside a maintenance window, on isolated test nodes, and must record the
maintenance window, isolation evidence and rollback method. Even when `--include-manual` is passed, the runner records only
`NOT_RUN`.

### 2.2 Risk level vocabulary (the single source of values)

This section is the **single** source of values for the "level" field. The
`- Level:` line at the start of every case in this document and the `risk:` in `testcases/fault-scenarios.yaml` share the table below,
and both sides are guarded in both directions by `RISK_VALUES` in `tools/run_fault_test_cases.py` and by
`tests/test_fault_scenario_catalog.py`:

- a value outside the table → the loader fails immediately with `unsupported test case risk`;
- a value in the table that neither the document nor the catalog uses → the test fails as well (blocking zombie values).

So **any new spelling must enter this table first**; a near-synonym must not be improvised inside some case
(the historical `live-workload` / `destructive-reboot` arose exactly that way and have been
merged into `live-non-destructive` / `destructive-provider-reboot` respectively).
Likewise, the early `live-service-restart` has been merged into `live-service-action`:
restarting a service is just one kind of action issued to that service, and the admission conditions of the two tiers (live hardware,
no node reboot, no job stop) are identical; keeping them apart only made case authors guess the boundary over and over.
The action table of §2.0.1 has always grouped `FABRIC_MANAGER_RESTART` and
`QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES` together under `live-service-action`.

Destructiveness increases from top to bottom; from `live-*` on, live hardware is needed.
`live-service-action`, `live-workload-restart`, `live-node-mutation` and all
`destructive*` levels need a maintenance window by default; whether read-only or pure signal-injection cases need a window is governed by the
per-phase notes of the machine execution order. Risk is labelled by the **actual maximum side effect**, not by the injection means.

| Value | What it touches | Representative case |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `non-destructive` | touches nothing: pure unit/component tests / fixture replay; can run in CI at any time. The runner selects only this tier by default | `GF-POL-001` |
| `read-only-signal-replay` | only **reads** live hardware or replays signals (late submission requests, forged headers, reading the FIFO); does not change node or job state | `GF-REGIONAL-AUTH-001` |
| `live-non-destructive` | runs end to end on live hardware, but injects no fault and does not change the existing state of nodes and jobs | `GF-REGIONAL-WORKLOAD-001` |
| `live-kernel-log-injection` | writes XID lines from user space into the real `/dev/kmsg`. The GPU itself is not broken, but the downstream policy is really driven | `GF-LIVE-KMSG-XID11-001` |
| `live-isolation` | cordons + taints one **idle** node (automatically uncordoned afterwards); no reset, no reboot, no job stop | `GF-REGIONAL-COLLECT-009` |
| `live-service-action` | issues controlled actions to services on the node, including really restarting that service process (e.g. Fabric Manager); no node reboot, no job stop | `GF-LIVE-XID74-ALLZERO-20260726`, `GF-LIVE-KMSG-XID45-SOLO-FM-20260724` |
| `live-workload-restart` | really restarts the training job/attempt; the node is untouched | `GF-LIVE-XID11-001` |
| `live-node-mutation` | changes devices or system components on the node (unbinding an EFA PCI function, deleting the device-plugin Pod), but does not reboot/replace the node | `GF-REGIONAL-COLLECT-017` |
| `destructive` | issues destructive actions to the GPU itself (GPU reset etc.), affecting all jobs on that node | `GF-LIVE-XID95-DUAL-RESET-RESUME-20260724` |
| `destructive-warm-spare` | really replaces the node, but only from the customer's own warm-spare pool; insufficient spares must fail and alert, never fall back to provider replace | `GF-REGIONAL-DESTR-003` |
| `destructive-provider-reboot` | really reboots the physical node via HyperPod `BatchRebootClusterNodes` | `GF-REGIONAL-DESTR-002` |

**The table deliberately has no `destructive-provider-replace`.** `BatchReplaceClusterNodes`
is the action forbidden by hard constraint 2 of §2.0; no path of this system ever calls it, so it can only appear in assertions as a
**disproof target** (e.g. `GF-REGIONAL-DESTR-008` asserts that there is no fallback when spares are insufficient),
and never as the level of a case itself.

### 2.3 Complete reusable acceptance entry points

The table below lists the entry points completed in this round, in the phase order of `testcases/regional-execution-order.yaml`.
Except for the two kinds of purely local/read-only entry points, every runner writes only `plan.json` by default; actual execution must additionally pass
`--execute`, the exact confirmation given in the plan, and a timezone-aware
`--maintenance-window-end`. The runner derives the predecessor case automatically from the formal order, reads
`<run-dir>/cases/<predecessor>/<predecessor>.json` by default and requires `verdict=PASS`,
and the top-level `release_id`/`cluster_id` of that evidence must equal the identity this runner reads from the release-state and
the target cluster (`RegionalLiveFixture.evidence_identity`): a PASS left over from before a release change or
cluster change is not a predecessor (`evidence_valid=false`) and cannot release execute.

The runner supports two explicit execution scopes:

- the default `formal`: strictly follows the formal order; the predecessor must be a formal `PASS`;
- `selective`: the administrator explicitly chooses a single case or a subset; the predecessor is recorded as
  `SKIPPED_BY_OPERATOR`, but the result proves only the selected case, not that the phase or the complete regional acceptance passed.

selective mode must also set a non-empty audit reference:

```bash
export GPU_FAULT_ACCEPTANCE_EXECUTION_SCOPE=selective
export GPU_FAULT_ACCEPTANCE_SELECTION_REFERENCE=CHG-12345
```

The `plan.json` schema 3 of the common live guard binds the scope, reference, arguments, connection contents, source identity and
success prechecks; at execute time, drift of any bound value is rejected. The selective
final report writes `execution_scope=selective`,
`formal_sequence_satisfied=false` and the same reference. The formal runner refuses to take a selective
`PASS` as a predecessor, so selective execution cannot forge a complete acceptance chain. The scope changes only the formal-order
gate; it does not relax the case's own identity, Profile, idle-node, maintenance-window, confirmation, stop-condition
or rollback gates. Both variables above must be cleared before returning to formal mode.

selective skips only the formal-order gate; it does not turn a missing or mismatched predecessor file into valid evidence. When a successor reuses
predecessor steps, it must verify case, release, cluster, completion result and scope from the same read,
and then use the document parsed in that read; the `evidence_sha256` in the report binds that read and must not carry over an old
`evidence_valid` and then re-read different content. `SUPERSEDED` may end a wait, but it does not equal a case PASS.
Marker-bearing Store queries may widen the scan start by the kmsg clock skew; the exact marker and event identity checks are not relaxed.
Kernel events whose correlation window has been cleared may only be re-normalised from the retained raw records and must match the event, node, boot, time and evidence reference of a persisted decision
or trusted marker; an arbitrary marker ID must not be clipped out to guess the event identity. Recovered records are marked
`recovered_from=raw_evidence`; multiple candidates or contradictory identity still fail.
These reads are not a cross-table atomic snapshot, and they do not fabricate evidence that has already expired or is missing.

| Formal order | Case | Entry point |
|---|---|---|
| Deployability | `BOOT-011..018` | `scripts/e2e/regional/run_boot_acceptance.py --case <case>` |
| Identity boundary | `AUTH-007/010/013..016` | `scripts/e2e/regional/run_identity_acceptance.py --case <case>` |
| Training baseline | `WORKLOAD-001..002` | `scripts/e2e/regional/run_workload_acceptance.py --case <case>` |
| Single-cluster isolation | `ISO-001` | `run_workload_acceptance.py --case GF-REGIONAL-ISO-001` |
| Single-cluster isolation | `ISO-003..005` | `run_identity_acceptance.py --case <case>` |
| Preemption and DAG | `PREEMPT-001..009` | `run_preemption_contracts.py --case <case>` |
| Preemption and DAG | `PREEMPT-012` | `run_preempt012_acceptance.py` |
| Single-cluster closed loop | `E2E-001` | `run_workload_acceptance.py --case GF-REGIONAL-E2E-001` |
| Blast radius | `BLAST-001..004` | `run_blast_acceptance.py --case <case>` |
| Notification | `NOTIFY-001..005` | `run_notification_acceptance.py --case <case>` |
| Capacity | `CAP-001..004` | `run_capacity_acceptance.py --case <case>` |
| Network | `NET-001` | `run_net001_collector_replay.py` |

The common plan/execute shape is:

```bash
python3 scripts/e2e/regional/<runner>.py \
  --case GF-REGIONAL-<CASE> \
  --run-dir "${RUN_DIR}" \
  <case-specific-targets> \
  --plan

python3 scripts/e2e/regional/<runner>.py \
  --case GF-REGIONAL-<CASE> \
  --run-dir "${RUN_DIR}" \
  <exactly the same case-specific-targets> \
  --execute \
  --confirm '<confirmation from plan.json>' \
  --maintenance-window-end "${MAINTENANCE_WINDOW_END}"
```

The focused pytest result of the `--plan` stage binds the content digests of the execution-related sources, tests, tools, deployment templates,
case catalog and dependency lock, including relevant untracked new files.
`--execute` additionally checks the CLI, kubeconfig contents, site profile and success prechecks;
identity drift of an approved plan requires a fresh plan; execution cannot continue by merely borrowing the old pytest result.

`PREEMPT-001..009` are deterministic isolated component/integration fixtures; they run directly and need no
live parameters:

```bash
python3 scripts/e2e/regional/run_preemption_contracts.py \
  --case GF-REGIONAL-PREEMPT-001
```

With `--run-dir <run-dir>` (optionally `--release-id`) it writes `cases/<id>/<id>.json` into the run
directory; only then can a PREEMPT case serve as the predecessor of a subsequent formal case.

`BLAST-001..004` only read the current site and do not modify the cluster; they execute directly but still require formal predecessor evidence.
`BLAST-001` additionally takes this round's `E2E-001` case directory and that round's CPU node baseline: `--e2e-dir` defaults to
`<run-dir>/cases/GF-REGIONAL-E2E-001` (or the environment variable `GPU_FAULT_E2E001_EVIDENCE_DIR`),
and `--trusted-cpu-baseline` defaults to the `cpu-nodes-before.json` recorded by E2E-001 in that directory (or
`GPU_FAULT_TRUSTED_CPU_BASELINE`).

case-specific targets must not be omitted:

- BOOT greenfield needs an isolated state-dir/ARN or an explicitly isolated site; BOOT-011 additionally takes the
  production site to prove that identities do not overlap, and BOOT-018 uninstalls the isolated site at the end by default.
- AUTH/ISO pass the primary/secondary cluster IDs explicitly; AUTH-014 reads the structured evidence of the probe outside the independent VPC;
  AUTH-015 accepts only a `0600` fleet master file on a trusted deployment host, two nodes and an immutable probe image.
- WORKLOAD/E2E pass site, cluster and state-dir explicitly; E2E-001 and PREEMPT-012 need a target node
  or an immutable host probe image. Every host-side action first has an independent systemd recovery timer.
- NOTIFY-001/002 use SES mail carrying the `DRILL` marker and structured receive/send window evidence,
  and do not repeat a reset for mail acceptance; NOTIFY-005 must be given three different GPU nodes.
- CAP creates only temporary Deployments, Secrets and an independent database, and deletes them in `finally`;
  NET-001 writes only a monitor-only XID 63, and the node's port-443 rule starts the host rollback timer before it is added.

These entry points write schema v2 `fault-acceptance` reports and do not describe a plan, pytest, API replay or user-space
`/dev/kmsg` injection as a hardware fault. Any cleanup residue changes the final verdict to `FAIL`.

## 3. Preconditions

### 3.0 Site parameters have exactly one source: `--site-profile`

The "formal entry point" runners of every chapter **contain no site topology at all** (account id, kubeconfig path,
EKS context, node names);
`test_collector_promoted_scripts_contain_no_site_specific_topology` blocks it.
These values live in a file that **never enters the repository**, normally right inside the private state directory:

```yaml
# /secure/<state-dir>/acceptance-site-profile.yaml   (mode 0600)
arguments:            # the key is the runner's long option name with the leading -- removed
  cluster-id: ...
  cpu-kubeconfig: ...
  gpu-kubeconfig: ...
  gpu-context: ...
  namespace: gpu-fault-system
  node: ...           # written as a list it expands into repeated --node
  region: us-west-2
  host-probe-image: ...
  site-file: ...      # only used by cases that read the site Profile (DESTR-003 etc.)
  hyperpod-cluster: ...
  fault-node: ...     # DESTR-003 uses --fault-node/--spare-node, not --node
  spare-node: ...
environment:          # only fill in keys the current shell has not exported yet
  GPU_FAULT_ACCEPTANCE_WINDOW_END: ...
  GPU_FAULT_ACCEPTANCE_EXECUTION_SCOPE: ...
  GPU_FAULT_ACCEPTANCE_SELECTION_REFERENCE: ...
```

```bash
python scripts/e2e/regional/run_collector_acceptance.py \
  --site-profile /secure/<state-dir>/acceptance-site-profile.yaml \
  --run-dir <run-dir> --case GF-REGIONAL-COLLECT-002 --plan
```

Precedence follows the runners' existing environment-fallback convention: **explicit command-line option > profile > current environment**.
When an option appears on the command line it overrides the same-named profile entry as a whole --
including `append` options such as `--node`: an explicit `--node` **replaces** rather than appends,
otherwise a case that requires "exactly two distinct nodes" would silently receive three.

The profile describes the **site**, not any single case, so it **only fills in the options the current runner actually defines**
and skips unknown keys outright: one profile that carries `node`, `fault-node` and `spare-node` at the same time is legal;
collection-type runners take only `--node`, DESTR-003 takes only `--fault-node`/`--spare-node`.
(Otherwise sharing one profile would make a runner that lacks some key exit 2 on "unknown argument".)
The fill-in happens at the moment of `parse_args` -- via the hook mounted in `add_live_arguments` --
not by rewriting `sys.argv`, so options a runner adds after that point are filled from the profile just the same.

`build_plan` records the profile path and its sha256 in `plan.json`, and
`authorize_execution` rejects the combination "plan with A, execute with B" --
a plan must name the target it was approved against.
If the profile is group/world writable, or contains any section other than `arguments`/`environment`,
it is rejected outright: this file decides which machine a destructive case reboots,
and a misspelled section name would silently drop every value inside it.
The profile may not carry `attempt`/`confirm`/`execute`/`plan` either (`site_profile.RESERVED_ARGUMENTS`,
checked once at load time and once when values are bound): those four are typed by hand on every run, and putting them in the profile would turn every `--plan`
into an execute against live hardware.

⚠ **Stop writing these values into launcher shells under `/tmp`.**
They vanish as soon as the jump host reboots, and the case evidence can then say "what happened" but not "on which machine it happened".

### 3.1 Environment variables

Every command must name the target cluster context explicitly; relying on the current default context is forbidden.

`CPU_KUBECONFIG` points into `/tmp` and disappears after a jump-host reboot; **do not assume it already exists**.
Rebuild it by reverse-looking-up from the HyperPod cluster name along the chain below; do not hand-write the EKS name (the control-plane EKS name carries
a random suffix generated by SageMaker and cannot be guessed):

```bash
export AWS_REGION=us-west-2
# the CPU HyperPod cluster that hosts the regional control plane
export CONTROL_PLANE_HYPERPOD='<cpu-control-plane>'
export CPU_KUBECONFIG=/tmp/gpu-fault-control-plane.kubeconfig

# confirm it is the only control-plane cluster and is InService
aws sagemaker list-clusters --region "${AWS_REGION}" \
  --query 'ClusterSummaries[].[ClusterName,ClusterStatus]' --output table

# HyperPod name -> EKS ARN -> kubeconfig
export CPU_EKS_ARN="$(
  aws sagemaker describe-cluster --region "${AWS_REGION}" \
    --cluster-name "${CONTROL_PLANE_HYPERPOD}" \
    --query 'Orchestrator.Eks.ClusterArn' --output text
)"
aws eks update-kubeconfig --region "${AWS_REGION}" \
  --name "${CPU_EKS_ARN##*/}" --kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}"

# must be three Ready CPU nodes
kubectl --kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" get nodes
```

The control-plane HyperPod's `NodeRecovery` is currently `Automatic`. This only affects the **CPU nodes that
host the control plane**; it has nothing to do with the `NodeRecovery` of the GPU cluster under test, so do not mistake it for
a violation of the `DESTR` group preconditions; the GPU-side value is taken from `hyperpod-cluster.json` in §3.3.

Remaining variables:

```bash
export NAMESPACE=gpu-fault-system
export SITE_FILE=/secure/gpu-fault/site.yaml

# the content-addressed Runtime Profile of the current release. Every workload, marker and fault injection
# must use this value; hard-coding hyperpod-v1 in a case is forbidden.
export RUNTIME_PROFILE_VERSION="$(
  PYTHONPATH=src python3 - "${SITE_FILE}" <<'PY'
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from gpu_fault.admin.site import load_site
print(load_site(Path(sys.argv[1])).release_config["runtime_profile"]["version"])
PY
)"

# the GPU cluster under test in this round (repeat the whole case set per cluster)
export CLUSTER_ID='<gpu-hyperpod-cluster>'
export GPU_EKS_CONTEXT='arn:aws:eks:us-west-2:123456789012:cluster/<gpu-eks-cluster>'
export HYPERPOD_CLUSTER_NAME="${CLUSTER_ID}"

# the second cluster identity used for isolation validation (see 3.4). Single-cluster site: AUTH-007/008 use
# auth-logical-<name> as a synthetic logical cluster the runner creates and tears down itself (same
# EKS as GPU_EKS_CONTEXT); ISO-003/004 may use any unregistered id
export CLUSTER_ID_B='<cluster_id of the second GPU cluster, or auth-logical-<name>>'
export GPU_EKS_CONTEXT_B='<EKS context of the second GPU cluster>'

export CONTROL_PLANE_URL="https://$(
  kubectl --kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" -n "${NAMESPACE}" \
    get service gpu-fault-api-nlb \
    -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].hostname}'
)"

kubectl --kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" get --raw=/readyz
kubectl --context "${GPU_EKS_CONTEXT}" get --raw=/readyz
```

### 3.2 Shared query functions

The control-plane API is reachable only inside the cluster, so all local queries are issued from inside the API Pod. Every query is read-only.

The four items below are shell **functions**, not commands: they exist only in the current shell. Save the §3.1 exports
and these four functions together in one file (for example `/tmp/gf-e2e/env.sh`) and `source` it once before every case.
This is especially necessary when running across several terminals or several logins -- skip this step and later cases fail with
"command not found" or an empty `CONTROL_PLANE_URL`, which looks like a problem in the system under test.

```bash
cp_pod() {
  kubectl --kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" -n "${NAMESPACE}" \
    get pod -l app=gpu-fault-api-ha -o json |
    jq -r '
      [.items[]
       | select(
           .metadata.deletionTimestamp == null
           and .status.phase == "Running"
           and (
             (.status.conditions // [])
             | any(.type == "Ready" and .status == "True")
           )
         )]
      | sort_by(.metadata.creationTimestamp)
      | last
      | .metadata.name // empty
    '
}

# cp_get /v1/collector-status/<cluster>
# Four required details; missing any one of them fails silently:
#  1. exec must carry -i, otherwise the heredoc never reaches the container and python reads an empty stdin and exits 0
#     → shows up as "command succeeded but no output", easily misread as "the endpoint returned nothing".
#  2. HTTPError must be caught, otherwise 403/404 likewise show up as no output.
#  3. In regional mode most GETs fall into the execution-token bucket and must carry that header;
#     the token is read from the API Pod's own environment and never enters the command line.
#  4. cp_pod must exclude old Pods whose deletionTimestamp is already set and pick the newest among the Ready
#     replicas; taking the first item of the Running list would, after a rolling update, hit the old Pod
#     that is being deleted and make acceptance commands issued right after a rollout randomly NotFound.
cp_get() {
  kubectl --kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" -n "${NAMESPACE}" \
    exec -i "$(cp_pod)" -- python - "$1" <<'PY'
import json, os, sys, urllib.error, urllib.request
url = "http://127.0.0.1:8080" + sys.argv[1]
headers = {}
token = os.environ.get("GPU_FAULT_EXECUTION_TOKEN")
if token:
    headers["X-GPU-Fault-Execution-Token"] = token
request = urllib.request.Request(url, headers=headers)
try:
    with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=15) as response:
        print(json.dumps(json.load(response), indent=2, ensure_ascii=False))
except urllib.error.HTTPError as exc:
    print("HTTP", exc.code, exc.read().decode(errors="replace")[:800])
    sys.exit(1)
PY
}

# cp_call <method> <path> [json-body]
# Control-plane-side write endpoints (execution-token bucket). Prints "HTTP <status>" and the response body,
# raises no exception, convenient for asserting 403/404/409/422.
cp_call() {
  kubectl --kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" -n "${NAMESPACE}" \
    exec -i "$(cp_pod)" -- python - "$@" <<'PY'
import os, sys, urllib.error, urllib.request

method, path = sys.argv[1:3]
body = sys.argv[3] if len(sys.argv) > 3 else None
headers = {}
token = os.environ.get("GPU_FAULT_EXECUTION_TOKEN")
if token:
    headers["X-GPU-Fault-Execution-Token"] = token
data = None
if body:
    data = body.encode()
    headers["Content-Type"] = "application/json"
request = urllib.request.Request(
    "http://127.0.0.1:8080" + path,
    data=data, headers=headers, method=method,
)
try:
    with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=20) as response:
        print("HTTP", response.status)
        print(response.read().decode(errors="replace")[:4000])
except urllib.error.HTTPError as exc:
    print("HTTP", exc.code)
    print(exc.read().decode(errors="replace")[:4000])
PY
}
```

Data-plane-side authentication cases need to construct arbitrary request headers, so they are all issued from inside the executor Pod.
The executor Pod already has python, the local private CA
(`GPU_FAULT_CONTROL_PLANE_CA_FILE`) and the cluster credentials; the global
`SSL_CERT_FILE` / `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` must stay unset.

```bash
gpu_pod() {
  kubectl --context "${1:-$GPU_EKS_CONTEXT}" -n "${NAMESPACE}" \
    get pod -l app=gpu-fault-cluster-executor \
    --field-selector=status.phase=Running \
    -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}'
}

# dp_call <method> <path> <cluster-header|-> <token|env|-> [json-body]
# Prints "HTTP <status>" and the response body, raises no exception, convenient for asserting 401/403/404/409/422/429
dp_call() {
  kubectl --context "${GPU_EKS_CONTEXT}" -n "${NAMESPACE}" \
    exec -i "$(gpu_pod)" -- python - "$@" <<'PY'
import json, os, ssl, sys, urllib.error, urllib.request

method, path, cluster, token = sys.argv[1:5]
body = sys.argv[5] if len(sys.argv) > 5 else None
headers = {}
if cluster != "-":
    headers["X-GPU-Fault-Cluster-ID"] = cluster
if token == "env":
    headers["Authorization"] = (
        "Bearer " + os.environ["GPU_FAULT_CONTROL_PLANE_TOKEN"]
    )
elif token not in {"-", ""}:
    headers["Authorization"] = token
data = None
if body:
    data = body.encode()
    headers["Content-Type"] = "application/json"
request = urllib.request.Request(
    os.environ["GPU_FAULT_CONTROL_PLANE_URL"] + path,
    data=data, headers=headers, method=method,
)
ssl_context = ssl.create_default_context(
    cafile=os.environ.get(
        "GPU_FAULT_CONTROL_PLANE_CA_FILE",
        "/etc/gpu-fault/tls/ca.crt",
    )
)
try:
    with urllib.request.urlopen(
        request, context=ssl_context, timeout=20
    ) as response:
        print("HTTP", response.status)
        print(response.read().decode(errors="replace")[:4000])
except urllib.error.HTTPError as exc:
    print("HTTP", exc.code)
    print(exc.read().decode(errors="replace")[:4000])
PY
}

# dp_call_receipt <method> <path> <cluster-header> <token> [json-body]
# For endpoints that enter the processor queue: first accept HTTP 202, then poll status_url until the real
# business terminal state. Only the HTTP/response body printed last is the result of the handler under test.
dp_call_receipt() {
  kubectl --context "${GPU_EKS_CONTEXT}" -n "${NAMESPACE}" \
    exec -i "$(gpu_pod)" -- python - "$@" <<'PY'
import json, os, ssl, sys, time, urllib.error, urllib.request

method, path, cluster, token = sys.argv[1:5]
body = sys.argv[5] if len(sys.argv) > 5 else None
headers = {"X-GPU-Fault-Cluster-ID": cluster}
if token == "env":
    headers["Authorization"] = (
        "Bearer " + os.environ["GPU_FAULT_CONTROL_PLANE_TOKEN"]
    )
elif token not in {"-", ""}:
    headers["Authorization"] = token
if body:
    headers["Content-Type"] = "application/json"
ssl_context = ssl.create_default_context(
    cafile=os.environ.get(
        "GPU_FAULT_CONTROL_PLANE_CA_FILE",
        "/etc/gpu-fault/tls/ca.crt",
    )
)
base = os.environ["GPU_FAULT_CONTROL_PLANE_URL"].rstrip("/")
request = urllib.request.Request(
    base + path,
    data=body.encode() if body else None,
    headers=headers,
    method=method,
)
with urllib.request.urlopen(
    request, context=ssl_context, timeout=20
) as response:
    status = response.status
    payload = response.read()
print("HTTP", status)
print(payload.decode(errors="replace")[:4000])
if status != 202:
    raise SystemExit(0)
accepted = json.loads(payload)
status_url = accepted.get("status_url") or (
    "/v1/processor/requests/"
    + accepted["processor_request_id"]
)
deadline = time.monotonic() + 120
while time.monotonic() < deadline:
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        base + status_url, headers=headers, method="GET"
    )
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(
            request, context=ssl_context, timeout=20
        ) as response:
            payload = response.read()
            if response.status == 202:
                time.sleep(0.5)
                continue
            print("HTTP", response.status)
            print(payload.decode(errors="replace")[:4000])
            raise SystemExit(0)
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as exc:
        print("HTTP", exc.code)
        print(exc.read().decode(errors="replace")[:4000])
        raise SystemExit(1)
raise SystemExit("processor receipt timed out")
PY
}
```

Passing `env` as `token` means use this cluster's real token; passing `-` means send no `Authorization`;
passing `Bearer xxx` can be used for forgery. **Writing a real token on the command line is forbidden**; it may only be read
from the Pod environment via `env`.

#### 3.2.1 marker trigger: constructing a step with a given `RecoveryAction` and **empty parameters**

Some cases need a "clean" step -- a `REPLACE_NODE` / `REBOOT_NODE` / `RESET_GPU` that carries **no parameters at all**
apart from `node_ids`. Neither XID injection nor
`/v1/admin/test/node-replacement` can do this; see [Why the synthetic endpoint cannot be used] below.
The only thing that can is the passive path **trusted marker + training terminal state**.

The chain (every link has been verified line by line):

```text
POST /v1/markers            (NodeMarker, trusted=true, recommended_action=X)
POST /v1/attempts/terminal  (TerminalEvent, allocation hits marker.scope)
  -> CompletionService._matching_markers()      service.py:469-505
  -> RecoveryPlanner.from_marker()              planner.py:87-135
       REPLACE_NODE branch: MARK_UNSCHEDULABLE / COLLECT_EVIDENCE /
       <X> / VALIDATE_NODE / RESTART_WORKLOAD, with parameters defaulting to {}
  -> PassiveWorkflowCompiler._steps()           passive.py:122-166
       dict(item.parameters) as is; only RESTART_WORKLOAD gets parameters appended
  -> ACTION_OPERATION[REPLACE_NODE] = WorkflowOperation.REPLACE_NODE
                                                passive.py:33
  -> WorkflowRequest(status=PENDING, fencing_token=1)
  -> WorkflowDispatcher picks it up automatically within 5 seconds   src/gpu_fault/execution/
```

**Why `/v1/admin/test/node-replacement` cannot be used.**
The type of `SyntheticNodeReplacementRequest.replacement_strategy` is
`Literal["HEALTHY_WARM_SPARE_ONLY"]` (`host_health.py:176-178`), and
`src/gpu_fault/app/` stuffs it into `diagnostic_parameters`,
so the step inevitably carries `replacement_strategy` and takes the warm-spare branch.
The other three places that inject this parameter -- `src/gpu_fault/orchestration/` (written unconditionally inside `escalate_failed_
hardware_remediation`), `:2507-2521` and `:3212-3227`
(both require the finding's `diagnostic_parameters` to already be
`HEALTHY_WARM_SPARE_ONLY`) -- **are all off the marker path**,
so the parameters produced by the marker path are always `{}`.

Preconditions (missing any one produces no workflow at all, rather than a failed workflow):

1. The `cluster_id` is registered as a regional cluster (visible in `/v1/regional/clusters`).
2. The `mode` of the corresponding capability in the profile is `OWN`/`DELEGATE`,
   otherwise `planner._owner()` raises `UnsupportedPlanError`.
   `REPLACE_NODE` requires `nodeReplace` of the current site Profile to be in an executable mode;
   `${RUNTIME_PROFILE_VERSION}` must be used, a historical version fails outright.
3. `TerminalEvent.terminal_status` must be `FAILED`/`TIMED_OUT`
   or contain a non-zero `rank_exit_status`, otherwise it goes to `NO_ACTION` (`service.py:245-262`).
4. `TerminalEvent.termination_initiator_incident_id` must be **left empty**,
   otherwise likewise `NO_ACTION` (`service.py:224-243`).
5. The difference between `marker.observed_at` and `event.ended_at` must lie within
   `marker_window` (default 10 minutes), and `expires_at > ended_at`.
6. `marker.scope.node_ids` must intersect `event.allocation[].node_id`.
7. `event_key = <cluster>/<attempt>/TrainingAttemptTerminal` is deduplicated globally;
   a rerun must use a new `attempt_id` (the same one returns `duplicate=true`).
8. `marker.incident_id` should point to an incident that **does not exist**.
   When `service.py:277-282` finds the incident it goes to `after_incident()`,
   and that path orchestrates only `RESTART_WORKLOAD`, producing no node-level step.
9. `severity` must be **lowercase** (`Severity` in `models.py:31-35` is
   `info`/`warning`/`critical`/`fatal`). Passing `CRITICAL` gives 422,
   and the 422 happens only on the marker-creation call -- the second call still returns `HTTP 200`,
   so it looks like "it worked" while what was actually hit is somebody else's marker. **Both
   HTTP status codes must be checked one by one; never look only at the last line.**
10. **A system-generated marker may already be competing on the same node.** In production
    `host_health.py` generates markers like `marker-host-<node>-<ts>-<metric>-node`
    for network-type metrics (for example `network_errors_delta`; `tcp_retransmits_delta`
    has been removed from `METRIC_RULES` -- retransmits are congestion control, not an error counter, and no longer produce markers).
    `service.py:264-270` takes the **maximum** by `ACTION_PRIORITY`
    (`planner.py:21-29`: `RUN_DIAGNOSTICS`=20 <
    `REBOOT_NODE`=40 < `REPLACE_NODE`=50 < `QUARANTINE`=60),
    so `REPLACE_NODE`/`REBOOT_NODE` can win, but
    `RESET_GPU`(30) is overridden by a `QUARANTINE` marker on the same node.
    When reading `matched_marker_ids` you must confirm that your own `marker-<suffix>`
    **is actually in the list**; if only somebody else's ids appear, this trigger did not take effect.

Failure-shape reference (to tell "precondition not met" from "stopped by a guard"):

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| Second call `HTTP 404` | `runtime_profile_version` not registered (`service.py:213` fetches the profile first) |
| Second call `HTTP 409` | `UnsupportedPlanError`: that capability in the profile is not `OWN`/`DELEGATE` |
| `HTTP 200` but `status=NO_ACTION` | Precondition 3/4 not met, or no marker matched |
| `HTTP 200` + `recovery_plan_id=null` | Same as above; **no workflow was produced at all**, this is not "stopped by a guard" |
| `HTTP 200` + `status=PLAN_CREATED` | Normal, go on to inspect the workflow |

> **⚠ The marker and terminal endpoints use different authorization buckets.**
> The original text said "both endpoints are inside `protected_cluster_paths`, `dp_call` must be used,
> and `X-GPU-Fault-Execution-Token` gets 403". **Only `/v1/attempts/terminal`
> is in that list** (`src/gpu_fault/app/`); `/v1/markers` is not,
> so by the default-deny of `regional_authorization_bucket()` it falls into the
> `execution-token` bucket (`src/gpu_fault/app/`) -- the per-cluster token is what gets 403 there.
> The credentials of the two endpoints are **different** and they must be called separately:

| Endpoint | Bucket | Credential | Which function |
|---|---|---|---|
| `POST /v1/markers` | `execution-token` | `X-GPU-Fault-Execution-Token` | `cp_call` (control-plane Pod, token taken from the Pod env) |
| `POST /v1/attempts/terminal` | `cluster-token` | per-cluster Bearer + `X-GPU-Fault-Cluster-ID` | `dp_call` (executor Pod) |

The real tokens on both sides are read only from the environment variables of their respective Pods and never enter the command line.
`GPU_FAULT_EXECUTION_TOKEN` exists in the API Pod environment,
`GPU_FAULT_CONTROL_PLANE_TOKEN` exists in the executor Pod environment.

> **⚠ `cp_get` must handle stdin and HTTP errors explicitly.**
> 1. `kubectl exec` **without `-i`**: the Python program in the heredoc never reaches the container,
>    python reads an empty stdin and exits `0` right away -- showing up as "command succeeded but no output",
>    which is very easily misread as "the endpoint returned nothing". This defect completely masked the 403 above.
> 2. `HTTPError` was not caught, so 403/404 also showed up as no output.
>
> The fixed versions are `cp_call`/`cp_get` below. **Any "the command finished with no output" symptom
> must first be cleared of this kind of fixture defect before the system under test is considered.**

```bash
# gf_marker_trigger <recovery-action> <node-id> <attempt-suffix> [profile-version]
# Prints two HTTP results; the second response body contains recovery_plan_id
# marker_id is written explicitly as marker-<suffix>, so rollback need not go back to look for the response body
gf_marker_trigger() {
  local action="$1" node="$2" suffix="$3"
  local profile="${4:-${RUNTIME_PROFILE_VERSION:?}}"
  local now expires
  now="$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"
  expires="$(date -u -d '+1 hour' +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"
  local incident="inc-marker-${suffix}"

  local marker_out
  marker_out="$(cp_call POST /v1/markers "$(cat <<JSON
{"marker_id":"marker-${suffix}",
 "source":"site-e2e-manual","trusted":true,
 "incident_id":"${incident}","observed_at":"${now}",
 "expires_at":"${expires}",
 "scope":{"node_ids":["${node}"]},
 "severity":"critical","recommended_action":"${action}",
 "mapping_version":"site-manual-v1"}
JSON
)")"
  echo "--- POST /v1/markers ---"
  echo "${marker_out}"
  # If marker creation fails, never go on to send the terminal event: it would hit somebody else's marker on the same node
  # (see precondition 10), the second call would still return 200, it would look like "success", but another path was actually tested.
  case "${marker_out}" in
    "HTTP 200"*) ;;
    *) echo "ABORT: marker creation failed, terminal event not sent" >&2; return 1 ;;
  esac

  echo "--- POST /v1/attempts/terminal ---"
  dp_call_receipt POST /v1/attempts/terminal "${CLUSTER_ID}" env "$(cat <<JSON
{"cluster_id":"${CLUSTER_ID}","environment":"hyperpod-eks",
 "job_id":"marker-trigger-${suffix}",
 "attempt_id":"attempt-${suffix}",
 "terminal_status":"FAILED","ended_at":"${now}",
 "allocation":[{"node_id":"${node}","gpu_uuids":[]}],
 "workload_ids":[],
 "runtime_profile_version":"${profile}",
 "restart_budget":0}
JSON
)"
}

# gf_marker_deactivate <recovery-action> <node-id> <attempt-suffix>
# Re-send an active=false marker with the same marker_id to overwrite it; the three arguments must exactly match the trigger
gf_marker_deactivate() {
  local action="$1" node="$2" suffix="$3"
  local now expires
  now="$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"
  expires="$(date -u -d '+1 hour' +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"

  cp_call POST /v1/markers "$(cat <<JSON
{"marker_id":"marker-${suffix}",
 "source":"site-e2e-manual","trusted":true,
 "incident_id":"inc-marker-${suffix}","observed_at":"${now}",
 "expires_at":"${expires}",
 "scope":{"node_ids":["${node}"]},
 "severity":"critical","recommended_action":"${action}",
 "mapping_version":"site-manual-v1","active":false}
JSON
)"
}

# gf_profile_probe [profile-version]
# The control plane has no GET endpoint for runtime-profile (among the 68 routes there is only POST /v1/runtime-profiles),
# so it can only be probed indirectly: handle_terminal calls get_profile() first at service.py:213,
# then save_event_if_absent() at :214, so when the profile does not exist the result is 404 and
# the event_key is **not** consumed; terminal_status=SUCCEEDED guarantees that even a 200 only goes to
# NO_ACTION (service.py:245-262) and produces no plan.
# How to read: HTTP 404 = that version is not registered; HTTP 200 + NO_ACTION = registered.
# Side effect: on a 200 it leaves behind one event for a throwaway attempt plus a NO_ACTION decision
# (`attempt_id` carries a timestamp and collides with no case's event_key); no rollback needed.
gf_profile_probe() {
  local profile="${1:-${RUNTIME_PROFILE_VERSION:?}}"
  local now
  now="$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"

  dp_call POST /v1/attempts/terminal "${CLUSTER_ID}" env "$(cat <<JSON
{"cluster_id":"${CLUSTER_ID}","environment":"hyperpod-eks",
 "job_id":"profile-probe","attempt_id":"probe-${profile}-$(date -u +%s)",
 "terminal_status":"SUCCEEDED","ended_at":"${now}",
 "allocation":[],"workload_ids":[],
 "runtime_profile_version":"${profile}","restart_budget":0}
JSON
)"
}

# gf_plan_id <trigger output file>  ->  take the last recovery_plan_id
# The first line of dp_call output is "HTTP <status>", so it cannot be fed to json.load directly
gf_plan_id() {
  python3 - "$1" <<'PY'
import re, sys
found = re.findall(
    r'"recovery_plan_id":\s*"([^"]+)"', open(sys.argv[1]).read()
)
print(found[-1] if found else "")
PY
}
```

`workload_ids` is passed as an empty array and `restart_budget` as `0`: this trigger exists only to validate the gate on node-level
steps and must not incidentally restart any real training job. The `RESTART_WORKLOAD` step is still
orchestrated (`from_marker` always appends it), but its `workload_ids` is empty,
so the namespace check of `RegionalRemoteWorkflowAdapter` matches nothing.
**Note**: if the preceding node-level step is `FAILED`, the workflow as a whole stops in `FAILED`
and later steps never execute -- which is exactly the shape disproof-type cases expect.

Rollback: the marker stays `active` indefinitely and must be deactivated explicitly, otherwise any later terminal event may
hit it again and generate a new workflow. At the end of the case re-send a marker with the same id and
`active=false` by its `marker_id` (`store.add_marker` overwrites by `marker_id`,
`src/gpu_fault/store/`).

### 3.3 Baseline snapshot (must be captured before every round of cases)

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/regional-baseline
kubectl --kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" get nodes -o json \
  > /tmp/regional-baseline/cpu-nodes.json
kubectl --kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" get jobs -A -o json \
  > /tmp/regional-baseline/cpu-jobs.json
kubectl --context "${GPU_EKS_CONTEXT}" get nodes -o json \
  > /tmp/regional-baseline/gpu-nodes.json
aws sagemaker describe-cluster --region "${AWS_REGION}" \
  --cluster-name "${HYPERPOD_CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  > /tmp/regional-baseline/hyperpod-cluster.json
aws sagemaker list-cluster-nodes --region "${AWS_REGION}" \
  --cluster-name "${HYPERPOD_CLUSTER_NAME}" \
  > /tmp/regional-baseline/hyperpod-nodes.json
```

The CPU control-plane baseline is used for the field-by-field comparison of the `BLAST` group; the HyperPod node baseline is used by
the `DESTR` group to judge whether the instance incarnation changed.

### 3.4 How to cover the isolation cases with only one GPU cluster

The `ISO` group and `AUTH-007/008` need two cluster identities. If the region has only one physical GPU cluster for now,
**the same EKS can be registered under a second `cluster_id`**: separate token, separate
`allowed_namespaces`, a second executor set running in another namespace.
`gpu-fault-admin join-cluster` refuses to register a second `cluster_id` for the same EKS/HyperPod/context,
so this second logical cluster is created and withdrawn by the runner under test itself within the lifetime of one case:

```bash
python3 scripts/e2e/regional/run_identity_acceptance.py \
  --case GF-REGIONAL-AUTH-007 --run-dir "${RUN_DIR}" --site "${SITE_FILE}" \
  --cluster-id "${CLUSTER_ID}" --secondary-cluster-id "${CLUSTER_ID_B}" \
  --secondary-registration synthetic --allow-synthetic-secondary --plan
```

- `--secondary-registration site` (the default) requires B to be a registered cluster in site.yaml; behaviour and
  evidence are exactly as before. `synthetic` is open only to `AUTH-007/008`, must be given together with
  `--allow-synthetic-secondary`, and `CLUSTER_ID_B` must match
  `auth-logical-<dns-label>` (lowercase letters, digits, hyphens, at most 50 characters) and may not share a name with any
  site cluster. `ISO-003/004` only compare the cluster-id binding; `CLUSTER_ID_B` may be any
  unregistered id and needs no synthetic registration.
- The plan phase is read-only: it records that B is not in site.yaml, the registration about to be published (`synthetic=true`, run id,
  expiry time, `allowed_namespaces=[B]`, loopback `agent_endpoint_allowed_cidrs`; the token is generated only at
  execution time and the evidence keeps only its sha256) and the Pod about to be created. If the registry already has a registration of that name, a
  namespace of that name already exists, the site has no durable registry, or the primary cluster's registration is unavailable, preflight fails and execution is not allowed.
- Execution phase: the runner uses the synthetic-registration builder of `scripts/perf/regional_capacity_registry.py`
  (the same field set as the `perf-cap-*` of the capacity load test, so both the perf sweep and the expiry pruning at registry load
  can reclaim it) to publish a durable revision that adds B; on the GPU data plane it creates a namespace named
  `${CLUSTER_ID_B}`, B's own `gpu-fault-regional-connection` Secret
  (copying A's `control-plane-url` and `ca.crt`, writing B's `cluster-id` and
  `cluster-token`, never copying A's token), the hold-script ConfigMap, and one
  `app=gpu-fault-cluster-executor` Pod: the image is taken from the deployed executor Deployment,
  the connection environment variables are the same as the executor's (including the artifact/compatibility Pin), the command is
  `scripts/e2e/regional/probes/auth_logical_secondary_hold.py`, and no claim loop is started --
  all of B's control-plane traffic is the claims the case itself issues by exec-ing into it. The case body treats this Pod as B's
