  ```bash
    --site-profile "${SITE_PROFILE}" --run-dir "${RUN_DIR}" --attempt 1 \
    --case GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-030 --expected-mode legacy --execute \
    --confirm VERIFY_DEPLOYED_STATE_TABLE_READ_ONLY \
    --maintenance-window-end "${MAINTENANCE_WINDOW_END}"
  ```

- Verdict: every enabled CPU role must have all replicas Ready; checking only the first API Pod is not enough.
  Use `/opt/gpu-fault/control-plane/bin/python` and the currently projected credentials to open a
  `default_transaction_read_only=on` session; the connection must be the writer, and readings from a lagging reader
  cannot serve as migration facts. Credentials are used only inside the Pod; the output contains only the database identity digest.
- Compare the schema version, the names and checksums of the consecutive migrations, and the existing dedicated-table structure;
  call the existing `state_table_status`, do not construct a Store, do not auto-ensure the schema.
- In `dual` the full payload-rebuild validation is executed on only one replica to limit scan load;
  backfill must be complete, with missing, mismatched, extra, invalid and noncanonical all zero.
  The remaining replicas confirm the same database digest, mode and revision; equal row counts by themselves do not prove that the dual writes are equal.
- `dedicated` allows old rows to linger for a release cycle; only with `legacy_purged=true` must old rows be zero.
  This case does not automatically clean old rows/indexes, nor does it interpret one read as a completed stable release cycle.
- After execution re-verify the release, Deployment UID/generation, Pod UID and mode identity.
  Drift, timeouts, missing replicas, read failures and empty results are all failures; after the SQL session closes there are no created resources to clean up.
  This is a point-in-time state proof; it does not replace real PostgreSQL regression tests of concurrent lease renewal, archiving, mode switching and HOT updates.

### GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-031

**Post-deploy workflow dedicated-table mode and dual-write consistency**

- The formal predecessor is BOOT-030, with the same risk and read-only boundary. Uses the same runner,
  with `--case` changed to `GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-031`, declaring the workflow `--expected-mode` independently.
  The two tables may be at different legitimate migration stages; the remote_command pass conclusion cannot be reused.
- Verdict: independently read the workflow mode, revision, backfill_complete and legacy_purged,
  and in `dual` compare the fully rebuilt workflow payload with the old table contents.
  A dedicated table that keeps only the immutable payload must correctly rebuild the state, lease, epoch, timestamp and pagination fields.
- All CPU replicas must connect to the same writer and use the schema matching the current release;
  the verdict, evidence and resource-cleanup rules are the same as BOOT-030. Missing items cannot be filled in with default zero values.
- No dispatcher, reconcile, archiving or audit deletion is executed; those behaviours are verified respectively by the dedicated-table Store
  contract, real PostgreSQL and the existing PREEMPT cases. What this case adds is the post-deploy wiring and
  integrity proof; it does not call a read-only audit a migration drill.

#### Independent lifecycle companion

The formal runners of BOOT-030/031 stay read-only. The following companion provides independent evidence for a real schema release,
fail-forward, and a retained-database reinstall after BOOT-019 `keep`; these mutations must not be
added to the read-only cases, nor may a read-only state PASS stand in for them. After the executor separately approves the lifecycle operation:

```bash
python3 -m scripts.e2e.regional.boot_store_lifecycle_evidence capture \
  --state-dir "${STATE_DIR}" --output "${PRIVATE_EVIDENCE_DIR}/store-before.json"
```

In the original state directory perform the approved public schema release, or `uninstall --cpu-cluster keep`
(without `--reset-database`) followed by a fresh deploy in the **same state directory**. The companion does not run
these commands automatically, nor does it fabricate a migration. After completion, or after entering a controlled failure state that requires fail-forward:

```bash
python3 -m scripts.e2e.regional.boot_store_lifecycle_evidence verify \
  --state-dir "${STATE_DIR}" \
  --before "${PRIVATE_EVIDENCE_DIR}/store-before.json" \
  --mode schema --output "${PRIVATE_EVIDENCE_DIR}/store-lifecycle.json"
```

`--mode` is chosen as `schema`, `fail-forward` or `reinstall` according to the operation approved for this run, not re-chosen according to
the observed result. Keep the original before; verify the writer, migration history, real schema advance and snapshot/
fail-forward, Aurora incarnation, the selected historical terminal-state records, and the proof Job's owner/UID and
explicit cleanup proof. A reinstall must additionally prove the retained handoff of the new namespace/installation.
If the selected historical records are zero, record zero; do not claim to have proven that non-existent data was retained. A normal FULL Profile
change, or a deploy into a new directory after BOOT-029 deleted the database, cannot satisfy this retained-database reinstall obligation.
When the corresponding lifecycle was not performed the companion stays `NOT_RUN`, and its standalone result is not a PASS for the whole case.

### GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-032

**Full uninstall of an independent acceptance site, interrupted resume and shared-resource protection**

- The formal entry point is `manual`, the risk is `destructive`, and the current evidence is `NOT_RUN`.
  Although the number belongs to BOOT, the execution position is the "full uninstall of the independent site" stage, with COLLECT-015 as predecessor;
  it must not be uninstalled early in the deploy stage by number.
- Runner: `scripts/e2e/regional/run_boot032_full_uninstall.py`.
  Parameters include `--run-dir`, `--fixture-id`, `--protected-site` and
  `--protected-cluster-id`. Run `--plan` first, and after review execute with the same parameters
  `--execute --confirm BOOT032_DELETE_SACRIFICIAL_CONTROL_PLANE`,
  providing an explicit `--maintenance-window-end`.
- Prepare the independent site separately; its audited config lives at
  `<run-dir>/cases/GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-032/sacrificial/site.yaml`.
  The physical cluster names and AWS ownership tags must follow this case's rules; the runner does not auto-create the site, does not backfill tags,
  and does not turn the continuous acceptance site into a destroyable site. The deploy-host interpreter must satisfy the native state-dir binding policy.
- The approval pins both sites, all contexts, physical cluster identities, live registry, resource registry and the node
  UID/instance/installed-unit lists. The two sets of resources must not overlap; global IAM ARNs are not split into different identities by site Region,
  and external references and PRESERVE resources must not be deleted by mistake.
- Uses the native audited `uninstall` flow, retaining confirmation, state reload, lock, supervision, ownership and policy validation.
  The first run returns `RESTART_REQUIRED` with exit code 75 after the native Kubernetes cleanup validation completes;
  **this is not PASS**. Keep the complete journal, and let a new process execute the same approved command again to resume.
  The native cleanup must use schema-v2 and complete
  `NODE_RUNTIMES_STOPPED` after the consumers and the GPU Executor have stopped; it uses only the saved fleet/UID proofs, does not look up old failed checkpoints,
  and does not query the database after the consumers have stopped. An old schema-v1 or a missing original proof must be reconciled first.
- Verdict: requires complete node and Kubernetes cleanup, the non-database cleanup barrier, an available Aurora final snapshot,
  CPU cluster deletion, and that the GPU cluster and explicitly retained resources still exist. Unreadability after the CPU API is deleted cannot
  serve as cleanup proof; the audited pre-deletion evidence and independent AWS read-back must be used.
- The identity and resources of the continuous acceptance site remain unchanged. After success a rerun can only re-verify;
  same-name rebuild, missing evidence, unknown reads or lost supervision all fail. The native cleanup and the final snapshot are irreversible outcomes;
  no rollback that rebuilds the site is promised, and "resuming" by deleting the journal or changing the target is not allowed.
- The local fake-transport regression covers these control flows; it does not mean an AWS/EKS/Aurora uninstall was executed.

### GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-024

**`remove-cluster` deregisters the site's only GPU cluster: full state machine, label-owned RBAC cleanup, second annotation clear and CPU-only steady state**

- Level: `live-service-action`. Deletes the product data plane on the target GPU cluster and its registration in the CPU
  control plane; does not reboot/replace nodes, does not stop training jobs (the precondition requires that the target cluster has
  no managed jobs); the underlying CPU/GPU EKS and HyperPod clusters are retained.
- Purpose: `BOOT-019` uses the runner on a two-cluster site to verify "deregister the second cluster / deregister the last cluster";
  this case uses the **real administrator command** on a site that manages only one GPU cluster to run the complete `remove-cluster`
  state machine, pinning several classes of gap that have only surfaced on live hardware: the dynamic Role/RoleBindings that the release engine renders
  by label into each workload namespace are not listed in the static installation inventory, so their renderer policy and ownership must first be proven through the shared
  read-only inspection before they are included in the cleanup snapshot of the current GPU context;
  the label by itself does not authorise deletion, nor may it let resources bypass the strict orphan check.
  The real RBAC deletion must wait for drain and Executor stop; a `DRAINING` ACK must not be treated as drained;
  a rerun that fails after `SITE_UPDATED` must still be able to resolve the ARN through the removal's own DISCOVERED evidence;
  after the cluster count reaches zero the previous snapshot and the site document must still render and `deploy` must pass via the CPU-only
  upgrade path; a terminating Node Installer Reconciler rewrites a node whose annotation was just cleared back to
  Retrying, so the annotation must be cleared once more after the namespace is gone.
- Code basis: `src/gpu_fault/admin/cluster_removal.py::remove_cluster` (state machine and
  parallel cleanup),
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/cluster_removal_rbac.py::inspect_workload_namespace_rbac`,
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/cluster_removal_rbac.py::delete_recorded_workload_namespace_rbac`,
  `deploy/control-plane/tools/collect_installed_resource_registry.py::attach_workload_rbac`,
  `deploy/control-plane/tools/cleanup_kubernetes.py::delete_workload_rbac`,
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/cluster_removal_kubernetes.py::clear_installer_annotations`,
  `src/gpu_fault_release/regional_admin_commands.py` (the deploy path for a zero-cluster site).

#### Preconditions and isolation

1. An isolated site whose `site.yaml` `spec.clusters` holds exactly one GPU cluster;
   `gpu-fault-admin status --state-dir <STATE_DIR> --full` all PASS. The formal BOOT-023
   evidence remains bound to the original continuous acceptance site; bind this run's independent site additionally through `boot024_epoch_preflight`:

   ```bash
   python3 -m scripts.e2e.regional.boot024_epoch_preflight \
     --site "${LIFECYCLE_SITE_FILE}" --protected-site "${SITE_FILE}" \
     --predecessor-evidence "${RUN_DIR}/cases/GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-023/GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-023.json" \
     --output "${PRIVATE_EVIDENCE_DIR}/boot024-epoch.json"
   ```

   The producer reads the independent site's committed NOOP, full health and failure-domain release facts separately, retaining the protected site's
   original BOOT-023 proof without rewriting its identity. Before executing the remove, validate the digest,
   target and at most 15 minutes of freshness with the same parameters plus `--check`; the administrator entry point must still re-run its own pre-mutation checks.
   This receipt is only a `READY` precondition, not a BOOT-024 PASS or a mutation authorisation; a missing proof is still recorded as
   `BLOCKED_PREREQUISITE`.
2. The target cluster has no PENDING/RUNNING/WAITING workflow, no open remote command,
   no budget claim; managed training jobs have finished. Nodes may carry cordon or spare labels
   (the removal does not change them) but must not carry `gpu-fault.io/quarantined`.
3. Baseline (read-only): the complete inventory of the GPU cluster's
   `kubectl get roles,rolebindings -A -o json`, including unlabelled foreign bindings;
   count only the product's resources that pass the renderer, namespace/SA UID and shared-reference validation
   (must be >0 and cover at least the system namespace and kube-system); the set of
   Node Installer annotations on each node; the Pod UIDs and
   `restartCount` of the three CPU control-plane Deployments; the member set of `clusters.json` in the registry Secret `gpu-fault-regional-clusters`;
   the cluster ID sets of `site.yaml` and the release state.
4. Negative control: in an approved workload namespace that does not belong to the product namespace being deleted,
   manually create a Role **without** that label; it must still exist after the removal.

#### Steps

1. Execute:

   ```bash
   gpu-fault-admin remove-cluster \
     --state-dir <STATE_DIR> \
     --gpu-cluster-arn <GPU_EKS_ARN> \
     --confirm REMOVE_GPU_CLUSTER
   ```

2. Observe `<STATE_DIR>/remove-cluster/<cluster_id>/state.json`: `completed_steps`
   accumulates in the order `DISCOVERED` → `CONTROL_REGISTRY_DRAINING` → `KUBERNETES_QUIESCED` →
   `KUBERNETES_REMOVED` → `CONTROL_REGISTRY_REMOVED` and `AWS_DETACHED` (parallel) →
   `AURORA_UPDATED` → `SITE_COMMIT_STARTED` → `SITE_UPDATED` →
   `RELEASE_STATE_UPDATED` → `VERIFIED`. The namespace must be confirmed deleted before the
   registry, key, IAM and network dependencies are withdrawn;
   the terminal `phase` is `COMPLETED`; `step_completed_at` has one entry per step; the same directory contains
   `installation-resources-before.json`, `installation-resources-after.json`,
   `kubernetes-cleanup-NNN.json` (`phase=CLEANUP_COMPLETED`, `status=COMPLETED`)
   and `site.before.yaml`.
   This original journal keeps the RBAC proof for each GPU context and the confirmed deletion progress.
   When `APPLICATION_OBJECTS_DELETED` begins it first confirms drain, Executor and the other required stop stages,
   then deletes the RoleBindings and Roles, and only last cleans up their SA/Deployment/namespace ownership anchors;
   permissions must not be withdrawn early before the first inventory check.
3. Interrupted resume (injected once within the same round): watch state.json in a loop, and as soon as `SITE_UPDATED`
   enters `completed_steps` send SIGINT to the command process; then rerun with **exactly the same parameters**.
   At this point `site.yaml` no longer contains the ARN; the command must resolve the same `cluster_id` through the removal's own DISCOVERED evidence
   and resume to `COMPLETED`, must not report `no managed GPU cluster matches`,
   and must not redo steps already in `completed_steps`.
4. After the removal completes, verify the GPU cluster: the system namespace does not exist; the count of RBAC with proven ownership is 0; the unlabelled Role from precondition
   4 still exists; no node carries a Node Installer annotation any more -- read twice with an interval after the
   namespace is gone, both empty, and no node was written as Retrying;
   the GPU EKS and HyperPod clusters themselves still exist (`PRESERVED` in
   `installation-resources-after.json`).
5. Verify the CPU control plane: the registry Secret's `clusters.json` is an explicit `[]`; every CPU Pod
   `/healthz` 200 with `regional_registry.secret_drift=false`; when the failure-domain map changes only
   `control-worker` may complete the audited template update, with the Deployment UID unchanged, and it reads the new empty member/Node
   map; the Pod UIDs and `restartCount` of ingress/spool are the same as the baseline;
   `site.yaml` `spec.clusters: []`; release
   state `cluster_ids: []`; `status --full` all PASS and `control_api` does not report
   `regional registry drift`.
6. Zero-cluster upgrade path: `gpu-fault-admin deploy --state-dir <STATE_DIR>`. The classification must be
   `NOOP` (DEPLOY_HOST_ONLY when the deploy-host identity changed); it must not fail on the previous snapshot capture
   ("images are inconsistent across") or on rendering the site document; afterwards
   `status --full` is still all PASS.
7. Run `remove-cluster` once more with the original parameters: the site no longer manages the cluster, so the command must return the completed
   record directly (`phase=COMPLETED`) without taking any action. "A second removal after the cluster has been re-attached must archive the old
   record and start from scratch" is verified by `BOOT-026` step 1.

##### Verdict

- All audited steps of the state machine enter `completed_steps`, terminal state `COMPLETED`; the rerun with original parameters after SIGINT
  resumes rather than rediscovering or erroring;
- all Role/RoleBindings covered by the renderer and UID proof are deleted (baseline >0 → 0), the unlabelled
  manual Role is retained; legitimate dynamic resources are not misjudged as orphans, while unknown ownership or foreign bindings must still be refused;
- inspection performs no mutation; the real deletion happens after drain and Executor stop, object by object using the
  original UID and the current resourceVersion, and progress is recorded only after disappearance is confirmed; recreated objects or unknown reads cannot pass;
- node annotations are empty after the namespace is gone, and no node is rewritten to Retrying by the terminating Reconciler;
- on the CPU side the registry is `[]`, `secret_drift=false`, no registry drift, the failure-domain map and
  worker release have converged, and the Pod UIDs and `restartCount` of unselected roles are unchanged;
- the zero-cluster `deploy` classifies as `NOOP` and succeeds; `status --full` all PASS before and after;
- the underlying CPU/GPU EKS and HyperPod clusters are retained.

##### Evidence

`cases/GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-024/GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-024.json`: the sha256 of each of state.json,
`installation-resources-{before,after}.json`, `site.before.yaml` and `site.yaml`,
and the registry `clusters.json` before and after; the per-context RBAC proof inside the original cleanup journal,
the confirmed deletion progress and its digest; the count of RBAC with proven ownership, the count of annotated nodes,
the PASS/FAIL counts of `status --full`; the `completed_steps` list. ARNs, cluster_id and
node names appear only as sha256 digests; per-step durations are not recorded.

##### Known limitations

- Only the removal of "the site's only cluster" is covered; on a multi-cluster site "other clusters are unaffected, the old token 403s immediately"
  is covered by `BOOT-019`.
- The removal does not clean the nodes' cordon and spare labels, nor does it delete the agent rows of that cluster's nodes in the store;
  the latter is precisely the precondition state that `BOOT-025` exploits.

### GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-025

**`join-cluster --gpu-cluster-arn` re-attach after removal: node subnet CIDRs, DNS gate retry, collector events during PENDING, executor ready before the first claim, wave safety looks only at live Agents, rollback after a forced failure and rediscovery on retry**

- Level: `live-service-action`. Reinstalls the product data plane on the same GPU cluster removed by `BOOT-024`
  and registers it back into the CPU control plane; the negative segment uses one reversible cluster DNS outage to force a release failure and
  automatic rollback; does not reboot/replace nodes, does not stop jobs (the cluster carries no product workload at this point).
- Purpose: the join negatives of `BOOT-019` are injected in-process by the runner; this case uses only administrator commands and
  a reversible environmental fault, pinning the gaps that appear only when "re-attaching after a removal" and each of which blocked
  the attach on its first live run: the Agent endpoint CIDRs must come from the subnets where the HyperPod nodes live (the cluster's `VpcConfig`
  and each instance group's `OverrideVpcConfig`), not only the EKS control-plane ENI subnets; the GPU
  endpoint DNS gate must wait until the private zone resolves inside the GPU VPC rather than failing on one NXDOMAIN;
  a cluster in `PENDING` in the registry must accept `/v1/collector-events` (claim still 423),
  otherwise `COLLECTORS_READY` is never reached; the executor's readiness must be able to read the execution owners before the first successful claim;
  the fleet wave safety gate may look only at nodes holding a live Agent
  and must not be stuck on the stale agent rows left by the removal; every join attempt must have its own
  `fleet_rollout_transaction`; the failure rollback must withdraw the `PENDING` registry entry, delete the
  kube context and fix `current-context`; a cluster token with no registry reference must be cleaned up,
  while a token still referenced by the rolled-back registry is retained bound to its original identity. The retry must archive the old attempt and
  **rediscover**, rather than reusing the old CIDRs or regenerating credentials that are still referenced.
- Code basis: `src/gpu_fault/admin/bootstrap_site.py::hyperpod_node_subnet_ids` and
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/bootstrap_site.py::discover_subnet_cidrs`,
  `deploy/control-plane/regional/probes/gpu_endpoint_gate.py` (`DNS_RESOLVE_WAIT_SECONDS`),
  `src/gpu_fault/cluster_executor/bootstrap.py::readiness_probe`,
  `src/gpu_fault_release/regional_release_fleet_rollout.py::live_agent_node_names`,
  `src/gpu_fault_release/regional_release_gpu_rollout.py::join_target`,
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/cluster_join_state.py::reset_completed_state`,
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/cluster_join_context.py::restore_current_context` and
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/cluster_join_context.py::ensure_kube_context`,
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/cluster_join_commit.py::rollback_membership`.

#### Preconditions and isolation

1. `BOOT-024` PASS: site `spec.clusters: []`, registry `[]`, no product
   namespace on the GPU cluster, node annotations empty; the store still holds the agent rows of that cluster's nodes (leases expired) --
   this is exactly the state the wave safety gate must face; do not clean it up by hand.
2. Site `spec.autoRollback` is true (the default).
3. Read-only record: `VpcConfig.Subnets` from `aws sagemaker describe-cluster` and every
   `InstanceGroups[].OverrideVpcConfig.Subnets`, `resourcesVpcConfig.subnetIds` from `aws eks describe-cluster`,
   and their respective CIDRs. If the two subnet sets are completely identical,
   the CIDR verdict degrades to "containment is enough"; note this in the evidence.
4. Baseline: the Pod UIDs and `restartCount` of the three CPU control-plane Deployments; the context list and `current-context` of the site kubeconfig
   (the file pointed to by the site environment variable `KUBECONFIG`).

#### Steps

1. Negative (forced failure and rollback). First scale the GPU cluster's `kube-system/coredns` to 0 (record the original
   replica count), then execute:

   ```bash
   gpu-fault-admin join-cluster \
     --state-dir <STATE_DIR> \
     --gpu-cluster-arn <GPU_EKS_ARN>
   ```

   Expected: `<STATE_DIR>/join-cluster/<arn_sha256_12>/state.json` records in order
   `PRECHECKED` → `DISCOVERED` → `LOCAL_INPUTS_READY` → `PREREQUISITES_READY` →
   `CANDIDATE_READY` → `RELEASE_STARTED`, then the GPU endpoint DNS gate fails because it never resolves within
   `DNS_RESOLVE_WAIT_SECONDS`, and the command exits non-zero; state.json has
   `phase=ROLLED_BACK`, no `rollback_errors`, and `completed_steps` retains only
   `PRECHECKED`/`DISCOVERED`. Verify the rollback result: the registry Secret has no
   `PENDING` entry for the cluster, `status --full` does not report `regional registry drift`; the product
   namespace on the GPU cluster has been deleted; the cluster's context does not exist in the site kubeconfig, and
   `kubectl config current-context` either points at another context or is empty -- it must not dangle at
   the deleted context; node annotations are empty, and the target in the registry cannot claim. Without a registry
   reference, this attempt's token file must be deleted; if the rolled-back registration is retained, only
   `retained_cluster_token` may keep the same token bound to the original cluster/EKS/HyperPod, the retry reuses it,
   and no other credential may be generated to impersonate the original registration. The temporary fleet master must be cleaned up. Verify only key names, digests and references;
   do not output credentials. Restore CoreDNS to its original replica count.
2. Positive retry (the same command): the old attempt in `state.json` is archived as
   `state.attempt-001.json`, `attempt=2`, `DISCOVERED` is recomputed rather than reused; then
   `RELEASE_STARTED` → `JOINED` → `COLLECTORS_READY` → `VERIFIED` → `SITE_UPDATED` →
   `RELEASE_STATE_UPDATED` → `REGISTRY_UPDATED` → `ACTIVATION_STARTED` → `ACTIVATED` →
   `FINAL_VERIFIED`, `phase=COMPLETED`, **in one run**, `step_completed_at` with one entry per step.
3. Observations during the attach (between `RELEASE_STARTED` and `ACTIVATED`):
   - the target's `subnet_cidrs` in the `DISCOVERED` evidence and the registry entry's
     `agentEndpointAllowedCidrs` contain the HyperPod node subnet CIDRs recorded in precondition 3;
   - while the registry entry's lifecycle is `PENDING`, deliveries from the GPU cluster's collectors to
     `/v1/collector-events` are accepted, and the executor's claim gets 423;
   - the `gpu-fault-cluster-executor` Pod is Ready before any successful claim (readiness
     reads the execution owners from the breadcrumb written when the claim loop starts, and no longer 503s with
     "executor advertised no execution owners");
   - the DNS gate probe keeps retrying after the first NXDOMAIN until resolution succeeds; if it resolves on the first try that also passes,
     but it must not fail on a single NXDOMAIN;
   - the fleet wave safety gate is not blocked by stale agent rows in the store (no
     `fleet wave safety blocked` may appear, nor waiting for the lease-margin of a non-existent Agent);
   - the `fleet_rollout_transaction` in the release state used by the join differs from the value in step 1;
   - the node barrier judged no node as `installer-active`/Retrying (when there is no
     Reconciler on the cluster, join first clears leftover annotations once).
4. Post-attach verification: the timestamp of `COLLECTORS_READY` is earlier than `ACTIVATION_STARTED` (proving that collector events during
   PENDING were accepted); `VERIFIED` reads the member snapshot through the CPU ingress Deployment `gpu-fault-api-ha`;
   check the CPU by the role boundary of BOOT-019: registry hot activation does not rely on restarts,
   a failure-domain map change allows only the audited roll of `control-worker`, the Deployment UID stays unchanged,
   and the new map matches the complete Node set; the Pod UIDs and `restartCount` of ingress/spool stay at baseline.
   Every CPU Pod `/healthz`
   `regional_registry.secret_drift=false`; the cluster ID sets in `site.yaml`, the registry and the release state
   agree; `status --full` all PASS; the Agent heartbeats of all nodes in the cluster
   converge and the executor claim no longer gets 423.

##### Verdict

- The forced failure happens after `RELEASE_STARTED`, the automatic rollback reaches `ROLLED_BACK` with
  `rollback_errors` empty; no `PENDING` residue in the registry, no kube context leak,
  `current-context` does not dangle, the target cannot claim; the unreferenced token is deleted, a token still referenced by the rolled-back registration
  is retained only bound to its original identity, the temporary fleet master is cleaned up;
- the retry archives the old attempt, rediscovers, and reaches `COMPLETED` in one run;
- the CIDRs contain the HyperPod node subnets; collector events during PENDING are accepted while claim gets 423; the executor
  is ready before the first claim; the DNS gate retries; wave safety looks only at live Agents;
  `fleet_rollout_transaction` differs between attempts;
- unselected CPU roles do not restart, the worker's new failure-domain map has been released and converged,
  `secret_drift=false`, the three cluster ID sets agree, `status --full` all PASS.

##### Evidence

`cases/GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-025/GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-025.json`: the sha256 of each of `state.attempt-001.json`
and the terminal `state.json`, the registry `clusters.json` (after rollback and after attach), and the release state;
the `attempt` number; the `completed_steps` list; the boolean conclusion of the CIDR containment;
the `restartCount` difference before and after; the `status --full` counts. ARNs, CIDRs, context names and node names appear only as
sha256 digests; per-step durations are not recorded.

##### Known limitations

- The forced failure is injected only at the DNS gate (after `RELEASE_STARTED`, before `JOINED`);
  the failure rollback after `JOINED` and before `ACTIVATION_STARTED`, and the second
  rollback of `ROLLBACK_FAILED`, are not injected in this case; the former is covered by the in-process injection of `BOOT-019`, the latter has unit tests only.
- The `--allowed-namespace` path that appends a workload namespace is not part of this case.

### GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-026

**A second `remove-cluster` archives the old record and runs from scratch; `deploy --gpu-cluster-arn` as the second join entry point re-attaches in batch**

- Level: `live-service-action`. The same actions as `BOOT-024`/`BOOT-025` performed once more each,
  only with the entry point switched to `deploy`; does not reboot/replace nodes, does not stop jobs.
- Purpose: both gaps appear only in the second round of "same cluster removed → attached → removed again → attached again":
  `remove-cluster` reads the previous round's `COMPLETED` record in the state directory and returns immediately,
  doing nothing; `deploy --gpu-cluster-arn` taking the batch join path reads the previous round's `COMPLETED`
  join record and is refused by the site non-membership field drift guard. At the same time it proves that the `deploy` entry point skips the whole rollout round when the site
  is `NOOP` against the current source and goes straight to the batch join, and that repeated execution is idempotent.
- Code basis: `src/gpu_fault/admin/cluster_removal.py` (a completed record is archived as
  `state.completed-<stamp>.json`),
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/cluster_join_state.py::completed_state_is_current` and
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/cluster_join_state.py::reset_completed_state` (`COMPLETED`
  is a finished state and is not constrained by the drift guard),
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/deploy_command.py::run_public_deploy` and
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/deploy_command.py::join_gpu_clusters`,
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/cluster_batch_join.py::join_clusters`.

#### Preconditions and isolation

1. `BOOT-025` PASS: the cluster is managed by the site again; `<STATE_DIR>/remove-cluster/<cluster_id>/state.json`
   is the `COMPLETED` record left by `BOOT-024`; `<STATE_DIR>/join-cluster/<arn_sha256_12>/state.json`
   is the `COMPLETED` record left by `BOOT-025`.
2. The emptiness requirements and baseline of `BOOT-024` preconditions 2 and 3 apply likewise.

#### Steps

1. Remove once more with exactly the same command as `BOOT-024`. Verify: the state directory gains
   `state.completed-<stamp>.json`, whose content equals the terminal record of `BOOT-024`; the new `state.json`
   walks all audited steps of BOOT-024 again from `STARTED` to `COMPLETED` and must not return the old record directly;
   the GPU-side and CPU-side checks of `BOOT-024` steps 4 and 5 all hold again.
2. Re-attach through the `deploy` entry point:

   ```bash
   gpu-fault-admin deploy --state-dir <STATE_DIR> --gpu-cluster-arn <GPU_EKS_ARN>
   ```

   Verify:
   - after the source hop finishes, the `mode` in `<STATE_DIR>/source-deploy-success.json` is not
     `APPLICATION_RELEASE` (the zero-cluster site is `NOOP` against the current source), and the command immediately enters the batch
     join instead of first running a full rollout round;
   - in the join state directory the `COMPLETED` record of `BOOT-025` is archived as
     `state.attempt-NNN.json`, the new record increments `attempt` and rediscovers from `STARTED`; it is neither
     judged `ALREADY_MANAGED` nor refused by
     `join-cluster source site non-membership fields drifted`;
   - the batch result printed by the command has `phase=COMPLETED`, `joined` contains the cluster, `already_managed`
     is empty;
   - the "during attach" and "post-attach" checks of `BOOT-025` steps 3 and 4 hold item by item, including the necessary
     failure-domain-map worker update; only the strict idempotent rerun in the next step requires zero rolls.
3. Run the very same `deploy` again unchanged: the batch result's `already_managed` contains the cluster, `joined`
   is empty; CPU/GPU Deployment generations are unchanged; `status --full` all PASS.
4. Try once more with `gpu-fault-admin join-cluster --state-dir <STATE_DIR> --gpu-cluster-arn <GPU_EKS_ARN>`:
   the result is likewise `ALREADY_MANAGED`; the two entry points judge consistently.

##### Verdict

- The second removal archives the old record and executes in full; the GPU-side and CPU-side terminal states are the same as after the first removal;
- `deploy --gpu-cluster-arn` goes straight to the batch join after the `NOOP` source hop and reaches `COMPLETED`;
  the old `COMPLETED` join record is archived rather than triggering the drift guard or being treated as already managed;
- repeated execution of the same `deploy` and of `join-cluster` both judge `ALREADY_MANAGED` and roll no
  Deployment;
- the `BOOT-025` verdicts during and after the attach hold item by item.

##### Evidence

`cases/GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-026/GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-026.json`: the sha256 of each of the archived record and the new record,
`source-deploy-success.json`, and the batch result JSON; the `attempt` number, the
counts of `joined`/`already_managed`; the same counts as `BOOT-025`. Identifiers appear only as digests; durations are not
recorded.

##### Known limitations

- The `deploy` entry point is verified only on the "remove first, then attach" path; "the site has an application-level change together with a new GPU
  ARN" (rollout first, then attach via `pending_gpu_cluster_arns`) is not part of this case.
### GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-027

**`uninstall --cpu-cluster keep --reset-database`: node uninstall after the consumers stop, interrupted-resume on the original schema-v2 journal, and the Aurora final snapshot**

- Level: `live-service-action`. Deletes every product resource of the site (Kubernetes objects, AWS resources,
  the Aurora cluster and its data), keeping only the CPU cluster declared as keep, the GPU clusters and EXTERNAL resources;
  no node reboot/replace.
- Purpose: every gap the whole-site uninstall exposed on live hardware is about "order": when the node Agent is
  uninstalled while the consumers or the Executor can still dispatch commands, a drain-after workflow is triggered and a
  LEASED command is left behind that nobody will complete; commands born after ingress stops cannot renew/report back,
  and after the lease expires the still-running consumer judges the parent workflow failed and mints a
  `workflow-drain-after-*` successor, so the drain never reaches 0. Therefore the whole site first sets the target
  clusters to `DRAINING` within the same registry revision (the API refuses new events and new claims; in-flight leases
  may still complete), then stops the producers; ingress and the consumers keep running until strictly drained, after
  which the consumers, ingress and the GPU Executor are stopped in turn, and only then are the nodes uninstalled. Once
  the control-plane consumers have stopped, the node phase uses only the fleet/UID proof saved in the original journal
  and no longer depends on the database. An interrupted resume may not guess at some other failed record, and an old
  schema-v1 may not be taken as proof of completion under the new order. Aurora is still deleted only after all the
  preceding verification has completed, reader first then writer, retaining one final snapshot bound to the identity of
  the original database.
- Code basis: `src/gpu_fault/admin/uninstall.py::uninstall`,
  `deploy/control-plane/regional/prepare-clean-redeploy.sh` (`--mode reset`:
  `drain_registry_clusters` publishes `DRAINING` in the same registry revision; node components live in the
  separate `NODE_RUNTIMES_STOPPED` phase),
  `deploy/control-plane/tools/cleanup_state.py` (schema-v2, exact phase_order, original fleet/UID binding),
  `deploy/control-plane/tools/cleanup_kubernetes.py` (cleanup protected by ownership and UID/resourceVersion),
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/aws_cleanup.py` (Aurora reader→writer→cluster deletion order).
  Offline contract: `tests/regional/test_clean_redeploy_script.py`.
  Whole-site uninstall and remove-cluster share the same dynamic RBAC inspection/inventory/delete
  contract: read-only proof enters the original per-context cleanup snapshot, and the strict orphan check grants no
  label-based exemptions; proven grants are deleted only after the drain and the Executor stop, and UID/RV validation
  completes before the ownership anchor is deleted.

#### Preconditions and isolation

1. `BOOT-026` PASS: the site manages one GPU cluster and every node Agent is online (what this case has to prove is
   precisely when they get stopped); no PENDING/RUNNING/WAITING workflow, open remote
   command or budget claim; no node carries `gpu-fault.io/quarantined` (the reset
   preflight would refuse).
2. Baseline: the AWS-side installed-resource registry (exported to `<STATE_DIR>/uninstall/` during uninstall); the
   reader/writer instance list of the Aurora cluster; the list of existing Aurora snapshots; the ARNs of the underlying
   CPU/GPU EKS and HyperPod clusters.
3. Do not manufacture orphan leases. When existing open/unknown commands are found, reconcile them first through the
   audited recovery flow; do not release them by bulk-failing them with SQL. A parked spare must additionally have the
   `previous-unschedulable` original baseline and Node UID owned by this run; an unknown baseline must block the cleanup.

#### Steps

1. First execution with an injected interruption:

   ```bash
   gpu-fault-admin uninstall \
     --state-dir <STATE_DIR> \
     --cpu-cluster keep \
     --reset-database \
     --confirm UNINSTALL_GPU_FAULT
   ```

   Watch `<STATE_DIR>/uninstall/kubernetes-cleanup.json` in a loop; as soon as
   `INGRESS_STOPPED` is recorded `COMPLETED` (both the control-plane consumers and ingress have been scaled to 0), send
   SIGINT to the foreground process group. At this point `<STATE_DIR>/uninstall/state.json` should have stopped at
   `REGISTRY_EXPORTED`.
2. Resume with exactly the same command and the original schema-v2 `kubernetes-cleanup.json`. Check:
   the phase_order matches the current order; the completed phases, run identity, site/namespace/Node UIDs and fleet
   inventory remain bound to the same transaction;
   no rebuild from `PREFLIGHT`, no lookup of some other "latest failed" journal, and no re-guessing of the fleet.
   With the original control-plane consumers already stopped, the node phase consumes only the saved fleet/UID proof
   and performs no database reads.
3. Order check (read the phase timeline in `kubernetes-cleanup.json` and the uninstall log):
   `PREFLIGHT` → `CLUSTERS_DRAINING` → `GPU_DATA_PLANE_SOURCES_STOPPED` →
   `QUEUES_DRAINED` → `CONTROL_CONSUMERS_STOPPED` → `INGRESS_STOPPED` → `GPU_EXECUTORS_STOPPED` →
   `NODE_RUNTIMES_STOPPED` → `CPU_AUXILIARIES_STOPPED` → `APPLICATION_OBJECTS_DELETED` →
   `NAMESPACES_DELETED` → `CLEANUP_COMPLETED` (`schema_version=2`). The uninstall of the node Agent and the
   Node Runtime must fall in the separate `NODE_RUNTIMES_STOPPED` phase; `QUEUES_DRAINED` is
   `COMPLETED` with no "did not drain within"; `CLUSTERS_DRAINING` precedes any GPU producer
   scale-down; `QUEUES_DRAINED` completes while `gpu-fault-api-ha` and `gpu-fault-control-worker` still have replicas,
   and only afterwards do the consumers scale to 0, then ingress scales to 0. The selected clusters publish exactly one
   batch revision; the durable lifecycle, credential digests and allowed scope of unselected clusters stay unchanged.
   The control-plane store holds no `drain-after-*` incident/workflow newly created in this round (query in the window
   before the first-round SIGINT, while `CONTROL_CONSUMERS_STOPPED` has not yet been reached).
4. Refusal of the old order and of unknown baselines is verified by the offline contract: schema-v1, or an old v2 with a
   different phase_order, both require explicit reconciliation; merely editing the version number or the order array,
   or fabricating completed phases, is not allowed; without the original fleet/UID or the parked-spare baseline it must
   not continue. The formal run does not rewrite the
   journal to manufacture negative conditions, nor does it run bulk orphan SQL. Spare restoration writes only the
   proven original scheduling values, must carry the Node UID/resourceVersion and read back, and may not uncordon
   indiscriminately.
5. `state.json` goes `STARTED` → `REGISTRY_EXPORTED` → `KUBERNETES_VERIFIED` →
   `NON_AURORA_DELETE_IN_PROGRESS` → `NON_AURORA_VERIFIED` → `CPU_VERIFIED` →
   `READY_TO_DELETE_AURORA` → `AURORA_DELETE_IN_PROGRESS` → `COMPLETED`.
   Audited pre-Aurora cleanup proof must exist before the database is deleted. By the current actual roles, delete the
   reader first and confirm it is gone, then delete the writer and confirm it is gone, and finally delete the cluster;
   this may not run in parallel with the preceding resource verification.
   At the end, the only thing left of that cluster is the single final snapshot that
   `final_snapshot_identifier` in `state.json` points to, in state `available`, and the total snapshot count is exactly
   one more than the baseline.
6. Command output: `cpu_cluster=keep`, `gpu_clusters=preserved`, `database_reset=true`,
   `aurora_cluster=deleted`, `aurora_deleted_last=true`,
   `delete_policy_residuals=0`, `aurora_final_snapshot` non-empty; the final registry that `final_registry`
   points to contains no `DELETE_PENDING`.
7. State-directory retention: `<STATE_DIR>/site.yaml`, `bootstrap-state.json`, `uninstall/`
   (including the original cleanup journal and the final registry) are still present; the CPU/GPU EKS and HyperPod
   clusters still exist, and the product namespace on the CPU cluster no longer exists.

##### Verdict

- Whole-site DRAINING precedes any component stop; ingress and the consumers are kept until the strict drain completes;
  node components are uninstalled only after the drain, the control-plane consumers and the GPU Executor have stopped.
  No new drain-after workflow or orphan command is created, and the node phase no longer queries the database;
- The original schema-v2 journal, exact phase_order and fleet/UID binding resume to `COMPLETED` without guessing at
  other checkpoints; an old order, unknown baselines and missing proof all require reconciliation, with no bulk orphan
  SQL or legacy fail-marking;
- Parked spares restore only the explicitly owned original scheduling values; the UID/resourceVersion guard and the
  read-back both hold;
- Aurora is deleted after the preceding cleanup verification completes, in the actual reader, writer, cluster order,
  each instance wave confirmed gone before continuing; only one available final snapshot belonging to the original
  database incarnation remains;
- The terminal output agrees with the final registry, residuals are 0; the underlying clusters and the state directory
  are retained.

##### Evidence

`cases/GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-027/GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-027.json`: the sha256 of each of `state.json`,
the original schema-v2 `kubernetes-cleanup.json`, the fleet/UID inventory and the final registry;
the phase sequence and continuity with the original journal; the spare-baseline restoration and the no-orphan-command
checks; the before/after difference in the Aurora snapshot count; the count fields of the command output. Snapshot
identifiers, ARNs and node names appear only as digests; per-phase durations are not recorded.

##### Known limitations

- The `--aurora-final-snapshot skip` path (legal in combination with `keep --reset-database`, produces no snapshot at
  all) is not executed in this case and is covered only by unit tests.
- The `--cpu-cluster delete` path is not part of this case; this case does not delete the CPU cluster.

### GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-028

**Fresh `deploy` bootstrap on empty clusters and `deploy --state-dir` resume after an interruption**

- Level: `live-service-action`. Re-creates every product resource of the site on the CPU/GPU clusters emptied by
  `BOOT-027`; no fault injection, no node reboot/replace.
- Purpose: `BOOT-016` proves that a first deployment "writes the complete registry before starting workloads" and that a
  rerun is `NOOP`; this case fills in the two segments it does not cover -- on clusters with **no installed control
  plane at all**, deploy's preflight checks, SNS mail confirmation and cold build of the runtime images must all go
  through and install both sides; and after an interruption midway, a resume on `--state-dir` alone must reuse the
  completed task checkpoints and not create a second set of resources.
- Code basis: `src/gpu_fault/admin/bootstrap_checkpoint.py::bind_bootstrap_inputs`
  (task digests and checkpoints), `src/gpu_fault/admin/monitoring_subscriptions.py`
  (SNS subscription confirmation gate), `src/gpu_fault/admin/release_artifacts.py::build_signed_release`,
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/deploy_command.py::run_prepared_deploy`.
  Input persistence ahead of source preparation is provided by `initial_deploy_request` in
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/deploy_identity.py`.

#### Preconditions and isolation

1. `BOOT-027` PASS: the CPU/GPU clusters exist but have no product namespace, no registry Secret,
   no Aurora cluster, no runtime/cache ECR. The isolation and permission requirements of `BOOT-016` apply equally
   (`NodeRecovery=None`, state-dir `0700`, signing material `0600`).
2. Use a **new, empty** `<STATE_DIR_FRESH>` (the old directory retained by `BOOT-027` is history only;
   its `bootstrap-state.json` is not reused).
3. The recipient of `<ADMIN_EMAIL>` can click the SNS confirmation mail during the run.
4. Baseline: the ECR repository list is empty, Aurora has no cluster, the target namespace does not exist.

#### Steps

1. First execution: first cover the input-persistence breakpoint ahead of source preparation, then cover the original
   infrastructure breakpoint:

   ```bash
   gpu-fault-admin deploy \
     --cpu-cluster-arn <CPU_EKS_ARN> \
     --gpu-cluster-arn <GPU_EKS_ARN> \
     --state-dir <STATE_DIR_FRESH> \
     --admin-email <ADMIN_EMAIL>
   ```

   Check that the private `initial-deploy-request.json` is written before source preparation, binding the original
   CPU/GPU ARN order, the e-mail address and the first-time configuration. Interrupt once while that file already exists
   and `site.yaml` has not yet been generated, then restore the original request with
   `deploy --state-dir <STATE_DIR_FRESH>`; conflicting parameters must be refused, the e-mail address is not guessed,
   and the record is not patched by hand. When the old state lacks this request, the original parameters must be
   supplied explicitly and reconciled.
   If this breakpoint was not actually exercised, record it separately as not tested; the later infrastructure
   interruption cannot stand in for it.
   Then check that the preflight does not treat "no installed control plane" as a failure; watch
   `<STATE_DIR_FRESH>/bootstrap-state.json` in a loop and, as soon as `phase` becomes
   `aws-infrastructure-ready`, send SIGINT to the foreground process group. Record the set of task names already
   `COMPLETED` at this point and the list of AWS-side resources already created (ECR, Aurora, NLB, IAM).
2. Resume on the state directory alone:

   ```bash
   gpu-fault-admin deploy --state-dir <STATE_DIR_FRESH>
   ```

   The ARNs and e-mail address are restored from the same bound state; tasks completed in step 1 are not executed again
   (same task digests, checkpoints reused, no second set added to the AWS resource list); `bootstrap-state.json`
   continues to `platform-prerequisites-ready` → `site-ready`.
3. SNS: the subscription of `<ADMIN_EMAIL>` on the site topic is first `PendingConfirmation`; after clicking confirm
   there is exactly one confirmed subscription and no duplicate pending request; the control-plane Pods have
   `GPU_FAULT_REQUIRE_CONFIRMED_SNS_SUBSCRIPTION=true`.
4. Images: check the release-bound `control_plane`, `executor` and
   `node_dependencies` descriptors and signatures separately; do not take one old shared runtime image as proof for all
   three. The corresponding descriptors of the first build are not registry reuse; later, with unchanged inputs, reuse by
   each one's own content identity is allowed and the overall classification is `NOOP`.
5. Release: `<STATE_DIR_FRESH>/release-deploy/<release-id>/state.json` goes from
   `bootstrap-started` to `complete` with status `COMPLETED`; the registry Secret's creation
   time precedes the CPU Deployments and any GPU workload (the same assertion as `BOOT-016`); the three CPU
   Deployments and the GPU-side executor/watcher/collector/reconciler are all Ready, and the node
   Agent heartbeats converge; `verification-report.json` and `stability-report.json` are healthy.
6. `gpu-fault-admin status --state-dir <STATE_DIR_FRESH> --full` is all PASS;
   the cluster ID sets in `site.yaml`, the registry `clusters.json` and the release state agree.
7. Rerun `deploy --state-dir <STATE_DIR_FRESH>` unchanged: classification `NOOP`, the CPU/GPU Deployment
   generations are unchanged.

##### Verdict

- With no installed control plane the preflight passes, and the bootstrap goes through `new` → `discovered` →
  `aws-infrastructure-ready` → `platform-prerequisites-ready` → `site-ready`;
- After the interruption, the `deploy --state-dir` resume reuses the completed tasks and no second set of AWS resources
  appears;
- SNS has exactly one confirmed subscription; the runtime images are cold-built and signed;
- Both sides are fully installed and `status --full` is all PASS; the rerun is strictly `NOOP`.

##### Evidence

`cases/GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-028/GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-028.json`: the sha256 of each of `bootstrap-state.json`
(at interruption and at completion), the release-deploy `state.json`, `verification-report.json`,
`stability-report.json` and the registry `clusters.json`; the before/after difference in the set of completed task
names; the before/after difference in AWS resource counts; the `status --full` counts. ARNs, account numbers and
repository names appear only as digests; durations are not recorded.

##### Known limitations

- This case records the interruptions at initial-request persistence and at `aws-infrastructure-ready` separately;
  interruptions during the release stage (the `bootstrap-*` phases)
  and their automatic cleanup are covered by the failure paths of `BOOT-016`/`BOOT-020`.
- Mail confirmation requires a manual click; the wait ceiling of `--wait-for-email-confirmation` is set by the operator
  per site convention and does not enter the verdict.

##### Cleanup

The single chain ends here: the site is in the freshly-deployed completed state and can serve directly as the isolated
site for later cases; no extra cleanup is needed. If `BOOT-029` follows, first uninstall the site installed by this case
with the command of `BOOT-027` step 1 (without injecting the interruption) -- that is the precondition of `BOOT-029`
and does not count towards its sequence.

### GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-029

**Administrator deployment lifecycle sequence: cold-build first `deploy` → `remove-cluster` → `join-cluster` → `uninstall keep + reset-database` → cold-build first `deploy` again**

- Level: `live-service-action`. On a pair of empty clusters, fully installs the product, deregisters and re-joins the
  only GPU cluster, uninstalls the whole site and deletes Aurora, then installs from zero again; no node reboot/replace,
  no stopping of training jobs (the GPU cluster is required to have no managed job throughout); the underlying CPU/GPU
  EKS and HyperPod clusters are retained.
  The second first-time deployment (S5) is executed **strictly by the text of the repository root README**: the README
  is the object under test, and no parameter, environment variable or precondition beyond the three steps it spells out
  is added.
- Purpose: `BOOT-024..028` each prove one verb and allow independent execution on their own preconditions. What an
  administrator actually experiences, however, is one **indivisible sequence**: from "nothing" to installed, changed,
  uninstalled, back to "nothing" and rebuilt. This case runs the five verbs once in that order and adds the verdicts
  that can only be verified when they are chained: (a) both first-time deployments are **cold** builds -- before the
  deployment the local BuildKit cache, the local images of every component, the site ECR images and the corresponding
  component buildcache tags all do not exist
  (a new site has no ECR repositories, and after the uninstall the repositories have been deleted too), none of the
  three images' build logs contains
  `CACHED`, and each has base-image pull evidence; the shared image's "six-step Dockerfile" is no longer hard-coded.
  (b) The uninstalled site can be rebuilt from zero, and the second round's
  `site_id`, completed task set and `status --full` conclusion are the same as the first round's -- the lifecycle is
  repeatable.
  (c) The README's deployment steps are themselves usable -- S5 runs only the commands the README writes out, and one
  missing required condition in the README makes S5 fail.
  The driver script `scripts/acceptance/admin-lifecycle-sequence.sh` is responsible for the order, cache cleanup,
  waiting for every command to exit, the cold-build assertions and private evidence recording; S5's README parsing,
  pristine source copy, allowlisted environment and `readme` receipt are handled by
  `scripts/e2e/regional/boot029_readme.py`;
  the **checklist** of each stage refers directly to the corresponding case and is not repeated here.
- Code basis: `src/gpu_fault/admin/bootstrap_checkpoint.py::bind_bootstrap_inputs` and
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/bootstrap_tasks.py` (`FOUNDATION_READY_PHASE`,
  `PLATFORM_READY_PHASE`), `src/gpu_fault/admin/cluster_removal.py::remove_cluster`,
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/cluster_join.py`, `src/gpu_fault/admin/cluster_join_commit.py`,
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/cluster_join_state.py::reset_completed_state`,
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/uninstall.py::uninstall`,
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/release_repositories.py` (`gpu-fault/runtime-<digest>` and
  `gpu-fault/runtime-cache-<digest>` repository naming),
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/release_artifacts.py::build_signed_release`
  (per-component selection of each one's own cache inputs and outputs),
  `scripts/release_image.py` (`docker buildx build --cache-from/--cache-to`),
  `src/gpu_fault/admin/aws_cleanup.py` (`ecr delete-repository --force`),
  `scripts/acceptance/admin-lifecycle-sequence.sh`,
  `scripts/e2e/regional/boot029_readme.py` (README parsing, `prepare_source_checkout`
  pristine copy, `clean_environment` allowlist). Offline contracts:
  `tests/regional/test_admin_lifecycle_sequence_script.py`,
  `tests/regional/test_boot029_readme.py` (the latter parses the repository's real README).

#### Preconditions and isolation

1. A pair of **empty** clusters: the CPU and GPU EKS/HyperPod clusters exist, but there is no product namespace, no
   registry Secret, no Aurora cluster, no `gpu-fault/runtime-*` ECR repository.
   Uninstalling the site left by a `BOOT-028` PASS with the command of `BOOT-027` step 1 (without injecting the
   interruption) yields this state; another pair of never-deployed clusters also works. The isolation and permission
   requirements of `BOOT-016` apply equally (`NodeRecovery=None`, state-dir `0700`, signing material `0600`).
2. Two state directories: `<STATE_DIR>` is a **new, empty directory** (S1–S4), `<STATE_DIR_SECOND>`
   is another new, empty directory (S5; the driver defaults to `<STATE_DIR>-second`). The driver refuses pre-existing
   bootstrap state when entering a first-deploy stage, so that an upgrade path is not mistaken for a cold start;
   a legitimate resume restores only the first non-PASS stage in the same bound receipt and no longer rejects its own
   existing state wholesale.
3. Use an isolated build host dedicated to this run and pass `--confirm-isolated-build-host` explicitly;
   the Docker prune affects the selected builder and must not be run on a shared build host.
   `gpu-fault-admin` is available; `docker`, `docker buildx` (any driver) and
   `aws` are logged in to the site account; `<CHECKOUT>` is the source checkout to deploy (`deploy` takes the working
   directory as the source root; S5 deploys from a pristine copy of it, so the working tree may be dirty). S5 inherits
   the operator's `PATH`
   (the README's premise is that the deployment machine **already has** `aws`, `cosign`, `docker`, `kubectl`, `helm`
   and similar tools installed; where they live is the operator's environment), only de-duplicating it in order and
   removing two kinds of directories: directories containing an executable
   `gpu-fault-admin`, and Python virtual-environment directories (the parent directory has `pyvenv.cfg`,
   or the path contains a `.venv`, `deployer-venv` or `.deployer-venv.versions` component); if it is empty after
   removal, refuse. The README's `. .venv/bin/activate` must be the only action that puts `gpu-fault-admin` on
   the PATH. AWS credentials may come only from the instance role,
   `AWS_PROFILE`/`AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE`/`AWS_CONFIG_FILE`, or the container/Web
   identity variables; `AWS_REGION` is not passed in (the README says the Region is derived from the ARN).
4. The recipient of `<ADMIN_EMAIL>` can click the SNS confirmation mail once in each of the two first-time deployments.
   For an unattended S1 give the driver `--email-wait-minutes <M>` (passed through as `--wait-for-email-confirmation`,
   **applies to S1 only**); S5 runs by the README's literal text without a wait parameter, see the note under S5
   about the two attempts.
5. Throughout, the GPU cluster has no PENDING/RUNNING/WAITING workflow, open remote command,
   budget claim or managed training job, and no node carries `gpu-fault.io/quarantined`.
6. Baseline (read-only): `aws ecr describe-repositories` shows no `gpu-fault/runtime-*`;
   `docker images` shows no `gpu-fault-runtime*`; `docker buildx du` is empty after cleanup;
   Aurora has no cluster; the target namespace does not exist on either cluster.

#### Steps

The driver runs the five stages in one go (S1–S5 below are the driver's `--stage 1`–`--stage 5`); every
`gpu-fault-admin` command runs in the foreground and **waits for the process to exit** before the next stage begins,
and any stage failure stops the run and prints the stage number. A resume is allowed only for the first non-PASS stage
under the original bound inputs; it may not skip a failure or replay completed stages at will; the source, repository,
ARNs, e-mail address, directories, cache and wait parameters must be identical, and the log digests of earlier PASS
stages must still verify. An original `RUNNING` without an exit receipt must be reconciled first; it may not be assumed
that the command has stopped:

```bash
scripts/acceptance/admin-lifecycle-sequence.sh \
  --state-dir <STATE_DIR> \
  --cpu-cluster-arn <CPU_EKS_ARN> \
  --gpu-cluster-arn <GPU_EKS_ARN> \
  --admin-email <ADMIN_EMAIL> \
  --repo <CHECKOUT> \
  --confirm-isolated-build-host
```

After all five stages PASS, uninstalling the second site and starting again with `--stage 5` is the S5 rerun: the
receipt keeps the already-passed S5 receipt under `reruns`, S5's attempt numbers keep counting up and mark the rerun
start with `rerun_from_attempt`, and no other stage may be rerun.

The optional `--aurora-final-snapshot retain|skip` controls S4; the default is `retain`.
Choose `skip` only when discarding the staging data has been approved; the policy is written into the sequence's input
digest and the S4 receipt, and a resume may not change it. The driver re-checks the bound uninstall journal and
requires its actual
`final_snapshot_policy` to match the choice. When `skip` is chosen, S4 records the
`GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-027` snapshot-retention companion as `NOT_RUN` and may not claim to have completed that case's
final-snapshot acceptance.

After an S1/S5 interruption, the same first-time deployment can be resumed only if the original sequence receipt allows
a retry and the original command's exit receipt has been obtained; when a `bootstrap-state.json` already exists,
`resumed_first_deploy` is recorded and the cold-build checks are re-run.
Leftover bootstrap files alone do not authorise a resume, and a directory with only `site.yaml` but no bootstrap
checkpoint may not be treated as empty. An original `RUNNING` without an exit receipt must still be reconciled first.

Each stage's state files remain after the stage ends; the manual checklists can be completed item by item, between
stages or after everything has finished, following the references below.

1. **S1: cold-build first deployment.** The driver clears the caches first:
   `docker buildx prune --builder <current buildx builder> -af`,
   `docker builder prune -af`, deletion of every local `gpu-fault-runtime*` image; then it resolves the site ECR
   repositories by `--previous-site-id` (if given) and, where the repositories exist, deletes the runtime repository's
   images proven by this run's site/resource tags together with every component cache tag, in batches of at most 100
   images; only an explicit `RepositoryNotFoundException` counts as absent, while permission or read errors block
   immediately. Then it runs:

   ```bash
   gpu-fault-admin deploy \
     --cpu-cluster-arn <CPU_EKS_ARN> \
     --gpu-cluster-arn <GPU_EKS_ARN> \
     --state-dir <STATE_DIR> \
     --admin-email <ADMIN_EMAIL>
   ```

   Check: the `phase` of `<STATE_DIR>/bootstrap-state.json` goes through `new` → `discovered` →
   `aws-infrastructure-ready` → `platform-prerequisites-ready` → `site-ready`;
   the checks of `BOOT-028` steps 3–6 hold item by item (SNS has exactly one confirmed subscription; the ECR runtime
   repository goes from empty to three release-bound images each with signature and build proof rather than registry
   reuse; the release-deploy `state.json` reaches `complete`/`COMPLETED`; the registry Secret is created before the
   Deployments; both sides are fully Ready; `status --full` is all PASS; the three cluster ID sets agree).
   The interruption and resume of `BOOT-028` steps 1–2 are **not** injected in this stage. The cold-build verdict reads
   the BuildKit output in the deployment log (the driver sets `BUILDKIT_PROGRESS=plain`) and binds the
   `control_plane`, `executor` and `node_dependencies` descriptors separately:
   `registry_reused=false`, each with no `CACHED` layer and with a base-image pull record.
2. **S2: deregister the only GPU cluster.**

   ```bash
   gpu-fault-admin remove-cluster \
     --state-dir <STATE_DIR> \
     --gpu-cluster-arn <GPU_EKS_ARN> \
     --confirm REMOVE_GPU_CLUSTER
   ```

   The driver asserts that `<STATE_DIR>/remove-cluster/<cluster_id>/state.json` ends in
   `phase=COMPLETED`. The checklist is `BOOT-024` step 2 (all `completed_steps`:
   `DISCOVERED` → `CONTROL_REGISTRY_DRAINING` → `KUBERNETES_QUIESCED` →
   `KUBERNETES_REMOVED` → `CONTROL_REGISTRY_REMOVED`/`AWS_DETACHED` →
   `AURORA_UPDATED` → `SITE_COMMIT_STARTED` → `SITE_UPDATED` →
   `RELEASE_STATE_UPDATED` → `VERIFIED`),
   step 4 (GPU side) and step 5 (CPU side). The SIGINT resume of `BOOT-024` step 3 and the zero-cluster `deploy` and
   idempotent rerun of steps 6–7 are not executed in this stage (optional; doing them does not affect later stages).
3. **S3: re-join the same GPU cluster.**

   ```bash
   gpu-fault-admin join-cluster \
     --state-dir <STATE_DIR> \
     --gpu-cluster-arn <GPU_EKS_ARN>
   ```

   The driver asserts that `<STATE_DIR>/join-cluster/<arn_sha256_12>/state.json` ends in
   `phase=COMPLETED`. The checklist is the step sequence of `BOOT-025` step 2 (`PRECHECKED` →
   `DISCOVERED` → `LOCAL_INPUTS_READY` → `PREREQUISITES_READY` → `CANDIDATE_READY` →
   `RELEASE_STARTED` → `JOINED` → `COLLECTORS_READY` → `VERIFIED` → `SITE_UPDATED` →
   `RELEASE_STATE_UPDATED` → `REGISTRY_UPDATED` → `ACTIVATION_STARTED` → `ACTIVATED` →
   `FINAL_VERIFIED`, with `attempt=1` when this stage has no forced failure), step 3 (during the join) and step 4
   (after the join). The forced CoreDNS failure and rollback of `BOOT-025` step 1 is an **optional sub-scenario**: to do
   it, execute it manually and restore CoreDNS before the driver enters S3, in which case S3 has `attempt=2`
   and the old attempt is archived as `state.attempt-001.json`.
4. **S4: uninstall the whole site and reset the database.**

   ```bash
   gpu-fault-admin uninstall \
     --state-dir <STATE_DIR> \
     --cpu-cluster keep \
     --reset-database \
     --aurora-final-snapshot retain \
     --confirm UNINSTALL_GPU_FAULT
   ```

   The driver asserts that `<STATE_DIR>/uninstall/state.json` ends in `phase=COMPLETED`. The checklist
   is `BOOT-027` step 3 (exact phase_order, DRAINING before the producers stop, ingress and the consumers kept until the
   strict drain completes, node components uninstalled within `NODE_RUNTIMES_STOPPED`), step 5 (`state.json`
   `STARTED` → `REGISTRY_EXPORTED` → `KUBERNETES_VERIFIED` →
   `NON_AURORA_DELETE_IN_PROGRESS` → `READY_TO_DELETE_AURORA` → `COMPLETED`, Aurora
   reader first then writer, the `retain` branch leaving exactly one final snapshot), step 6 (command output fields) and
   step 7 (state directory and underlying clusters retained, product namespace gone). The SIGINT resume of `BOOT-027`
   steps 1–2 is an independent interrupted-resume sub-scenario; do not manufacture orphan leases. An explicit `skip`
   branch still checks the other cleanup steps, but the snapshot-retention companion is `NOT_RUN`. Additional check after
   the uninstall: the site's
   `gpu-fault/runtime-<digest>` and `gpu-fault/runtime-cache-<digest>` ECR repositories no longer exist
   (`aws ecr describe-repositories` reports `RepositoryNotFoundException`) -- this is the source of S5's
   "site ECR images and buildcache tags do not exist".
5. **S5: cold-build first deployment again.** The driver repeats S1's cache cleanup; this time it reads the `site_id`
   from `<STATE_DIR>/bootstrap-state.json` (retained by the uninstall) and resolves the two ECR
   repositories from it: normally the repositories have already been deleted by the uninstall and only "absent" is
   recorded; if a repository still exists (product defect or manual residue) it must first pass strict ownership
   validation against the original site/resource tags before its component images and every component
   cache tag are cleaned up; it may not continue on a read failure or unknown ownership. Then it deploys to
   `<STATE_DIR_SECOND>` **by the text of the repository root README**
   (`scripts/e2e/regional/boot029_readme.py`):
   - **Command source.** The driver locates two fenced code blocks tagged `bash` in `<CHECKOUT>/README.md` by heading
     (not by line number): the build block under `## 构建和验证` ("Build and verify") and the first-deploy block under
     `## 部署：先区分角色` ("Deploy: distinguish the roles first"); the command text is not hard-coded in the driver --
     whatever the README writes is what gets executed. In the build block only the non-verification lines are executed
     -- `make deploy-host-setup-online` and `. .venv/bin/activate`
     (or `source .venv/bin/activate`) -- while verification lines such as `make … check` and `make …-check` are skipped
     and recorded (deploy runs the release gates itself; checks are not part of the deployment steps); then the deploy
     block is executed. The deploy block must start with `gpu-fault-admin deploy`, and the four placeholders
     `<cpu-eks-or-hyperpod-arn>`, `<gpu-eks-or-hyperpod-arn>`, the example path
     `/secure/gpu-fault` and `<operations-email>` must each appear exactly once; they are replaced by
     `<CPU_EKS_ARN>`, `<GPU_EKS_ARN>`, `<STATE_DIR_SECOND>` and `<ADMIN_EMAIL>` respectively;
     no `--wait-for-email-confirmation` or any other parameter is added. A missing heading, a missing code block, a
     wrong placeholder count, or a build block that lacks the two lines above or has them in reverse order fails the
     stage immediately and names the heading.
     S5 therefore executes exactly and only the README's three steps: `make deploy-host-setup-online`,
     `. .venv/bin/activate`, and the four-argument `gpu-fault-admin deploy`.
   - **Pristine source copy.** The three steps run in a copy of `<CHECKOUT>` constructed the same way as the deploy
     source snapshot (`scripts/staging_source_snapshot.py::prepare_source_checkout`):
     `git worktree add --detach … HEAD`, apply `git diff --binary HEAD`, copy the untracked
     but non-ignored files, and a dirty working tree becomes one snapshot commit; the ignored `.venv` and `dist/` are not
     carried over. Before execution, assert that the copy has no `.venv` and that `git status --porcelain` is empty, and
     record the copy's source commit. Every attempt creates a fresh copy (`venv_preexisted=false`); the script and the
     copy live under
     `<STATE_DIR>/acceptance/stage-5-readme/attempt-<N>/`.
   - **Allowlisted environment.** The generated script enters the copy directory under `set -euo pipefail` and executes
     line by line; the environment is not the driver's environment but an allowlist: only `HOME`, `USER`, `LOGNAME`,
     `LANG`, `LC_*`, `TMPDIR`, `TERM`, `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, `DOCKER_*`, `AWS_PROFILE`,
     `AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE`, `AWS_CONFIG_FILE`, `AWS_CONTAINER_*` and
     `AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_*` are kept; `PATH` is the operator PATH described in precondition 3 minus the venv directories,
     in which an ordinary tool directory that also provides `gpu-fault-admin` (such as `/usr/local/bin` holding kubectl,
     helm and an old deploy-host link) is replaced in place by a stand-in directory that links only the remaining
     executables and contains no `gpu-fault-admin`; all `GPU_FAULT_*`, `PYTHONPATH`, `VIRTUAL_ENV` and
     `AWS_REGION`/`AWS_DEFAULT_REGION` are dropped. If the README flow cannot work without a condition the README does
     not state, this stage must fail -- that is exactly the README defect this case is looking for, and it may not be
     remedied in the driver.
   - **Mail confirmation.** The README command has no wait parameter. In the notification precheck during its first
     minute, deploy creates the site SNS topic, sends the confirmation mail to `<ADMIN_EMAIL>` (and sends it only once)
     and **checks only once**: while the subscription is still PENDING it neither builds nor deploys, prints
     `email notifications are not confirmed yet; nothing was deployed` together with the rerun command line, exits with
     a non-zero status, and records the PENDING request in `<STATE_DIR_SECOND>/bootstrap-state.json`.
     S4 deleted the topic along with the site, so S5's first attempt necessarily stops here (unless the recipient has
     already confirmed the subscription on the same topic by some other route): the driver records S5 attempt 1 FAIL
     and prints
     `--stage 5`; after the recipient clicks confirm, resume: attempt 2 is handled as
     `resumed_first_deploy` because bootstrap state already exists (no repeated cache cleanup -- no build has happened
     yet), redoes the three steps in a new pristine copy, and this time the precheck reads CONFIRMED and the deployment
     completes. The validity period of the confirmation mail is determined by SNS; the wait and the click do not enter
     the verdict.
   The cold-build verdict is the same as S1. The checklist is the same as S1, plus the cross-round comparison:
   the `site_id` in the two directories' `bootstrap-state.json` is the same (the same CPU cluster derives the same site
   identifier) and the `completed_tasks` sets are the same; the AWS-side installed-resource list has the same number of
   entries as S1 (no second set, and none missing); the `status --full` PASS count is the same as S1;
   the rerun `deploy --state-dir <STATE_DIR_SECOND>` of `BOOT-028` step 7 is strictly `NOOP`.

##### Verdict

- The five stages each execute once in the order 1→2→3→4→5, every command is waited to exit, and the driver stops at the
  first failure and reports a resumable stage number;
- The three images of both S1 and S5 satisfy the cold build: each has no `CACHED`, the base image is pulled, and the
  release-bound descriptor is built rather than reused; before both deployments the local caches/images and the site
  ECR tags do not exist (before S5 the ECR repositories themselves have already disappeared with the uninstall);
- The `state.json` of S2, S3 and S4 ends in `COMPLETED`, and the referenced `BOOT-024`/`025`/`027`
  checklists hold item by item under the originally approved policy; `skip` does not prove BOOT-027's final-snapshot
  retention;
- Every administrator command's non-zero exit must propagate as a stage failure, and an old `COMPLETED` journal may not
  override the exit code; the schema-2 stage receipts bind this run's target, attempt and original journal baseline,
  and success is not guessed from the latest mtime. One run's private sequence lock may not be reused concurrently;
- The S5 site and the S1 site agree on `site_id`, `completed_tasks`, AWS resource count and
  `status --full` PASS count; `status --full` is all PASS and the rerun is `NOOP`;
- Every command text S5 executes comes from the README: in the `readme` receipt, `readme_sha256`,
  `build_block_sha256` and `deploy_block_sha256` match the actual README and its two code blocks,
  `executed_lines` is exactly `make deploy-host-setup-online`, `. .venv/bin/activate`
  and the placeholder-substituted `gpu-fault-admin deploy`, `skipped_verification_lines` contains only
  verification lines, `venv_preexisted=false`, the environment variable names are within the allowlist, `PATH` is the
  operator PATH minus the venv directories, and the tool directory containing `gpu-fault-admin` is replaced by a
  stand-in (the receipt records only the kept/removed/stand-in counts and sha256);
  a README missing a step, or a flow depending on a condition the README does not state, is FAIL, and the driver may not
  be changed to make it pass;
- The underlying CPU/GPU EKS and HyperPod clusters are retained throughout; training jobs and nodes are untouched.

##### Evidence

`cases/GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-029/GF-REGIONAL-BOOT-029.json`: the driver-written
`<STATE_DIR>/acceptance/admin-lifecycle-sequence.json` (per-stage PASS/FAIL,
stage log sha256, each component's `cold_build`/descriptor/registry-reuse and base-image
proof, original journal binding, snapshot policy, unexecuted companions and each terminal `phase`;
ARNs, e-mail address and directory paths appear in it only as sha256;
S5 additionally has the `readme` receipt: the sha256 of the README and its two code blocks, `executed_lines` and
`skipped_verification_lines` -- in which ARNs, e-mail address and directories are replaced by `sha256:<digest>` --
the sha256 of the generated script, the pristine copy's source commit and baseline commit, whether a snapshot commit
was made, `venv_preexisted`, the kept environment variable names, the PATH kept/removed/stand-in counts and the sha256
of the kept string, and the attempt number) and its own sha256; the sha256 of each of the two `bootstrap-state.json`,
the remove/join/uninstall `state.json` files and the two `verification-report.json`; the boolean conclusion of whether
the `completed_tasks` sets are the same; the before/after difference in AWS resource counts; the PASS/FAIL counts of
both rounds of `status --full`. Cluster names, account numbers and repository names appear only as digests; per-stage
durations are kept only in the driver's private JSON and do not enter this document or the directory.

##### Known limitations

- The interrupted-resume and forced-failure rollback sub-scenarios of `BOOT-024`/`025`/`027`/`028` are not injected by
  the driver and remain governed by their own cases; `BOOT-026` (second deregistration and `deploy --gpu-cluster-arn`
  batch re-join) is not part of this sequence.
- The cold build is asserted for the single platform `linux/amd64` only. If the current buildx builder uses the
  `docker` driver, the base-image layers live in the daemon's image store and are unaffected by `docker builder prune`,
  so the `FROM` step may show no `extracting` line -- in that case the base image must be deleted manually before
  running S1/S5, otherwise the driver stops with
  "base image was not pulled".
- On a truly fresh site S1 has no resolvable `site_id`, so on the ECR side only the baseline check of precondition 6 is
  available; for reused clusters, `--previous-site-id` lets the driver resolve and clean up on its own.
- S1's mail confirmation requires a manual click or `--email-wait-minutes`; S5 has no wait parameter, its first attempt
  exits by deploy's own precheck while the subscription is PENDING, and after confirmation it resumes with `--stage 5`;
  the wait ceiling and the time to click do not enter the verdict.
- Every S5 attempt re-runs `make deploy-host-setup-online` (rebuilding the venv in a new pristine copy and fetching
  dependencies online); its duration counts towards that attempt; the README does not describe an offline bundle route,
  and S5 does not take one.

##### Cleanup

The chain ends here: `<STATE_DIR_SECOND>` is a freshly-deployed completed site and can serve directly as the isolated
site for later cases; `<STATE_DIR>` is history only and is not reused.

## 5. AUTH: Per-cluster credentials and identity anti-spoofing

The authorization requests in this group are issued from the GPU data plane through `dp_call` (section 3.2) and verify the control plane's authorization ladder.
Most requests are rejected or read-only; AUTH-008 creates a run-owned no-op command as the positive claim control,
and AUTH-016 involves an audited token rotation, so the group as a whole cannot be treated as a stateless change.

Code basis:
`src/gpu_fault/app/middleware/auth.py::install_regional_authorization`
(the 401/403 ladder and the header/payload cluster binding) and
`src/gpu_fault/app/authorization.py::ExplicitAuthorizationRegistry`
(classification of protected routes).

Every `/v1/regional/executors/claim` request that is **expected to reach the claim handler and return 200**
must also carry the current release's:

```python
from gpu_fault.regional_compatibility import CURRENT_REGIONAL_EXECUTOR_PROTOCOL_VERSION

claim_identity = {
    "executor_protocol_version": CURRENT_REGIONAL_EXECUTOR_PROTOCOL_VERSION,
```
