    `mutation_submitted_by_control_plane: false` and
    `requires_external_confirmation: true`
    (`src/gpu_fault/adapters/`);
  - **the executor log contains no Kubernetes write operation against that Job**;
  - an alert notification is received (advisory channel) stating that recovery has been delegated;
  - after writing that operation_id into `confirmed_adapter_operation_ids` and replaying,
    the step turns `SUCCEEDED` and details contain `externally_confirmed: true`
    (`:3305-3316`).
- Meaning of failure: with the profile at `DELEGATE` this system still touched the job → fail-closed is broken.
- Cleanup: delete the isolated test database, and confirm that the current site Profile's path, version and digest were unchanged throughout.

**Group D (positive acceptance of the runtime guard): a violating annotation makes the workload step `FAILED`**

- Positioning: accepts the **second line of enforcement** of the ⚠ paragraph in §2.0.1. Group A proves "a compliant configuration is let through",
  group D proves "a violating configuration is refused"; only together do the two groups show that the guard really reads the annotation
  -- group A alone cannot distinguish "read it and judged it compliant" from "never read it at all".
- Destructiveness: **low**. The guard runs before `_mark_terminating_pods()` and every patch,
  so this group produces no Kubernetes write operation against the training job;
  the only cost is a leftover `FAILED` incident/workflow.
  To avoid affecting real jobs, **use a one-off single-node Job**, not the group A PyTorchJob.
- Steps:
  1. Submit a one-off single-node Job (1 GPU is enough) and confirm that it is managed by this system
     (carrying `gpu-fault.io/managed=true` and `gpu-fault.io/attempt-id`).
  2. Put the violating annotation on it:
     `kubectl annotate job <name> -n <ns> \`
     `sagemaker.amazonaws.com/enable-job-auto-resume=true`.
     Read back to confirm it took effect.
  3. The profile stays at the default `OWN` / `gpu-fault-kubernetes-adapter` (**do not change the profile**;
     this is the key difference from group C: group C changes the profile but not the annotation,
     group D changes the annotation but not the profile).
  4. Inject XID 11 against the node hosting that Job to trigger a workflow containing `STOP_WORKLOADS`.
  5. Record the step result and details, then inspect the Job's `spec.suspend` and Pod UIDs.
- Verdict:
  - the `STOP_WORKLOADS` step is `FAILED`, with an error containing
    `enable-job-auto-resume is enabled`;
  - the step details contain `managed_job_recovery_workloads`, whose value lists **only** the
    `namespace/kind/name` of that violating workload;
  - details contain `required_annotation` =
    `sagemaker.amazonaws.com/enable-job-auto-resume`,
    `required_annotation_value` = `absent or false`,
    and `remediation_commands` (a directly copy-and-run `kubectl annotate … -`);
  - **the Job's `spec.suspend` is untouched and every Pod UID is unchanged** --
    proving that the guard took effect before any write operation;
  - the executor log contains no Kubernetes write operation against that Job.
  - **Mandatory strengthening**:
    after deleting the annotation, replay the same injection with a new record_id;
    the step turns to the normal path and runs through `RESTART_WORKLOAD`.
    Rationale: running only the main body cannot distinguish "the guard re-reads cluster state every time" from
    "the guard permanently blacklists that workload", and the latter would mean a job whose configuration has been fixed can never recover again.
- Coverage note: `RESTART_WORKLOAD` and `STOP_WORKLOADS` share the
  `_set_workloads()` entry point, and the unit tests already cover both by parametrisation
  (`tests/execution/test_kubernetes.py::test_kubernetes_refuses_workload_with_hyperpod_auto_resume`),
  so E2E only needs to verify one path.
- Meaning of failure: the step is not `FAILED`, or `spec.suspend` is modified → the runtime guard is broken,
  and a violating configuration would let this system and HyperPod write the same job simultaneously. **Blocks go-live.**
- Rollback: delete the one-off Job; confirm that no managed job carrying that annotation remains
  (go back to group B step 1 and re-check once).



  Group C must be executed on an isolated control plane with an independent database. Do not pause production workers, manually release production
  workflow leases, or overwrite the current site Profile.

### GF-REGIONAL-DESTR-014

> The current implementation uses an independent Agent recovery protocol that spans the reboot. Only after the independent
> invocation of the persisted recovery service/timer has reported ARMED bound to this Node UID, the original boot ID, the release and the runtime
> may the original Agent enablement link be disabled and injection begin. An ordinary transient timer does not constitute this proof.
> The current local tests are not a live pass; real execution still requires a full maintenance window and the original destructive approval.

**Two-node repair of the same job: one branch wraps up with a reboot after a known failure, the other keeps manual protection while its reboot outcome is unknown**

- Level: `destructive-provider-reboot`. Two real `BatchRebootClusterNodes`
  calls (one for node-b, one for node-c); the reboot switch stays at its default (enabled);
  **no warm spare is declared, and calling `BatchReplaceClusterNodes` is forbidden.**
- The reusable formal entry point is
  `scripts/e2e/regional/run_destr014_branch_exhaustion.py`. By default it only generates the
  plan; before execute it must read `DESTR-008=PASS` (chain: `010 → 001 → 002 → 009 →
  012 → 003 → 008 → 014`), and it requires the administrator to explicitly name the two fault
  nodes, their GPU PCI BDFs and the device file that is held on node-b:

  ```bash
  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/run_destr014_branch_exhaustion.py \
    --run-dir "${RUN_DIR}" --attempt 1 --plan \
    --cpu-kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-kubeconfig "${GPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-context "${GPU_EKS_CONTEXT}" \
    --namespace "${NAMESPACE}" --cluster-id "${CLUSTER_ID}" \
    --region "${AWS_REGION}" --site-file "${SITE_FILE}" \
    --hyperpod-cluster "${HYPERPOD_CLUSTER_NAME}" \
    --host-probe-image "${NODE_INSTALLER_IMAGE}" \
    --predecessor-evidence "${PREDECESSOR_EVIDENCE_DIR}" \
    --fault-node "${FAULT_NODE}" --fault-pci-bdf "${FAULT_PCI_BDF}" \
    --fault-device "${FAULT_DEVICE}" \
    --sibling-node "${SIBLING_NODE}" --sibling-pci-bdf "${SIBLING_PCI_BDF}" \
    --verify-max-attempts 6 --managed-recovery-timeout-seconds 600 \
    --variant unknown-reboot

  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/run_destr014_branch_exhaustion.py \
    --run-dir "${RUN_DIR}" --attempt 1 --execute \
    --confirm DESTR014_EXECUTE \
    --maintenance-window-end "${MAINTENANCE_WINDOW_END}" \
    --cpu-kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-kubeconfig "${GPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-context "${GPU_EKS_CONTEXT}" \
    --namespace "${NAMESPACE}" --cluster-id "${CLUSTER_ID}" \
    --region "${AWS_REGION}" --site-file "${SITE_FILE}" \
    --hyperpod-cluster "${HYPERPOD_CLUSTER_NAME}" \
    --host-probe-image "${NODE_INSTALLER_IMAGE}" \
    --predecessor-evidence "${PREDECESSOR_EVIDENCE_DIR}" \
    --fault-node "${FAULT_NODE}" --fault-pci-bdf "${FAULT_PCI_BDF}" \
    --fault-device "${FAULT_DEVICE}" \
    --sibling-node "${SIBLING_NODE}" --sibling-pci-bdf "${SIBLING_PCI_BDF}" \
    --verify-max-attempts 6 --managed-recovery-timeout-seconds 600 \
    --variant unknown-reboot
  ```

  `--fault-node` is node-b (XID 46 → `RESET_GPU`, escalated in place to a reboot and then wrapped up),
  `--sibling-node` is node-c (XID 79 → `RESTART_NODE`; the Agent does not come back after the reboot,
  no proof of action completion can be obtained, the record stays `BLOCKED / NEEDS_OPERATOR`, and no
  replacement is appended);
  `--fault-device` is the `/dev/nvidiaN` on node-b that corresponds to
  `--fault-pci-bdf`. `--verify-max-attempts` is written into the
  **executor** env window; `--managed-recovery-timeout-seconds` is written into the **control-plane**
  env window (`control_plane_env_window.py`, landing on `gpu-fault-control-worker` -- the managed
  recovery window is read by the control plane, which derives the wait ceiling of
  `RESTART_NODE`/`REPLACE_NODE` from it; the executor does not read it, setting it on the executor has
  no effect whatsoever, and the control plane would wait the default 1800 s). The latter must not be
  lower than the default step timeout of 600 s, and twice its value must not exceed the job lifetime,
  otherwise the control plane refuses to start and the runner refuses already at `configure`.
  `--variant` currently has a single value, `unknown-reboot`; "no new Agent heartbeat" is no longer
  treated as a known failure that executes a replacement.
  The administrator may also run only this case in the selective mode of §2.3; in that case
  DESTR-008 is recorded as `SKIPPED_BY_OPERATOR`, the verdict of this case is still judged by every
  assertion in this section, but it must not be used to claim that the "Warm spare" stage has passed
  in full, nor can it serve as the predecessor of a later formal case.

  The recovery helper and the private journal live under `/var/lib/gpu-fault-acceptance/`; their
  persisted service/timer live under `/etc/systemd/system/`. `OnBootSec`, `OnCalendar` and
  `Persistent=true` make recovery independent of the runner, the probe Pod and the Agent venv.
  The original enablement link is preserved by inode; recovery only permits the Agent of the original
  runtime and may not reset, reboot, switch to a warm spare or restart the job. The fixed recovery
  time and the expiry must fall inside the approved window and cannot be extended.
  If automatic recovery fires before the scenario completes, this case FAILs; if the host comes back
  only after the recovery deadline, manual handling is required.
  Manual handling is performed by the `--release` mode of the same runner (it generates no plan and
  only reads this attempt's own plan/journal/result records):

  ```bash
  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/run_destr014_branch_exhaustion.py \
    --run-dir "${RUN_DIR}" --attempt 1 --site-profile "${SITE_PROFILE}" \
    --release --confirm RELEASE_GF_REGIONAL_DESTR_014_HOLD
  ```

  It performs the following in order and is re-runnable: first verify identity (the live release id
  and the Node UIDs of both nodes must match the plan; boot ids may differ; any mismatch is refused);
  for each node whose boot id has changed, run
  `gpu-fault-admin submit-remediation --disposition confirm-node-action --node <node>`
  (confirming the reboot outcome from the boot-id change and the Agent-return evidence; a node with
  no pending action -- the fault node of the known-failure branch -- is refused by the product and
  recorded as skipped); `submit-remediation --disposition restore`
  lets the product initiate the restore for that incident itself (the record stays BLOCKED after
  confirmation until the product's restore and workflow-reconcile complete; when the incident no
  longer has any node it quarantined itself, the product refuses, this is recorded as skipped, and the
  next step recovers via the owner); after that restore workflow ends, run a validated restore for
  every node still quarantined via its current owner incident (a node taken over by the support-after
  incident, whose owner is ESCALATED, goes through the same validation-first restore workflow);
  `workflow-reconcile --incident-id` wraps up that record and the records under the follow-up
  incident (it only qualifies once the incident is RECOVERED and has a validated restore successor,
  which is why it comes after restore); delete the drill PyTorchJob; run `disarm-holder` on a freshly
  created probe Pod; close the executor and control-plane env windows from their respective records;
  finally close the drill incident with the node-quarantine evidence. The report is appended to
  `cases/GF-REGIONAL-DESTR-014/destr014-release.json`;
  if any step fails or any incident remains open it exits 1 and lists the residue. The manual
  equivalent is still the three admin verbs above plus the two window-closing helpers; until the
  record is wrapped up, new faults on nodes under its name open no workflow, and the release preflight
  `workflow_safety` refuses to release.
  Re-running an existing attempt can only continue the cleanup: it must prove that the timer/service/
  pending jobs have stopped, that the original Agent is restored and that the probe is gone before it
  closes the journal, and it produces no second PASS. The old unbound
  `restore-agent`/`disable-agent-restart` no longer operate on services and must be reconciled manually.
  However, if the boot ID bound by the original journal has been superseded by a new boot of the node
  (the sibling has rebooted and the current boot ID differs from it), that unfinished journal no
  longer owns any host state on the current boot -- the installer has rebuilt the Node Agent and the
  probe's new-boot decision table has retired the old boot's host state --
  so the resume is no longer refused as an "identity change"; instead the old journal is moved to
  `<stem>.rebooted-<run id>.json` as an archive, this attempt is rerun from scratch, and its lineage
  (archive path, original run_id, phase, boot_id,
  host_request) is kept in the new journal's `run.retired_journals` for cleanup and verdict evidence;
  a journal whose boot ID is unchanged (node not rebooted) or which is already recorded as lost still
  refuses to resume. Likewise, an unfinished journal whose boot ID is unchanged but which provably
  never touched the host (no `host_*` record of any kind -- no `host_binding`/`host_ack`/`host_request`
  -- none of `holder_armed`, `agent_disabled`, `injection_started`, `physical_outcome_unknown` set in
  `run`, `incident_id` and `marker` empty -- i.e. the attempt died at the window-opening step before
  arming anything) likewise owns no host state on the current boot: the old journal is moved to
  `<stem>.abandoned-<run id>.json` as an archive, this attempt is rerun from scratch, the lineage is
  likewise recorded in `run.retired_journals` with `reason: never armed on the host`; the
  window-opened flags (`env_opened`, `control_env_opened`) do not prevent retirement, since the two
  windows each have their own record and guard and are closed through them. Any journal that has ever
  armed anything on the host is still refused under the original rule.

  When the node comes back with a **new boot ID** (the product's `RESTART_NODE` has really rebooted
  it), the probe no longer requires the original runtime identity to match item by item -- when the
  installer returns it rewrites the unit, the enablement link and the venv, and the old boot's ctime
  can never reappear -- but judges file by file according to the ownership of the enablement link:
  - The link has been rebuilt by the installer at the standard path (target is the installer unit,
    any inode) and the Agent is `enabled`+`active`: record `restored_by=reboot-installer`, go
    straight to `RESTORED`, do not touch that link, and only reclaim the probe's own residue (timer,
    service, helper copy and the 45 s start-limit drop-in; after deleting the drop-in run
    `daemon-reload` first, then allow any subsequent Agent start), without waiting for the recovery
    time -- the start limit must not outlive its purpose;
  - The link is missing: still restore only at the recovery time using the preserved original-inode
    copy and start the same Agent in a bounded way, exactly as recovery on the original boot;
  - The link is neither the original inode nor the installer link: never touch it; at expiry mark
    `EXPIRED`, reclaim the probe residue and hand over to manual handling.
  The expiry and recovery-time decisions are made before any identity check that can only hold on the
  original boot; the strict identity check on the original boot is unchanged (a rebuilt link or a
  drifted unit is always refused). While the node is NotReady no exec is issued to it: the persistent
  timer runs independently on the node itself, and the runner only talks to the probe again after
  `wait_node_ready`. The recovery record's `boot_id_observed`,
  `restored_by` and `retired` are returned with the `status`/`restore`/`cleanup` reports, and the
  controller journal distinguishes the two kinds of recovery as `RESTORED` / `RESTORED_BY_REBOOT`.
  Detailed resource ownership, cross-reboot conditions and the lost-contact boundary are described in
  [DESTR-014 Recovery Safeguard](../components/destr014-recovery-safeguard.md).

  Each of the two environment variables may only be changed with its baseline-carrying window helper
  (one for the executor, one for the control plane);
  **do not `kubectl set env` by hand and rely on memory to wrap up**:

  ```bash
  # Read-only: report the current value of both variables on the Deployment and on every ready replica
  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/executor_env_window.py \
    --site-profile "${SITE_PROFILE}" \
    --baseline "${STATE_DIR}/executor-env-window.json"

  # Open the window (record the baseline first, then change, then poll until every ready replica has the new value)
  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/executor_env_window.py \
    --site-profile "${SITE_PROFILE}" \
    --baseline "${STATE_DIR}/executor-env-window.json" \
    --open --confirm OPEN_EXECUTOR_ENV_WINDOW \
    --set GPU_FAULT_GPU_CLIENT_VERIFY_MAX_ATTEMPTS=6

  # The managed recovery window lives on the control plane: open the control-plane window separately (this rolls every control-worker replica;
  # it must be opened before injection and closed after the workflow reaches a terminal state)
  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/control_plane_env_window.py \
    --site-profile "${SITE_PROFILE}" \
    --baseline "${STATE_DIR}/control-plane-env-window.json" \
    --open --confirm OPEN_CONTROL_PLANE_ENV_WINDOW \
    --set GPU_FAULT_HYPERPOD_MANAGED_RECOVERY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=600

  # Close the windows only after the physical outcome has been reconciled and the shared recovery no longer holds an operator hold.
  # Do not run these restore commands just because the runner has finished or the workflow is BLOCKED.
  # Restore exactly per the baseline: variables unset at the factory are deleted, not written back to their default values.
  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/executor_env_window.py \
    --site-profile "${SITE_PROFILE}" \
    --baseline "${STATE_DIR}/executor-env-window.json" \
    --close --confirm CLOSE_EXECUTOR_ENV_WINDOW
  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/control_plane_env_window.py \
    --site-profile "${SITE_PROFILE}" \
    --baseline "${STATE_DIR}/control-plane-env-window.json" \
    --close --confirm CLOSE_CONTROL_PLANE_ENV_WINDOW
  ```

  The executor helper recognises exactly one variable name, `GPU_FAULT_GPU_CLIENT_VERIFY_MAX_ATTEMPTS`;
  the control-plane helper's whitelist is the six timing variables of `DESTR-018` (see §DESTR-018).
  Both are hard-coded in the scripts; they are not tools for "changing arbitrary env on a live
  Deployment". Their shape is the same as
  `scripts/e2e/regional/synthetic_replacement_route.py`: opening/closing only counts as done once
  **every ready replica reports the same value**; a `kubectl rollout status` return is not the verdict
  condition. Compressing these two values merely shortens the waits from about 5 minutes and 30 minutes
  to about 30 seconds and 10 minutes; it changes no verdict semantics.
- Purpose: the unit layer already pins the branch ladder and the counts
  (`src/gpu_fault/execution/branch_escalation.py`); what live acceptance must add are the three things
  the unit tests cannot prove:
  1. The shape and timing with which a real Node Agent makes `RESET_GPU` fail **at the RESET step** --
     the barrier (`src/gpu_fault/adapters/node_action/barriers.py`) records
     `clients are still active` as WAITING and increments
     `gpu_client_quiesce_attempt` (the pre-commit client re-check refuses the reset, the Agent does
     not execute the reset, the ledger has no `RESET_GPU` row) or `gpu_reset_commit_attempt` (the
     committed reset is refused), until `GPU_FAULT_GPU_CLIENT_VERIFY_MAX_ATTEMPTS` is reached and it
     becomes FAILED; the verdict accepts both shapes;
  2. When the node returns to Ready but the new Agent identity/completion confirmation is missing, the
     timeout proves only that the wait reached its ceiling; it cannot prove that the physical action
     failed or stopped. The step keeps its outcome-unknown details, the workflow wraps up as
     `BLOCKED / NEEDS_OPERATOR`, and it must not continue to `REPLACE_NODE`;
  3. While the sibling branch's outcome is unknown, the join (`RESTART_WORKLOAD`) is never executed,
     the job is **not** restarted, the restart budget is untouched, and the already wrapped-up node-b
     returns to scheduling as usual.
  Any drift in any of these would re-launch a job that should have been handed to operations, or leave
  the workflow never closing.
- Preconditions:
  1. `DESTR-003` and `DESTR-008` have finished and have returned the spare via `--release`:
     this case requires that the cluster contains **no** node carrying the `gpu-fault.io/spare` label;
     `preflight_errors` lists any leftover spare labels and refuses to execute.
     Keep this isolation premise to prevent the fixture from being mixed with the warm-spare
     scenario; the unknown-outcome direction here must stop before `REPLACE_NODE` is selected, and
     "zero warm spares make the replacement fail" is no longer a live pass condition.
  2. Two idle GPU nodes node-b and node-c in the same instance group with the same instance type,
     8 GPUs each; neither hosts a controller or an executor arbiter replica
     (both `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES` and the reboot will hit them). The runner's read-only preflight
     shares the same placement read with DESTR-015: it lists the running (not terminating)
     `gpu-fault-cluster-executor`, `gpu-fault-completion-watcher` and
     `gpu-fault-node-installer-reconciler` Pods on both nodes, plus the nodes hosting every endpoint
     of `k8s-app=kube-dns` in kube-system; if either target node hosts one of those replicas, or the
     two nodes together hold all kube-dns endpoints (rebooting the two in succession would cut cluster
     DNS), `preflight_errors` refuses to execute and the placement snapshot is written to
     `preflight.json`.
  3. On the executor side `GPU_FAULT_ENABLE_HYPERPOD_ADAPTER=true`,
     `GPU_FAULT_ENABLE_HYPERPOD_SPARE_FAILOVER=true`,
     `GPU_FAULT_CLUSTER_EXECUTOR_REMOTE_STATE=true`,
     `GPU_FAULT_ENABLE_NODE_ACTION_ADAPTER=true`,
     `GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_HYPERPOD_REBOOT=true` (default),
     `GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_HYPERPOD_REPLACE=false` (invariant);
     HyperPod `NodeRecovery=None`.
  4. The windows have been opened with the helpers above: both variables read 6 and 600 on every ready
     replica.
  5. The site's `GPU_FAULT_MULTI_NODE_AGGREGATION_WINDOW_SECONDS` is large enough that the two XIDs
     the runner writes in succession still land in the same job DAG; the runner prints the current
     value in the plan.
  6. No synthetic replacement route is needed: the unknown-outcome direction here must not append
     `REPLACE_NODE`, and `GPU_FAULT_ENABLE_SYNTHETIC_REPLACEMENT_TESTS` should stay unset.
- Steps:
  1. Record the full baseline of both nodes: HyperPod instance ID, EC2 instance ID,
     Kubernetes labels/taints/`unschedulable`, the `boot_id` and generation registered by the Node
     Agent, Node Agent ledger row count, total cluster node count, CloudTrail window start; confirm
     that neither node carries the `gpu-fault.io/quarantined` taint or an ownership annotation,
     otherwise `FAIL/INCOMPLETE` -- a dirty baseline must not be recorded as PASS.
  2. Use `managed_workload_fixture` to render a two-replica PyTorchJob, 8 GPUs per replica, pinned
     to node-b and node-c respectively, and submit it through `gpu-training-submit`
     (`--restart-budget 1`); confirm Running, a healthy NCCL all-reduce, and a source attempt
     observation containing 16 unique GPU UUIDs.
  3. The runner uses `host_probe_fixture.py` to start one host probe on each node
     (`scripts/e2e/regional/probes/destr014_node_probe.py`):
     - node-c: use the persisted recovery fixture; first obtain the `ARMED` proof bound to the
       original Node/boot/release/runtime, then remove the original Agent enablement link; the
       current Agent is not stopped, it is merely prevented from auto-starting after the reboot.
       The fixed recovery deadline cannot be extended, and the ownership of the original link inode
       and of the recovery service/timer must be preserved; the old unbound disable/restore commands
       and transient timers are no longer used as substitutes;
     - node-b: `arm-holder` -- watch the Node Agent ledger
       (`/var/lib/gpu-fault/node-actions.db`); as soon as this drill's successful
       `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS` row appears, open `--fault-device` in a `systemd-run` transient unit
       and wait for SIGTERM; the holder is a **host process** detached from the Pod cgroup, because
       QUIESCE has already stopped kubelet and a Pod cannot start; it carries a `--max-hold-seconds`
       ceiling.
     Both probes answer over `kubectl exec`, so they only **arrange** the actions and do not wait
     for results on the channel; node-c's current Agent keeps serving, so the channel is unaffected.
  4. Write XID 79 to node-c first, then write XID 46 to node-b within the aggregation window
     (`destructive_node_probe.py write-xid79 / write-xid46`, each with its own BDF,
     marker and drill id). The order must not be reversed: hitting node-c first lets its reboot
     start early, so node-c's wait is already running while node-b is wrestling with the holder.
  5. Observe the control plane: both XIDs land in the same `workflow_request_id`, `dag_enabled=true`,
     the shared `STOP_WORKLOADS` has `node_ids` exactly `[node-b, node-c]`;
     the node-b branch is `MARK_UNSCHEDULABLE → QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES →
     VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS → RESET_GPU …`, the node-c branch is
     `MARK_UNSCHEDULABLE → RESTART_NODE → VALIDATE_* → RESTORE_SCHEDULING`,
     and the join is `RESTART_WORKLOAD`.
  6. node-b: `RESET_GPU` is WAITING repeatedly, `details.gpu_reset_commit_attempt`
     climbs to 6 and then FAILED, with an error containing `clients are still active`; the remaining
     steps of the original branch enter `superseded_step_indexes`, and
     `[RESTART_NODE, VALIDATE_GPU, VALIDATE_HOST, VALIDATE_FABRIC,
     RESTORE_SCHEDULING]` is appended, with the join now depending on the new branch tail.
     `RESTART_NODE` submits a real reboot (CloudTrail `BatchRebootClusterNodes` with `Username` equal
     to the executor role); the holder disappears with the reboot; the Node Agent re-registers with a
     **new** `boot_id`; all three `VALIDATE_*` and `RESTORE_SCHEDULING` are SUCCEEDED, node-b has no
     taint and is schedulable.
  7. node-c: `RESTART_NODE` submits a real reboot (the second `BatchRebootClusterNodes`);
     the node returns to `Ready=True`, but the control plane **never** receives a new `boot_id`
     (the Agent has been disabled); the step stays WAITING until
     `GPU_FAULT_HYPERPOD_MANAGED_RECOVERY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (compressed to 600 s by the control-plane
     window) and then keeps the FAILED step together with `step_waiting_timeout_seconds`, and it must
     also carry normalised unknown-outcome evidence such as
     `outcome_unknown/manual_confirmation_required`.
     No `REPLACE_NODE` is appended, node-c does not perform restore-scheduling, and neither Ready nor a
     CloudTrail-received request may be used to infer that the physical action ended safely.
  8. Wait until every non-join step has settled or been retired: workflow `BLOCKED`,
     `blocked_kind=NEEDS_OPERATOR`; `branch_escalation_counts == {node-b: 1}`,
     node-c has no added rung. `exhausted_branch_ids` contains exactly node-c's branch;
     `RESTART_WORKLOAD` was never started; `workflow_lifetime_exceeded` was not triggered.
  9. Check the job and the budget: the two Pod UIDs of the PyTorchJob are the same as in step 2 or
     have disappeared with `STOP_WORKLOADS`, **no new attempt**; the restart budget reading equals the
     baseline; `RESTART_WORKLOAD` has no `details.notification_context`.
  10. Check quarantine and escalation: the incident is `QUARANTINED` or `ESCALATED`; node-c stays
      cordoned and carries the `gpu-fault.io/quarantined` taint whose value is the first 24
      characters of `sha256(incident_id)`; the manual-reconciliation reason and the original command
      identity are preserved; there is **no** new reboot / replace workflow under that incident.
      node-b returning to scheduling must not release node-c's protection.
  11. **Core disproof assertion**: query CloudTrail over the window recorded in step 1:
      `BatchRebootClusterNodes` **exactly twice**,
      `BatchReplaceClusterNodes` and `BatchDeleteClusterNodes` both `[]`
      (enumerated verb by verb, no contains); the `list-cluster-nodes` total node count equals the
      baseline.
  12. The `BLAST-001` comparison is still IDENTICAL.
  13. The plan, pre-injection, post-terminal and post-cleanup snapshots are bound to the same
      release-state and key CPU/GPU Deployment template digests; any drift fails closed.
- Verdict: `scenario_verdict=PASS` may be recorded only if steps 5-13 are all satisfied;
  while the physical outcome and the cleanup are not yet reconciled the public verdict must be
  `BLOCKED`, and the formal sequence must not continue.
  Any of the following is a blocker:
  `RESTART_WORKLOAD` was executed or the job shows a new attempt; `BatchRebootClusterNodes`
  is not exactly twice; any `BatchReplaceClusterNodes` / `BatchDeleteClusterNodes` appears;
  node-c is still WAITING indefinitely after the bounded wait, or an unknown outcome is treated as an
  ordinary failure and replacement/restore continues;
  node-b's `RESET_GPU` fails before `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS`
  (meaning the holder was raised too early -- the round is invalid rather than a defect);
  `branch_escalation_counts` is not equal to `{node-b: 1}`.
  Another class of blocker is a **product defect rather than a valid BLOCKED**: the `RESTART_NODE`
  escalated from node-b, when the executor re-checks the shared STOP receipt before submitting, is
  refused because node-c's boot id has changed as a result of the product's own submitted, not yet
  confirmed reboot (`reason=STOP_OWNERSHIP_DRIFT`,
  `ownership_check_boundary=EXECUTOR_PRE_SUBMIT`, `node_action_not_started=true`),
  so node-b is quarantined without ever rebooting. The receipt re-check rule is: for a node under the
  same receipt that is not the target of this action, if its latest `RESTART_NODE` is still WAITING,
  carries a real provider submission (`action=reboot`, `requires_external_confirmation`,
  `submitted_nodes` complete for every target, not a cached duplicate submission) and the
  `stop_receipt_sha256` of its `stop_reboot_authorization_v1` equals the current receipt digest and is
  bound to that node's UID and the receipt boot id,
  then any new boot id on that node is treated as the outcome of that reboot rather than drift; when
  no such record exists, it is bound to a different receipt digest, the record has terminated (FAILED
  or an unconfirmed SUCCEEDED), the node UID has changed, or the node itself is the target of this
  action, it is still refused as drift. node-b's reboot must still be submittable after node-c has
  re-registered with a new boot id; otherwise this case records FAIL rather than BLOCKED.

**Additional data-plane verdict** (extra observations when run on a real cluster):
in node-b's ledger the successful `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS` row is followed by several failed
`RESET_GPU` rows and no successful one, and `kernel_reset_journal` has no reset record for that BDF
-- node-b's GPU **was not reset**, only quiesced; the start/end times of the holder's transient unit
fall after the successful VERIFY row and before the first failed RESET row. On node-c,
`systemctl is-enabled gpu-fault-node-agent.service` reads `disabled` after the reboot and
`is-active` reads `inactive`; `/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id` has changed while the `boot_id`
recorded by the control plane has not, which shows that the window lacking Agent confirmation was
observed -- not a proof of physical failure.
The installer reconciler may reinstall and re-`enable` the Agent after the step's wait ceiling
(`sibling_reboot_proof.restored_by=reboot-installer`); that is product self-healing and does not
change the verdict, provided the control plane received no new `boot_id` within the wait ceiling.
This direction must not use a warm-spare-shortage alert as a success condition, because no
replacement should ever be attempted.

- Cleanup (`finally`, fixed order):
  1. `disarm-holder`: stop the transient unit and confirm the holder process no longer exists (the
     reboot has usually already removed it; this step is an idempotent confirmation).
  2. Restore the same Agent using the original persisted recovery journal: on the original boot verify
     the original runtime/inode and a fresh heartbeat; on a new boot accept the installer-restored
     Agent or restore from the original-inode copy per the rules above, and write the observed boot
     ID and `restored_by` into `sibling_reboot_proof`;
     confirm the recovery service/timer/pending job have stopped and the drop-in has been reclaimed
     with the probe.
  3. `operator_hold` has two parts, listed one by one in `hold_reasons`: **the product side still
     holds the recovery** (workflow not terminal or `BLOCKED/NEEDS_OPERATOR`, remote command not
     terminal, outcome unresolved -- the same rule as the supervised recovery on the CPU side) and
     **node-c's physical outcome is unproven** (no new boot ID observed, Agent not restored and not
     restorable, node not back). While either remains, do not lift node-c's quarantine, do not delete
     the protected workload, and do not close a configuration window that would change the recovery
     execution environment; preserve the original command, workflow, watchdog and diagnostic
     evidence, and clean up only the holder/probe that is permitted and provably belongs to this run;
     a direct `restore-quiesce`, taint deletion or annotation deletion is forbidden. The public
     verdict is `BLOCKED`.
  4. Only when both parts are clear at the same time -- the product has let go, and node-c is back
     with a new boot ID with its Agent `enabled`+`active` per the recovery record -- is the physical
     outcome considered reconciled; the runner then waits for quiescence along the product's
     supervised path, deletes the test workload, restores from quarantine and closes the windows. A
     cleanup-continuation rerun re-reads the product-side hold: after manual reconciliation on the
     product side, when the CLOSED recovery record proves the Agent restore on the new boot, the
     continuation completes the remaining recovery but produces no new scenario PASS. While the
     product side still holds, the runner does not approve the reconciliation on its own.
  Unreconciled state, lost supervision or residue can never issue a full PASS.
- Known limitations:
  - The original obligation "escalate to REPLACE_NODE after a known reboot failure, exhaust zero warm
    spares, FAILED overall" is kept in a separate deterministic contract and requires explicit
    failure proof such as `node_action_not_started`.
    `tests/regional/test_acceptance_recovery_outcomes.py` distinguishes recoverable, exhausted and
    unknown; this disabled-Agent live drill provides no proof of a known failure or of a real
    warm-spare replacement.
  - This case only proves the unknown-outcome classification under the approved 600-second wait
    value; it does not prove that the default wait is reasonable, nor does it guarantee that the whole
    formal acceptance chain can finish without manual reconciliation.
  - `disable` without `--now` relies on "the reboot definitely happens": if node-c's reboot is not
    submitted, the failsafe timer re-`enable`s the Agent at expiry and the round is recorded
    `INCOMPLETE`.
  - The exactly-two `BatchRebootClusterNodes` assertion assumes no other case runs in parallel within
    this window; running `COLLECT-004` / `COLLECT-015` in the same window pollutes the count.

### GF-REGIONAL-DESTR-013

**Hard-constraint disproof: `NodeRecovery` is always `None`, and no `BatchReplaceClusterNodes` occurs at any point**

- Level: `non-destructive` (pure disproof, produces no change).
- The reusable read-only entry point is
  `scripts/e2e/regional/audit_destr013_replacement_invariant.py`.
  A UTC time window covering the complete destructive stage must be supplied explicitly, and it must
  read `HA-004=PASS`:

  ```bash
  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/audit_destr013_replacement_invariant.py \
    --run-dir "${RUN_DIR}" --attempt 1 \
    --cpu-kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-kubeconfig "${GPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-context "${GPU_EKS_CONTEXT}" \
    --namespace "${NAMESPACE}" --region "${AWS_REGION}" \
    --hyperpod-cluster "${HYPERPOD_CLUSTER_NAME}" \
    --executor-role-arn "${GPU_EXECUTOR_ROLE_ARN}" \
    --window-start "${ACCEPTANCE_WINDOW_START}" \
    --window-end "${ACCEPTANCE_WINDOW_END}"
  ```

  The audit performs only Kubernetes get/exec, AWS describe/simulation/CloudTrail lookup, an STS
  identity read inside the executor
  and local manifest parsing; it modifies no cluster, IAM or provider resource.
  `--cpu-kubeconfig` (or `GPU_FAULT_CONTROL_KUBECONFIG`/`CPU_KUBECONFIG`; `--cpu-context`
  optional) is now required: the audit reads
  `GPU_FAULT_ENABLE_SYNTHETIC_REPLACEMENT_TESTS` on every stable Ready API replica, and any replica
  still carrying that variable (a synthetic-replacement-route window that DESTR-003/008 did not close)
  is a FAIL. `--run-dir` is not just the evidence destination: the run timestamps of every evidence
  record of the earlier cases under `cases/GF-REGIONAL-DESTR-*` must fall within
  `--window-start/--window-end`, otherwise the window is rejected. Unreadable JSON, illegal or
  timezone-less time fields that are present, or an existing case with no time evidence at all can
  never be silently skipped; this audit's own older output does not count as proof of predecessor
  coverage.
  When the window end is less than 15 minutes from now (CloudTrail delivery lag) it refuses by
  default; passing `--accept-recent-window` continues the collection but records only
  `INCOMPLETE/FAIL`, `cloudtrail_provisional: true` and `formal_sequence_satisfied: false`, exits
  with code 1, and cannot advance the formal acceptance sequence. If the window contains no
  successful `BatchRebootClusterNodes` issued against the target cluster, from the target
  Region/account, by the actual executor role (positive control), it likewise refuses -- an empty set
  cannot distinguish "the cluster was quiet" from "wrong region/time period" -- unless
  `--expect-no-reboots` declares that no reboot case ran in this round (declaring it and then finding
  reboot events is likewise FAIL).
  The forbidden verbs are still checked conservatively across the SageMaker events in the region and
  are not ignored because the actor differs. Duplicate/incomplete pagination and missing or illegal
  event identities all fail, and the evidence does not save the raw CloudTrail credential context.
- Target binding: the CLI's HyperPod name and Region must map uniquely to the CPU durable registry;
  its EKS ARN must simultaneously match the HyperPod orchestrator, the HTTPS endpoint/CA of the
  actual GPU kubeconfig, and EKS DescribeCluster. The actual ServiceAccount IRSA, the Pod's
  cluster/Region, the web-identity credential method and the STS identity must match the declared
  role.
  The images, component digests and Executor pins of the fully submitted release, and the
  release/cluster identity of HA-004, must also agree; any replica not Ready, a rollout in progress,
  or UID/registration drift during the read all fail.
  Stop when read-only permissions are missing; never escalate privileges automatically. The report is
  written to disk as FAIL first; after command supervision is lost, probing stops and recovery is
  demanded.
- Purpose: carries the acceptance of the §2.0 hard constraints, **replacing the retired
  `DESTR-004`**.
  It does not verify "whether replace works" -- that action does not exist in this system;
  it verifies "that the action indeed does not exist, and that no configuration can make it appear".
- Positioning: **a read-only audit at the end of the stage "failover and constraint disproof"**.
  This case produces no change; HA-003/004 in the same stage still contain real failover or recovery
  actions and must respect their own maintenance windows.
  This case should run after the stages "destructive capability acceptance (including non-destructive
  fail-closed negative cases)" and "Warm spare", because it must cover the **full period** of
  CloudTrail for all earlier destructive cases.
- Scope: this case only disproves the **node-level** constraints (constraints 1 and 2).
  The **task-level** constraint (constraint 3, disabling HyperPod auto-resume) is carried by
  `DESTR-012` group B (configuration disproof) and group D (runtime guard live test);
  only the three together form the complete acceptance of the §2.1 hard constraints.
- Steps:
  1. **Cluster side**: `DescribeCluster` confirms `NodeRecovery == "None"`.
     Record the raw output (that field alone may be excerpted).
  2. **Switch side**: use the installed component interpreter to read only the following restricted
     switches from every executor replica, without exporting the full environment:
     - `GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_HYPERPOD_REPLACE=false`
     - `GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_WITH_AUTOMATIC_NODE_RECOVERY` unset or `false`
     - `GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_HYPERPOD_MUTATION` unset
     All three agree on **all replicas** (inconsistency between replicas is itself a FAIL).
  3. **IAM side**: check whether the executor's role holds
     `sagemaker:BatchReplaceClusterNodes`.
     Expected: **not held**; if it is still held, this case is a direct `FAIL` and blocks go-live.
  4. **CloudTrail side**: query with a time window **covering the full period of the stages
     "destructive capability acceptance (including non-destructive fail-closed negative cases)" and
     "Warm spare"**,
     enumerating the verbs (`BatchReplaceClusterNodes`, `ReplaceClusterNodes`),
     **without contains** -- otherwise read-only calls such as `ListClusterNodes` pollute the result
     and make the assertion permanently non-empty (a trap `BOOT-005` has already stepped on).
  5. **Manifest side**: confirm that `cluster-action-executor.yaml` explicitly sets
     `GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_HYPERPOD_REPLACE=false` and does not contain the legacy
     `GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_HYPERPOD_MUTATION`; the deployment kustomize/patch chain must not override it
     either.
- Verdict:
  - Step 1 is `None`;
  - Step 2: all three items satisfied and consistent across replicas;
  - Step 4 result is `[]`;
  - Step 5: no override.
  - Step 3 must be an explicit or implicit deny; if the executor role holds
    `sagemaker:BatchReplaceClusterNodes`, direct `FAIL`.
  - The two items merged from the former `DESTR-011`: reboot can still be enabled independently
    (every executor replica has `GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_HYPERPOD_REBOOT=true`; disabling replace must not
    drag reboot down with it); the report records the number of executor replicas and the per-replica
    `ALLOW_HYPERPOD_REPLACE=false`; writing only "none found enabled" does not constitute evidence.
- Meaning of failure:
  - Step 1 not `None` → the cluster is outside the supported scope and **must not be onboarded**.
    Blocks go-live.
  - Step 4 non-empty → someone called replace; regardless of the caller it is a constraint breach.
    The caller and the trigger path must be identified before continuing. Blocks go-live.
  - Step 2 inconsistent across replicas → configuration delivery is unreliable, which is worse than
    a single wrong value.
- Note (must be written into the report):
  the `[]` conclusion of this case **covers only the time window it queried**.
  It cannot prove "it will not be called in the future either" -- that needs the configuration-class
  evidence of steps 2/3/5 to support it.
  Without any one of the three kinds of evidence the conclusion is incomplete.


#### Execution time window

Record a common `ACCEPTANCE_WINDOW_START` before the stage "destructive capability acceptance
(including non-destructive fail-closed negative cases)" begins, and record
`ACCEPTANCE_WINDOW_END` before this case queries. The CloudTrail query must cover the complete window
between these two timestamps; do not use historical fixed dates from the documentation or "the last
30 minutes".

**Query shape for step 4**: `aws cloudtrail lookup-events`
with `--lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=<verb>`,
**enumerating verb by verb**; the verb table is
`BatchReplaceClusterNodes`, `ReplaceClusterNodes`,
`BatchDeleteClusterNodes`, `DeleteCluster`, `UpdateCluster`
(the last three are incidental corroboration for constraints 1/2, are not part of the original
verdict, and are listed separately).
A single `lookup-events` call spans at most 90 days; this window is far smaller,
but note that it is **sharded by region**, so `--region us-west-2` must be explicit.
**Do not use any contains/prefix matching** --
read-only verbs such as `ListClusterNodes` and `DescribeClusterNode` pollute the result
and make the assertion permanently non-empty (`BOOT-005` already stepped on this).

**Evidence-capture requirement for step 2**: it must be taken **per replica**, not just from the
Deployment's `spec.template` -- the latter is the desired value,
while what this case must prove is "the value actually in effect on every running replica",
and the two disagree while a rolling upgrade is incomplete.
Also, among the three switches, the passing criterion for `GPU_FAULT_ALLOW_WITH_AUTOMATIC_NODE_RECOVERY`
is "**unset** or `false`",
so the evidence capture must distinguish "value is false" from "key does not exist";
when `env | grep` finds nothing, that must not be judged FAIL outright.


### GF-REGIONAL-DESTR-015

**Two nodes of the same job faulting in the same window: two-branch parallel GPU reset, single join restarts the job**

- Level: `destructive`. Each of the two nodes performs one real `RESET_GPU` (through the executor and
  the Node Agent, including quiesce/restore); **no reboot, no warm spare declared,
  no provider API called at all**.
- The reusable formal entry point is
  `scripts/e2e/regional/run_destr015_parallel_branch_join.py`. By default it only generates the
  plan; before execute it must read `DESTR-012=PASS` (chain: `010 → 001 → 002 → 009 →
  012 → 015`), and it requires the administrator to explicitly name the two nodes; the GPU PCI BDF
  defaults to the first GPU enumerated by each node's host probe, or can be given with
  `--pci-bdf-a/--pci-bdf-b`:

  ```bash
  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/run_destr015_parallel_branch_join.py \
    --run-dir "${RUN_DIR}" --attempt 1 --plan \
    --cpu-kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-kubeconfig "${GPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-context "${GPU_EKS_CONTEXT}" \
    --namespace "${NAMESPACE}" --cluster-id "${CLUSTER_ID}" \
    --region "${AWS_REGION}" --site-file "${SITE_FILE}" \
    --host-probe-image "${NODE_INSTALLER_IMAGE}" \
    --predecessor-evidence "${PREDECESSOR_EVIDENCE_DIR}" \
    --node-a "${NODE_A}" --node-b "${NODE_B}"

  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/run_destr015_parallel_branch_join.py \
    --run-dir "${RUN_DIR}" --attempt 1 --execute \
    --confirm DESTR015_EXECUTE \
    --maintenance-window-end "${MAINTENANCE_WINDOW_END}" \
    --cpu-kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-kubeconfig "${GPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-context "${GPU_EKS_CONTEXT}" \
    --namespace "${NAMESPACE}" --cluster-id "${CLUSTER_ID}" \
    --region "${AWS_REGION}" --site-file "${SITE_FILE}" \
    --host-probe-image "${NODE_INSTALLER_IMAGE}" \
    --predecessor-evidence "${PREDECESSOR_EVIDENCE_DIR}" \
    --node-a "${NODE_A}" --node-b "${NODE_B}"
  ```

  `--node-a` hosts the PyTorchJob's Master replica, `--node-b` hosts the Worker replica;
  the two must differ, and each must have 8 allocatable GPUs. The administrator may also run only
  this case in the selective mode of §2.3; in that case DESTR-012 is recorded as
  `SKIPPED_BY_OPERATOR`, the verdict of this case is still judged by every assertion in this section,
  but it cannot serve as the predecessor of a later formal case.
- Purpose: for multi-node training, "several nodes of the same job fault at the same time → each is
  repaired in parallel → one join restarts the job" is a core promise of this system, but the positive
  path so far had only unit and integration evidence
  (`PREEMPT-017`, `tests/hyperpod/test_e2e_distributed_xid_reset.py`), and
  `DESTR-014` currently proves the **negative** protection under an unknown reboot outcome, where the
  join is not executed. What live acceptance must add are the four things the unit tests cannot prove:
  1. Two XID 46 events reported through the real Collector land in the **same** job DAG within the
     multi-node aggregation window (`src/gpu_fault/orchestration/workflow_merge.py`
     `PARALLEL_BRANCH` disposition, `src/gpu_fault/orchestration/dag_branching.py`
     `append_parallel_job_branch`), rather than two mutually independent node workflows;
  2. The two branches of the real executor have evidence of parallel dispatch, and the two
     independently observed `nvidia-smi --gpu-reset` process intervals really overlap under a
     conservative clock-error bound.
     The start/end times of the whole branch cannot prove that the reset processes overlapped;
  3. The shared `STOP_WORKLOADS` stops only once, the join (`RESTART_WORKLOAD`) executes **once**
     only after both branches have completed `RESTORE_SCHEDULING`, and the restart budget is
     deducted only once;
  4. The quiesce/reset/restore of both nodes appear exactly once each in the Node Agent ledger, the
     boot_id is unchanged, and both nodes return to schedulable with no quarantine residue.
  Any drift in any of these would restart the job twice, restart it on a node that is still
  quarantined, or leave it waiting for a restart forever.
- Preconditions:
  1. `DESTR-012` PASS (on its chain, the real reset of `DESTR-001` and the job restart of `DESTR-009`
     have each been established).
  2. Two idle GPU nodes node-a and node-b of the same instance type, 8 GPUs each,
     Ready, schedulable, with no gpu-fault taint or ownership annotation; both Node Agents are ACTIVE
     and their allowed_operations contain `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES`,
     `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS`, `RESET_GPU`, `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES`; neither hosts a controller or an
     executor arbiter replica.
  3. In the Runtime Profile `gpuReset` is `OWN` (owner `gpu-fault-node-agent`) and
     `workloadStop`/`workloadRestart` are `OWN` (owner
     `gpu-fault-kubernetes-adapter`).
  4. The site's `multi_node_aggregation_window_seconds` (read by the runner from the release state
     and written into the plan) is at least 5 s: the two kmsg writes are executed **concurrently** by
     two probes, and the measured time difference is usually 1-2 s, but with a narrower window the
     same-window landing cannot be guaranteed and preflight refuses outright.
  5. The cluster has no other GPU workload, and the processor queue and remote command queue are
     empty.
  6. No synthetic replacement route is needed and no executor env window is needed; this case changes
     no runtime parameter.
  7. Within the approved window both nodes must support the required read-only strace execution
     witness; it is bound to the Agent PID, the executable digest, the Node UID/boot/generation, and is
     calibrated through a real NVIDIA query.
     Premise: `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES` stops that node's kubelet, and until
     `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES` no `kubectl exec` can reach that node, while this case quiesces both nodes
     in parallel; therefore the witness cannot be a streaming exec session but must **run detached**
     as a `systemd-run` transient unit on the host (unit name derived from the run id, `RuntimeMaxSec`
     bounded by the maintenance window and the case budget, stopping itself at expiry, read-only and
     never touching the Agent), persisting its observations to
     `/var/lib/gpu-fault-acceptance/destr015/<run>/`, arranged with a single exec before injection
     (`arm`) and read back with a single exec after the node is Ready again
     (`collect`). If either node cannot be armed, the unit does not report armed within the time
     limit, or the arm receipt is not bound to the scope (run/node/boot/GPU/unit/state directory/
     program digest), refuse before injection and record the refusal reason given by the host; do not
     fall back to merely comparing control-plane timestamps.
- Steps:
  1. Record the full baseline of both nodes: Kubernetes UID, `boot_id`, labels/taints/
     `unschedulable`, Node Agent ledger row count, quiesce state, gpu-fault timers, list of active
     services; the plan is bound to the release-state and the key CPU/GPU Deployment template
     digests, and a mismatch on recomputation before execute is refused.
  2. Use `managed_workload_fixture` to render a two-replica PyTorchJob, 8 GPUs per replica, pinned to
     node-a and node-b respectively, and submit it through `gpu-training-submit` (`--restart-budget
     1`); confirm Running, a healthy NCCL all-reduce heartbeat, and a source attempt observation
     containing 16 unique GPU UUIDs.
  3. The runner uses `host_probe_fixture.py` to start one host probe on each node
     (`scripts/e2e/regional/probes/destructive_node_probe.py`), takes a `snapshot`
     baseline and selects each node's target PCI BDF. Then, through the same probe Pods, it runs one
     `arm` each to set the two independent detached exec witnesses
     (`scripts/e2e/regional/probes/destr015_witness_probe.py`, delivered with a fixed digest by the
     `reset-interval-detached` role of `late_ownership_probe_bundle.py`) to ready: the probe checks
     the Agent PID, the boot id, the existence of the target GPU and the scope digest, writes the
     program copy and `state.json` into the state directory, starts the transient unit and waits for
     it to write `armed.json` (host monotonic/realtime stamps, tracee/producer identity, executable
     digest), and then returns the arm receipt together with host clock samples; the runner records
     its own monotonic stamps before and after the request, forming the first bounded clock
     exchange. Injection is allowed only after both `arm`s succeed.
  4. The two probes execute `write-xid46` **concurrently** (same marker, drill id with a per-node
     suffix) and record their respective write timestamps; the difference between the two must be
     smaller than the aggregation window, otherwise the round is recorded
     `INCOMPLETE` (the injection did not land in one window; not a defect).
  5. Observe the control plane (via store/API only; from injection until both nodes are Ready again,
     the runner issues no exec to either node): the incidents of both events point to the same
     `workflow_request_id`,
     `dag_enabled=true`, `dag_revision>=1`; the shared `STOP_WORKLOADS` has `node_ids` covering both
     nodes; each node has one branch
     `MARK_UNSCHEDULABLE → QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES → VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS →
     RESET_GPU → RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES → VALIDATE_GPU → RESTORE_SCHEDULING`,
     and the join is `RESTART_WORKLOAD` whose `depends_on_step_indexes` contains the
     `RESTORE_SCHEDULING` of both branches.
  6. Poll to the terminal state: every step of both branches exactly once and SUCCEEDED. Then wait
     for both nodes to be Ready again (a node not Ready within the budget means its witness record is
     lost and FAILs, still without exec), confirm the probe Pods are usable, and run one `collect`
     each: the probe checks that the current boot id matches `state.json` (a changed boot id is
     refused), writes `finish.request` to the unit and waits for it to write `final.json` (trace
     digest and byte count, calibration count, reset process exec/exit
     interval, the realtime−monotonic envelope from continuous sampling, host clock stamps, exit
     reason), and returns it with the current host clock, forming the second bounded clock exchange.
     Verdict requirements: each node's `armed`/`final` records are bound to the scope, the unit and
     the same witness id; the boot id of the scope, the arm receipt, both records and the collect
     receipt are all identical; the recorded host monotonic stamps fall inside the
     [arm request, collect response] window (arm, unit and collect share one monotonic clock on the
     same boot, so the comparison is exact); the witness is bound to its own new successful ledger
     row, workflow/incident/fencing/GPU, and via the offset bound of the two exchanges (200 ppm plus a
     50 ms margin) the conservative inner intervals of the two reset processes' exec/exit are derived,
     and the two inner intervals must overlap; the offset uncertainty is written into the evidence.
     `RESTART_WORKLOAD` executed exactly once, SUCCEEDED, with `started_at` no earlier than the
     completion time of both `RESTORE_SCHEDULING`, and details source/target GPU counts both 16;
     workflow SUCCEEDED, incident RECOVERED;
     `superseded_step_indexes` empty, `branch_escalation_counts` empty,
     `exhausted_branch_ids` empty, `workload_withdrawn_at` empty, no
     `terminal_failure_reason`.
  7. Check the job and the budget: the two Pod UIDs of the new attempt differ from step 2, still land
     on the same two nodes, all Running and Ready; restart budget `budget=1`, `restart_count=1`.
  8. Check the data plane: both `boot_id`s unchanged; each ledger gained exactly one SUCCEEDED
     `RESET_GPU`, one `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES` and one `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES`,
     no `RESET_ALL_GPUS_NVSWITCHES` row, no duplicate `command_id`; no quiesce state or fail-safe
     timer residue; every service active at baseline is back to active.
  9. Check scheduling: both nodes Ready, schedulable, with no `gpu-fault.io/` taint or ownership
     annotation.
  10. **Disproof assertion**: in CloudTrail `BatchRebootClusterNodes`,
      `BatchReplaceClusterNodes` and `BatchDeleteClusterNodes` are all empty;
      the control-plane API/control-worker/processor logs contain no Kubernetes write operation
      targeting this job; the `BLAST-001` comparison is still IDENTICAL.
  11. The plan, pre-injection, post-restart and post-cleanup snapshots are bound to the same
      release-state and key Deployment template digests; any drift fails closed.
- Verdict: steps 5-11 all satisfied. Any of the following is a blocker: the two events land in two
  workflows (if the two write timestamps already differ by more than the aggregation window, record
  `INCOMPLETE` rather than a defect); any branch shows
  `RESTART_NODE`/`REPLACE_NODE`/`RESET_ALL_GPUS_NVSWITCHES`/`QUARANTINE`/
  `ESCALATE_SUPPORT`; `RESTART_WORKLOAD` executed other than exactly once or earlier than either
  `RESTORE_SCHEDULING`; the reset process intervals do not overlap or a reliable witness is missing;
  the job is restarted twice or lands on a third node;
  either `boot_id` changes; either node is still quarantined after cleanup.

**Additional data-plane verdict** (extra observations when run on a real cluster): in the ledgers of
both nodes the `started_at` of the successful `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES` rows should be close to each
other (dispatched in the same dispatcher cycle), there is exactly one successful `RESET_GPU` row each
with `attempt=1`; in `kernel_reset_journal` there is at most one kernel-sourced reset row for the
target BDF. These are auxiliary proofs of action count and order and
cannot prove parallelism on their own. The primary evidence of parallelism is the independently
captured process intervals in `physical-reset-intervals.json`,
not the GPU chip's internal execution time; the raw argv does not enter ordinary evidence.

- Cleanup (`finally`, fixed order; failure of any step makes the case FAIL):
  1. Reuse `DESTR-009`'s `wait_for_cleanup_quiescence`: wait until the workflow, the remote commands
     and the source attempt observation are all terminal and quiet for 15 s.
  2. Delete the test PyTorchJob and confirm it no longer exists.
  3. If either node is still cordoned/carries an ownership annotation/carries a `gpu-fault.io/` taint
     (meaning some branch failed), follow the `DESTR-003` `cleanup_case` approach: after
     `wait_incident_idle()`, restore scheduling via the validated-restore workflow of the owning
     incident.
     **Under no circumstances may taints or annotations be deleted by hand to lift the quarantine.**
  4. For each node: first wait for kubelet to answer again (same rule as the `DESTR-016` cleanup: if
     not Ready within the budget, the witness may be considered released only when the boot id has
     changed or the unit's bounded lifetime has elapsed, otherwise record it as unknown); once Ready,
     first stop the witness unit via `disarm` and delete its program copy, then delete the probe
     Pod/ConfigMap; if the node never becomes Ready, **issue no exec to it**, keep the witness state
     and probe resources for manual reconciliation, and FAIL the case. Finally delete the warm-up Pod
     and check for zero residue. When supervision is lost or an in-flight action is unknown, do not
     automatically restore services or lift the quarantine.
  5. Recompute the release-state and Deployment template digests and check they match the plan.
- Known limitations:
  - What this case proves is **same-window** arrival (merged into a DAG at ingest). If the second
    node's fault arrives only after `STOP_WORKLOADS` has completed, the control plane no longer sees
    an active attempt container on that node (`families/evidence.py` `attempt_observation` matches
    only observations that are PENDING/RUNNING with a non-terminated container), and the event takes
    the node-scope path and opens an **independent** idle-node reset workflow instead of merging into
    the job DAG; the "dynamic append during RUNNING" described in `PREEMPT-018/020` is reachable
    only in the short window before STOP has completed. The live behaviour of "late sibling node
    repaired independently, concurrently with the job restart" has no case yet and no explicit
    expectation defined, and is not included in this case.
  - The process intervals are converted conservatively from the continuous clock samples inside the
    unit, the two bounded arm/collect exchanges and the 200ppm plus 50ms margin; there is no
    intermediate calibration between the two exchanges (the node is unreachable), the offset
    uncertainty grows with the interval at 200ppm and is written into the evidence truthfully; a
    clock jump, an incomplete trace, identity drift or an unbounded error can never PASS.
    No promise is made to detect arbitrary external clock tampering, nor are the process intervals
    described as an exact overlap of the silicon action.
    Actual configuration such as `max_concurrent_commands=1` must not be masked by the overlap of
    the branches' total intervals.
  - Running `COLLECT-004` / `COLLECT-015` in the same window pollutes the CloudTrail empty-set
    assertion.


#### Supplementary acceptance of physical ownership after STOP

After an ordinary DESTR-015 PASS with completed cleanup, obtain a separate approved physical
maintenance window and run the supplementary acceptance with
`scripts/e2e/regional/run_late_ownership_acceptance.py`.
It does not replace the ordinary two-node repair with a single job restart, nor can it be inserted at
the phase-6 position of PREEMPT-033. Always use `--case GF-REGIONAL-DESTR-015`, and review the plan,
execute and clean up separately in the following order; stop when the previous trial is not PASS or its
cleanup is incomplete:

The pre-injection calibration only proves that the authenticated read-only NVIDIA query can be
observed independently: a successful query is allowed, as is an accurate, authenticated
active-compute-client refusal with first-attempt details. The latter is still a failed VERIFY,
not a passed no-client barrier; the real `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS` must come after STOP and quiesce.
Authentication, transport, an unknown outcome or a missing actual query trace can never count as a
passed calibration.

1. `--scenario unchanged-owner`: after the real STOP, Agent enqueue and final check, each of the two
   approved nodes completes exactly one reset exec, proving that the measurement chain can observe
   the actual action.
2. `--scenario ownership-drift`: once the command is enqueued but the final permit has not yet been
   issued, add an owner reference to this run's paused Job under the original workload UID/RV
   condition; the final validation refuses accurately, and neither node has a reset exec. This does
   not replace the real workload UID.
3. `--scenario late-sibling`: on the same check barrier, create a bounded GPU Pod with a same-origin
   owner on the second participating node, proving an actual GPU PID/cgroup; the check for all
   participants refuses, and not even the first node may execute the reset. This negative branch
   does not quiesce the second node first.

Each scenario uses an independent, non-nested `--run-dir`; the site, the two nodes, the BDFs, the
Profile, the release, the GPU context and the other preflight parameters follow the constraints of
this section. The explicit `--predecessor-evidence` still points at the DESTR-012 predecessor
evidence of the ordinary run and cannot be placed inside the supplementary trial's output directory.
In addition, `--ordinary-destr015-evidence` must supply the ordinary run's original
`cases/GF-REGIONAL-DESTR-015/GF-REGIONAL-DESTR-015.json`. The entry point enforces validation of its
success, complete cleanup, and the release, cluster, node and runtime bindings; the ordinary run
directory and the supplementary directory must not be nested.
Run `--plan` first each time; execution needs `--execute --confirm PHYSICAL_LATE_OWNERSHIP_EXECUTE`
and a full `--maintenance-window-end`; a plan must not be reused from one scenario for another.

Evidence is written to each scenario's
`cases/GF-REGIONAL-DESTR-015/late-ownership/<scenario>/{result,receipts}.json`,
without overwriting the ordinary `<case>.json`. The manual evidence index must keep the paths and
digests of all three trials together with the original ordinary case and the cleanup results.
PREEMPT-033 may simply reference this supplementary evidence for the same mechanism; the three physical
trials need not be repeated merely for an alias; its ordinary software wrap-up case is still judged
separately.

This proof binds the controlled change **after Agent enqueue and before the final permit**, and uses
an independent continuous exec trace rather than inferring no-action from a zero count in the ledger.
The final challenge lasts at most 90 seconds, the permit at most 3 seconds and is bounded by the
original command's deadline; after the permit, the local safety conditions and the expiry are
re-verified. It is not an atomic transaction from Kubernetes to the kernel, and it does not guarantee
refusal of changes that occur only after an arbitrary later API read, permit or OS scheduling.
Lost contact, an unknown ACK, an incomplete read/trace or an unproven end of an in-flight action FAILs
and keeps the manual-reconciliation state.
The product STOP's own pause fields and ownership annotations are validated by derivation from the
original intent under this STOP's credential; arbitrary modifications read back later must not be
re-registered as approved state.
The detailed protocol and limitations are in [Physical Late-Ownership Acceptance](../components/late-ownership-acceptance.md).

### GF-REGIONAL-DESTR-016

**A second fault on the same node arrives while a physical step is in progress: the same-tier XID is absorbed, the higher-tier XID 79 preempts the reset workflow, takes over the quiesce and completes a real reboot**

Barrier location must use the remote command the workflow actually references, and must verify the incident, the fencing and the
specific `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS` step. A verification inside a compound command may go through WAITING/LEASED re-claims;
an attempt count alone or an operation of the same name cannot prove that the barrier still holds. The full progress of the compound command must also prove that the reset tail
has not yet started; missing progress, an error pointer or multiple candidates all forbid releasing the follow-up injections.

- Level: `destructive-provider-reboot`. One `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES` is really executed on
  an idle GPU node, then the **successor** workflow really reboots that node once through HyperPod
  (`BatchRebootClusterNodes`), and `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES` is performed after the reboot.
  **No GPU reset is submitted, no warm spare is declared, and no replace/delete is authorized at any point.**
- The reusable formal entry point is
  `scripts/e2e/regional/run_destr016_preempting_reboot.py`. By default it only produces the plan;
  before execute it must read `DESTR-002=PASS` (chain: `010 → 001 → 002`; DESTR-002 is the only
  case that has already proven a live reboot on the **same** node), and it requires the administrator to name the node explicitly.
  The target GPU's PCI BDF defaults to the first card enumerated by the host probe, and the device opened by the holder defaults to
  the same card's `/dev/nvidiaN`; both can be set separately with `--pci-bdf` and `--holder-device`:

  ```bash
  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/run_destr016_preempting_reboot.py \
    --run-dir "${RUN_DIR}" --attempt 1 --plan \
    --cpu-kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-kubeconfig "${GPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-context "${GPU_EKS_CONTEXT}" \
    --namespace "${NAMESPACE}" --cluster-id "${CLUSTER_ID}" \
    --region "${AWS_REGION}" --site-profile "${SITE_FILE}" \
    --host-probe-image "${NODE_INSTALLER_IMAGE}" \
    --hyperpod-cluster "${HYPERPOD_CLUSTER}" \
    --executor-role-arn "${EXECUTOR_ROLE_ARN}" \
    --predecessor-evidence "${PREDECESSOR_EVIDENCE_DIR}" \
    --node "${NODE}"

  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/run_destr016_preempting_reboot.py \
    --run-dir "${RUN_DIR}" --attempt 1 --execute \
    --confirm DESTR016_EXECUTE \
    --maintenance-window-end "${MAINTENANCE_WINDOW_END}" \
    --cpu-kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-kubeconfig "${GPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-context "${GPU_EKS_CONTEXT}" \
    --namespace "${NAMESPACE}" --cluster-id "${CLUSTER_ID}" \
    --region "${AWS_REGION}" --site-profile "${SITE_FILE}" \
    --host-probe-image "${NODE_INSTALLER_IMAGE}" \
    --hyperpod-cluster "${HYPERPOD_CLUSTER}" \
    --executor-role-arn "${EXECUTOR_ROLE_ARN}" \
    --predecessor-evidence "${PREDECESSOR_EVIDENCE_DIR}" \
    --node "${NODE}" --max-hold-seconds 2400
  ```

  `--max-hold-seconds` is the **bounded** lifetime of the GPU device holder's systemd transient unit
  (the probe accepts 60–3600 s, default 1800 s; `configure` rejects values below "the conditional pre-authorization validity
  `PRE_AUTHORIZATION_VALID_SECONDS` (1200 s) plus `MIN_HOLD_MARGIN_SECONDS`
  (300 s)" -- the pre-authorization must live inside the holder's lifetime): even if the runner crashes, the holder exits on its own and the node is not
  stuck on the barrier forever. The administrator may also run only this case in the selective mode of §2.3; in that case
  DESTR-002 is recorded as `SKIPPED_BY_OPERATOR`, this case's verdict is still judged against every assertion in this section,
  but it cannot serve as the predecessor of a later formal case.
- Purpose: real faults rarely arrive alone. When the same node reports another one after the physical repair has **already started** (GPU services already
  quiesced), the control plane must get two things right at once, and until now both had only unit and
  integration evidence:
  1. **The same-tier event is absorbed**: the second XID 46 is recorded into the same workflow of the same incident, without opening
     a second parallel repair or appending steps (the `ABSORB` / `WIDEN_IN_PLACE` dispositions in
     `src/gpu_fault/orchestration/workflow_merge.py`);
  2. **The higher-tier event preempts on a dirty boundary**: XID 79's `RESTART_NODE` (rank 50) is strictly stronger than
     `RESET_GPU` (rank 30, `src/gpu_fault/models.py::RecoveryAction`), so
     `workflow_merge.py:474-489` writes `preempt_predecessor` and
     `strictly stronger recovery action: rank 30 -> 50` onto the successor;
     `src/gpu_fault/execution/executor.py::ProductionWorkflowExecutor._supersede_if_safe` cancels the remote command on the barrier after judging the
     `PreemptionBoundary` as a **whole**;
     `executor.py:1237-1300` hands the quiesce to the successor -- it appends a
     `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES` carrying `preemption_quiesce_handoff_after_reboot`,
     makes it depend on `RESTART_NODE`, re-points the steps that used to depend on `RESTART_NODE` (`VALIDATE_GPU`)
     to depend on this step, and writes `quiesce_handoff_from_workflow_id`.
  What live acceptance adds are the four points a unit test cannot prove: the remote command on the barrier is **really** cancelled
  (`status_source=workflow-preempted`); the handoff restore **really** runs after the reboot,
  against the **new generation** of the Node Agent
  (`src/gpu_fault/adapters/node_action/barriers.py::NodeActionBarrierMixin._maintenance_generations` refuses to inherit the predecessor's
  maintenance generation); the preempted reset **never submitted a single GPU reset**; and the node
  finally returns to schedulable with no quarantine residue. Drift in any one of them leaves behind a quiesced, ownerless
  quarantined node.
- Preconditions:
  1. `DESTR-002` PASS (the real reset of `DESTR-001` on its chain is established).
  2. One idle GPU node: Ready, schedulable, no `gpu-fault.io/` taint or
     ownership annotation, at least 1 allocatable GPU, carrying no business workload, no recent XID events,
     and no unclosed incident attached (ESCALATED/QUARANTINED etc.) -- otherwise the injected
     XID 46 would be merged into that incident instead of opening a new workflow; the runner refuses before injection and names
     the `workflow-reconcile --close-incident` / `--close-quarantined` closing means;
     the whole GPU cluster has no other GPU workload.
  3. The node's Node Agent is `ACTIVE` and `allowed_operations` contains
     `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES`, `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS`, `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES`.
     `VALIDATE_GPU` is executed by the validation adapter and does not need to be in the Node Agent operation allowlist.
  4. In the Runtime Profile `gpuReset` is `OWN` (owner `gpu-fault-node-agent`),
     `nodeReboot` is `OWN` (owner `gpu-fault-hyperpod-adapter`, adapter
     `regional-cluster-executor`), and the profile has no warnings.
  5. The processor queue and the remote command queue are empty; workflow preemption is not disabled on the control plane.
  6. The `GPU_FAULT_WORKFLOW_STEP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` actually in effect on the control plane is long enough: both
     escalation injections must land inside the WAITING window of `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS` (the runner reads the
     measured value from the replica environment and refuses if it is insufficient); the
     `GPU_FAULT_NODE_WORKFLOW_MAX_LIFETIME_SECONDS` actually in effect must accommodate this case's estimated duration
     (the successor workflow **inherits** the lifetime deadline of the preempted workflow and does not restart the clock).
  7. At least 1 hour of maintenance window remains; `--maintenance-window-end` must be given explicitly.
  8. No synthetic replacement route is needed, and no control-plane or executor environment variable is changed.
- Steps:
  1. Record the node's full baseline: Kubernetes UID, `boot_id`, labels/taints/
     `unschedulable`, GPU capacity, Node Agent identity (boot_id, artifact digest,
     lifecycle), ledger rows, quiesce state, fail-safe timer, active service list,
     host `boot_id` and GPU inventory; the plan binds the release-state and the key CPU/GPU
     Deployment template digests, recomputed before execute, refusing on any mismatch.
  2. Start two host probes: the shared injection probe
     (`scripts/e2e/regional/probes/destructive_node_probe.py`, used for
     `snapshot`/`write-xid46`/`write-xid79`) and this case's dedicated holder probe
     (`scripts/e2e/regional/probes/destr016_node_probe.py`). The three injections each use a
     **different** marker (the store probe takes the last matching event). Premise: `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES`
     stops kubelet, so the `kubectl exec` channel the probes rely on to answer is cut with it, and no exec reaches the node between the quiesce and
     `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES` -- exactly the moment at which the barrier holds lies inside
     that window. Therefore only the first XID 46 is written on the spot by the runner via `kubectl exec`; the second
     XID 46 and the XID 79 use **conditional pre-authorization**: before the quiesce the runner hands the authorization once
     to the holder probe, and whether to write is decided by the probe on the node against the local ledger (see step 3);
     the runner only observes their landing through the control-plane store and never execs into the node again after the barrier.
  3. First `arm-holder`: the holder probe polls the local Node Agent ledger as a systemd transient unit
     until a new, successful `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES` row added by **this drill** appears, and only then opens a read-only handle on the target
     `/dev/nvidiaN` and holds it until `--max-hold-seconds`. The baseline command_id and
     the arm timestamp are both recorded in this run's state file under `/var/lib/gpu-fault-acceptance`;
     if `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS` has already succeeded **before** the holder started, the probe records
     `arm_race_lost` and this round is judged FAIL (no dirty boundary to preempt; not defect evidence).
     After `arm-holder` returns and **before** the first XID 46 is written, the runner execs once more to
     `pre-authorize`, delivering the conditional pre-authorization: bound to run_id, node, baseline boot id, the held
     device, the drill_id and marker of the reset injection, `--maintenance-window-end`, the agent maintenance window length
     measured on the control plane, the earliest offset of each of the two writes
     (`--absorb-after-seconds`/`--escalate-after-seconds`, both counted from the holder start, i.e. from the moment the
     quiesce row lands in the ledger), the expected ledger shape (quiesce/verify operation names,
     the `clients are still active` refusal text, the forbidden reset/restore operations) and the
     pre-authorization's own expiry time. The probe checks every binding (one mismatch refuses and does not arm), records the
     set of workflows already present in the ledger as the baseline, then places one systemd transient
     timer for each of the two writes. When a timer fires, `fire-injection` evaluates the **barrier condition** on the node every few seconds:
