     exactly one workflow added after the pre-authorization appears in the ledger, its
     `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES` row is SUCCEEDED, its `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS` row has executed and
     the failure reason of the latest attempt contains `clients are still active` (the holder keeping the device open is exactly what it
     refuses on -- this is the barrier), there is no `RESET_GPU`/`RESET_ALL_GPUS_NVSWITCHES`/
     `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES` row; the boot id has not changed; the holder unit is still active; the current time is earlier than both
     the pinned window derived from the quiesce row time plus the maintenance window length and the pre-authorization expiry; the absorption
     (XID 46) precedes the escalation (XID 79). The relative delays are only the **earliest** moments and never constitute authorization.
     If the condition does not hold, nothing is written; if the condition can no longer hold (a reset/restore row appears, verify succeeds,
     the boot id changes, the holder exits, workflow ambiguity) or the authorization expires, the reason is recorded, the other timer is cancelled
     and the holder is stopped. Before writing, `fire_requested_at` and the matched ledger facts are persisted to the
     state file, so a lost ACK is never replayed.
  4. Write the first XID 46 and wait for the incident to open a `RESET_GPU` workflow whose
     `official_steps` are exactly the eight steps `FREEZE_EVIDENCE → MARK_UNSCHEDULABLE →
     QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES → VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS → RESET_GPU →
     RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES → VALIDATE_GPU → RESTORE_SCHEDULING`.
  5. Wait until the **dirty boundary** holds: `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES` has SUCCEEDED and has not been RESTOREd,
     `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS` is parked in `WAITING` with a remote command id, `RESET_GPU` has never
     executed; the barrier remote command has `status=WAITING`, its `result_details` have
     `gpu_client_quiesce_attempt >= 1` and a `reason` containing `clients are still active`
     (`src/gpu_fault/adapters/node_action/step_execution.py::NodeActionExecutionService._fold_result`); that
     step has exactly **one** remote command under this workflow. At the same time the runner uses the store-side
     `barrier_authorization` to record the barrier identity (workflow, incident, fencing token,
     generation, both command ids) and the observation time (`barrier-authorization.json`; recorded once more before the escalation as
     `barrier-authorization-escalate.json`), for comparison against the host's write records in step 11;
     this record is evidence only and is not, and cannot be, delivered to the node.
  6. After the pre-authorized second **same-tier** XID 46 lands, verify the absorption: the incident and
     `workflow_request_id` are unchanged, no new incident and no new workflow is created,
     the counts of `official_steps` and `step_executions` do not grow, `official_action` is still
     `RESET_GPU`, and the new event's reason points at this node and XID 46.
  7. After the pre-authorized XID 79 lands, verify the preemption: the preempted reset workflow is `SUPERSEDED`; the incident points at
     a **new** `RESTART_NODE` workflow (neither the same row reused nor a second incident);
     the successor's `preemption_reason` contains `strictly stronger recovery action`;
     `dag_enabled=true`, `dag_revision>=1`, `inherited_step_indexes` contains
     `MARK_UNSCHEDULABLE`, `quiesce_handoff_from_workflow_id` points at the preempted workflow;
     the successor's **last step** is a `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES` carrying
     `preemption_quiesce_handoff_after_reboot`, depending on `RESTART_NODE`, and `VALIDATE_GPU` depends on that step.
  8. Verify the wrap-up of the preempted workflow: its barrier remote command becomes `FAILED`,
     `status_source=workflow-preempted`, `error` points at the successor's `request_id`; it never
     dispatched a `RESET_GPU` remote command; its `WAITING` step execution record itself is **not rewritten**
     (`WorkflowStepStatus` has no CANCELLED state; the cancellation happens on the remote command).
  9. Poll to the terminal state: `RESTART_NODE`, the handoff `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES`,
     `VALIDATE_GPU`, `VALIDATE_HOST`, `VALIDATE_FABRIC`, `RESTORE_SCHEDULING`
     all SUCCEEDED (`RESTART_NODE` may poll in WAITING first, but has exactly one success row);
     workflow SUCCEEDED, incident RECOVERED, no `terminal_failure_reason`.
  10. Verify the live reboot: both the host `boot_id` and the Kubernetes Node boot id changed,
      the Node UID is unchanged; the GPU holder vanished with the reboot (its systemd unit is no longer active);
      the Node Agent re-registered with a new `boot_id`, artifact digest unchanged, state `ACTIVE`;
      after the reboot both probe Pods must be recreated (`restartPolicy: Never`) before a snapshot can be taken.
  11. Verify the data plane: the ledger has no SUCCEEDED `RESET_GPU` or
      `RESET_ALL_GPUS_NVSWITCHES` row; `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES` and
      `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES` each have a success row (`VALIDATE_GPU` is executed through the GPU validation adapter,
      not through the Node Agent, so it does not appear in the ledger; its success is taken from the workflow record of step 9);
      `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS` has at least one failure row (proving the holder really blocked the barrier);
      no quiesce state and no NVIDIA compute client residue; every service active at baseline is back to
      active; the GPU inventory is back to the baseline count. In the `injections_fired` read back by the holder probe's
      `holder-status`, the `fire_requested_at` of both writes must be **later** than the moment the runner
      observed the barrier in the store (the absorption is compared against the first observation, the escalation against the re-observation before escalation),
      and the workflow, incident and boot id matched on the host must agree with the store observation
      (`fired_after_barrier_errors`) -- all these host reads happen after the node is Ready.
  12. Verify scheduling: the node is Ready, schedulable, with no `gpu-fault.io/` taint or ownership
      annotation.
  13. **Disproof assertions**: CloudTrail has exactly one `BatchRebootClusterNodes` with the executor role as actor;
      `BatchReplaceClusterNodes` and `BatchDeleteClusterNodes` are empty.
  14. Plan, pre-injection, post-reboot and post-cleanup bind the same release-state and key Deployment
      template digests; any drift fails closed.
- Verdict: all of the checks above are satisfied. Any of the following is a blocking item: the holder loses the arming race, the barrier never
  reached WAITING (recorded as FAIL; this round had no preemptable dirty boundary); the second XID 46 opens a second workflow or
  a second incident, or changes the step table; XID 79 does not preempt, or the successor has no quiesce handoff,
  or the handoff restore is not after the reboot; the preempted workflow dispatched or submitted any GPU
  reset; the ledger shows a SUCCEEDED `RESET_GPU` or `RESET_ALL_GPUS_NVSWITCHES`;
  any host-recorded write is earlier than the runner's barrier observation, or matched a different workflow/incident/
  boot id; the barrier condition never held before the pre-authorization expired (the holder released itself; this round had no escalation write);
  CloudTrail shows not exactly one reboot, an actor other than the executor role, or any
  replace/delete; the node is still quarantined after cleanup; any cleanup step fails.
  If the remaining maintenance window is already insufficient before injection, the step timeout actually in effect on the control plane cannot fit both
  injections, or the agent maintenance window cannot fit the earliest escalation offset, preflight refuses outright (not a defect).

**Additional data-plane verdict** (observed additionally when run on a real cluster): the failure rows of
`VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS` in the ledger should be several consecutive rows with increasing `attempt`, and their
`command_id` must equal the barrier command of the preempted workflow -- this proves that "waiting for clients to exit" happened on the real
node and not only in control-plane timestamps; the `started_at` of the handoff `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES` success row
must be later than the boot time of the host's new `boot_id`; in `kernel_reset_journal` the target
BDF must show no kernel-sourced reset row at all (this case has no GPU reset anywhere).

- Cleanup (`finally`, fixed order; any failing step makes the case FAIL):
  1. `disarm-holder` (idempotent): first wait for the node to become Ready again -- after the quiesce only a restore or a
     reboot brings kubelet back, and never exec while the node is unreachable; once the node is back, recreate the probe Pod,
     then stop the holder, the arm unit and both injection timers, `reset-failed` them, and confirm the units are no longer active.
     If the node never comes back, the release is considered done only if the boot id has changed (transient units die with the boot) or the holder's
     bounded lifetime has elapsed; otherwise record a cleanup failure. The holder must go first, otherwise the
     quiet wait below may be blocked by ourselves.
  2. `wait_incident_idle()`: wait until the workflow and all remote commands are terminal and quiet.
  3. If the node is still cordoned/carries an ownership annotation/carries a `gpu-fault.io/` taint, restore scheduling through the validated-restore workflow on the owning incident in the same way as
     `DESTR-003` `cleanup_case`.
     **Under no circumstances may taints or annotations be deleted by hand to lift the quarantine.**
  4. Delete both probe Pods/ConfigMaps and verify zero residue.
  5. Recompute the runtime identity (release-state and Deployment template digests) and check it agrees with the plan.
- Known limitations:
  - The boundary this case preempts is the WAITING of `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS` (quiesce applied and not
    restored). The single-node `RESET_GPU` step itself never parks in WAITING, so "a physical step in progress"
    means the **physical step sequence** is in flight, not that a reset call is interrupted; "preempted halfway through
    a reset call" is unreachable in the current implementation and no assertion should be written on it.
  - The disposition of the second XID 46 is `ABSORB` for the same GPU UUID and `WIDEN_IN_PLACE` when there is no UUID or a different card.
    The **observable outcome** of both is the same (same incident, same workflow,
    unchanged step table); this case only asserts these shared observations, not the disposition label.
  - `SUPERSEDED` is persisted when the preempted workflow's executor next reaches a step boundary,
    so it may lag the creation of the successor workflow by up to one lease period; the runner budgets for this;
    readers must not treat this lag as a defect.
  - This case only proves a second fault on the **same node**. A same-tier event landing on **another** node takes the parallel
    branch path (see `DESTR-015`); a late-arriving sibling-node fault after `STOP_WORKLOADS`
    opens an independent workflow (see the known limitations of `DESTR-015`).

### GF-REGIONAL-DESTR-017

**Generation fence after an out-of-band reboot: the node is rebooted from outside the system while RESET_GPU is waiting, the in-flight command of the old generation is rejected, and no reset is executed on the new boot**

- Level: `destructive`. One idle GPU node is **really rebooted once**; the reboot is initiated by a
  systemd timer on the node (`systemd-run --on-active=<n>s systemctl reboot`),
  **without going through the control plane and without calling any provider API** (an OS reboot is not
  `BatchRebootClusterNodes`). This case performs no real `RESET_GPU`: what it asserts is precisely that that reset
  never lands.
- The reusable formal entry point is
  `scripts/e2e/regional/run_destr017_out_of_band_reboot_fence.py`. By default it only produces the
  plan; before execute it must read `DESTR-002=PASS` (a live reboot has already been established on the same
  node), and it requires the administrator to name the node explicitly; the GPU PCI BDF defaults to the
  first card enumerated by that node's host probe and can also be set with `--pci-bdf`:

  ```bash
  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/run_destr017_out_of_band_reboot_fence.py \
    --run-dir "${RUN_DIR}" --attempt 1 --plan \
    --cpu-kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-kubeconfig "${GPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-context "${GPU_EKS_CONTEXT}" \
    --namespace "${NAMESPACE}" --cluster-id "${CLUSTER_ID}" \
    --region "${AWS_REGION}" --site-file "${SITE_FILE}" \
    --host-probe-image "${NODE_INSTALLER_IMAGE}" \
    --predecessor-evidence "${PREDECESSOR_EVIDENCE_DIR}" \
    --node "${NODE}"

  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/run_destr017_out_of_band_reboot_fence.py \
    --run-dir "${RUN_DIR}" --attempt 1 --execute \
    --confirm DESTR017_EXECUTE \
    --maintenance-window-end "${MAINTENANCE_WINDOW_END}" \
    --cpu-kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-kubeconfig "${GPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-context "${GPU_EKS_CONTEXT}" \
    --namespace "${NAMESPACE}" --cluster-id "${CLUSTER_ID}" \
    --region "${AWS_REGION}" --site-file "${SITE_FILE}" \
    --host-probe-image "${NODE_INSTALLER_IMAGE}" \
    --predecessor-evidence "${PREDECESSOR_EVIDENCE_DIR}" \
    --node "${NODE}" \
    --reboot-delay-seconds 30 --max-hold-seconds 1200
  ```

  `--reboot-delay-seconds` (30..600) is the interval "from the holder opening to the earliest permitted reboot": the reboot
  is armed on the node as a conditional pre-authorization **before** the injection (see step 3); when the time comes the probe decides from the local
  ledger whether the barrier holds, and the interval is only the earliest moment, not an authorization; it must also make the reboot fall inside the already
  pinned maintenance window -- before arming, the runner validates against the agent maintenance window measured on the control plane, and while the barrier is
  WAITING it re-checks the remaining window from the store (without exec); if there is not enough time it records `INCOMPLETE` rather than
  forcing through. `--max-hold-seconds` must be no lower than the pre-authorization validity `PRE_AUTHORIZATION_VALID_SECONDS`
  (900 s). The administrator may also run only this
  case in the selective mode of §2.3; in that case `DESTR-002` is recorded as `SKIPPED_BY_OPERATOR`, this case's verdict is still judged against
  every assertion in this section, but it cannot serve as the predecessor of a later formal case.
- Purpose: the generation / boot-id fence is the last gate of "never touch hardware on the wrong generation",
  but until now it had only unit evidence (`GF-ATTEMPT-GENERATION-FENCE-*`,
  `test_same_incident_stale_node_generation_is_always_rejected`,
  `test_registry_addressing_fences_on_agent_generation`,
  `tests/execution/test_retired_generation.py`,
  `tests/execution/test_abandoned_generation.py`); no live case has ever really swapped a node's boot id while a
  workflow was in flight. What live acceptance adds are the four things a unit test cannot prove:
  1. the copy of `agent_generations[node]` pinned when `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES` succeeded
     (the maintenance-window pinning logic in `src/gpu_fault/adapters/node_action/step_execution.py`)
     really disagrees with the new generation after the node's out-of-band reboot, and
     `maintenance_agent_fence` therefore refuses to dispatch, rather than "carrying on dispatching after reconnecting";
  2. the refusal happens **before** `RESET_GPU`: on the new boot the Node Agent ledger has no
     `RESET_GPU` success row for this round, and the kernel journal has no reset record for the target BDF;
  3. the old generation's in-flight command is not patched up to `SUCCEEDED` -- it ends as failed/expired and its
     `command_id` is not reused (the Node Agent's 7-day replay does not turn it into a success);
  4. the failure compensation (`RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES`) is exempt from the window but **not exempt from the generation check**,
     so it is likewise blocked by the fence, and the workflow fails closed and hands over to a human instead of staying in
     WAITING with unlimited renewals.
  Drift in any one of them means the control plane may execute a hardware operation on a node that has just rebooted and whose state is unknown,
  or record an unfinished repair as a success.
- Preconditions:
  1. `DESTR-002` PASS ("real reboot + Agent re-registering with a new boot id" is already established on the same
     node).
  2. One idle GPU node with 8 cards, Ready, schedulable, no `gpu-fault.io/` taint
     or ownership annotation; Node Agent ACTIVE with allowed_operations containing
     `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES`, `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS`, `RESET_GPU`,
     `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES`; the node hosts neither controller nor executor arbiter replicas, nor
     any GPU workload.
  3. In the Runtime Profile `gpuReset` is `OWN` (owner `gpu-fault-node-agent`);
     this case needs no `nodeReboot` ownership, because the reboot does not go through the control plane.
  4. `systemd-run` (transient unit) is available on the node, and the probe image is the node installer
     image; kubelet comes back automatically after the node reboots (proven by `DESTR-002`).
  5. The processor queue and the remote command queue are empty and the cluster has no other in-flight incident; the target node must not carry
     any unclosed incident (ESCALATED, QUARANTINED, DETECTED, ACTION_PENDING,
     SAFETY_PENDING) -- while the node is still held by such an incident, a newly injected XID would be merged into that
     incident instead of opening a new workflow; the runner refuses before injection and names the closing means in the error:
     `gpu-fault-admin workflow-reconcile --close-incident` (ESCALATED) or
     `--close-quarantined` (QUARANTINED).
  6. The remaining maintenance window must be significantly larger than "arming interval + reboot return time"; the runner cross-validates in both directions with the pinned
     `maintenance_window_expires_at` and `--maintenance-window-end`.
- Steps:
  1. Record the node's full baseline: Kubernetes UID, `boot_id`, labels/taints/
     `unschedulable`, the Node Agent record (`generation`, `incarnation_id`,
     `retired_incarnation_ids`), ledger rows, quiesce state, gpu-fault timer,
     active service list, GPU inventory and target BDF; the plan binds the release-state and the key
     CPU/GPU Deployment template digests, recomputed before execute, refusing on any mismatch.
  2. The runner starts two host probes (same node, different run ids, so the ConfigMap/Pod names do not
     collide): `probes/destructive_node_probe.py` handles injection and snapshots,
     `probes/destr017_node_probe.py` handles the holder and the out-of-band reboot.
  3. Use `destr017_node_probe.py arm-holder --after-ledger-op
     QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES` to arm a **bounded** GPU device occupant: as a systemd
     transient unit it polls the Node Agent ledger and only opens `/dev/nvidiaN` after the
     `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES` success row of **this round** appears. It must wait until after the quiesce,
     because the quiesce itself sweeps device occupants; the occupant's job is to make the immediately following
     `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS` fail and retry continuously, parking the workflow stably in WAITING.
     The probe records the command_id matched by the holder, the arming time and the pre-reboot `boot_id` in this run's
     state file on the node; in the cleanup phase the runner calls `destr017_node_probe.py clear-state --run-id <run id>`
     to delete it (only when the holder or the reboot was ever armed), otherwise the next `--plan` of the same attempt would read a
     stale holder match or reboot marker.
     After `arm-holder` returns and **before** XID 46 is written, the runner execs once more to
     `pre-authorize-reboot --delay-seconds <n>`. Premise: `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES`
     stops kubelet, no exec reaches the node between the quiesce and the restore, and the moment the barrier is
     WAITING lies exactly inside that window, so the authorization can only be given in advance, and it is **conditional** -- bound to
     run_id, node, baseline boot id, the held device, drill_id and marker,
     `--maintenance-window-end`, the agent maintenance window length measured on the control plane, the earliest reboot
     offset, the expected ledger shape (quiesce/verify operation names, the `clients are still active`
     refusal text, the forbidden reset/restore operations) and the pre-authorization expiry time. The probe checks every binding
     (one mismatch refuses and does not arm), records the set of workflows already present in the ledger as the baseline, **first**
     writes the pre-reboot `boot_id` into the marker file, then arms a one-shot `fire-reboot` with
     `systemd-run --on-active=<n>s`, and returns immediately (a synchronous reboot would kill the probe's own exec channel).
  4. Use `destructive_node_probe.py write-xid46` to software-replay one XID 46 text line into `/dev/kmsg`,
     and confirm the Collector reports it and a node-scoped `RESET_GPU` workflow is opened; this is not a hardware-generated
     XID. The 8-step plan is
     `FREEZE_EVIDENCE → MARK_UNSCHEDULABLE → QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES →
     VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS → RESET_GPU → RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES → VALIDATE_GPU →
     RESTORE_SCHEDULING`.
  5. Read the details of the successful `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES` execution and take this node's generation N from
     `agent_generations` together with `maintenance_window_expires_at` (the window start time is
     recorded as well); confirm `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS` has entered WAITING with an error text that is a retry reason of the
     "GPU device clients are still active" kind.
  6. The runner re-checks from the store that the remaining window fits the reboot offset (no exec; kubelet is already stopped), and uses
     `barrier_authorization` to record the barrier identity (workflow, incident, fencing token,
     generation, both command ids) and the observation time (`waiting-verify.json`); this record is evidence only and
     is not, and cannot be, delivered to the node. Meanwhile, once its time comes, `fire-reboot` on the node evaluates
     the **barrier condition** every few seconds: exactly one workflow added after the pre-authorization appears in the ledger, its
     `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES` row is SUCCEEDED, its `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS` row has executed and
     the failure reason of the latest attempt contains `clients are still active` (the holder keeping the device open is exactly what it
     refuses on -- this is the barrier), there is no `RESET_GPU`/`RESET_ALL_GPUS_NVSWITCHES`/
     `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES` row; the boot id has not changed; the holder unit is still active; the current time is earlier than both
     the pinned window derived from the quiesce row time plus the maintenance window length and the pre-authorization expiry, and past
     the earliest offset after the holder opened. Only when the condition holds does it write `fire_requested_at` and the matched ledger
     facts into the marker file and then execute `/bin/systemctl reboot`; if the condition can no longer hold
     (a reset/restore row appears, verify succeeds, the boot id changes, the holder exits, workflow
     ambiguity) or the authorization expires, it records the reason, cancels the reboot and stops the holder.
  7. Wait for the node to return to Ready with a **new** `boot_id`, and for the Node Agent to re-register with generation N+1
     (the old incarnation enters `retired_incarnation_ids`).
  8. Poll to the workflow's terminal state. During this, any one of four kinds of fail-closed text is allowed as the record of
     "how the waiting step ended" (window expired, device occupant, wait ceiling, transport failure);
     the runner only records the variant and does not pin one of them; but `agent generation changed from N to N+1` **must** appear in some step error or in the workflow's terminal
     error -- this is the hard assertion of this case,
     and it comes from the `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES` compensation that is window-exempt but not generation-exempt.
  9. Terminal-state checks: the fenced original workflow must be `FAILED`; the original incident may be
     `QUARANTINED`, or `RECOVERED` with the legitimate recovery-successor evidence described in the next step;
     `RESET_GPU` never SUCCEEDED -- the compound carrier command has carried the `RESET_GPU`
     member since its creation, and carrying alone is not dispatch: there must be no command whose first step is a reset, and the carrier's
     `batched_results` must contain no result of the `RESET_GPU` member (the executor never
     reached that step); the old generation's command has no SUCCEEDED result;
     `RESTART_NODE`/`REPLACE_NODE`/
     `RESET_ALL_GPUS_NVSWITCHES` do not appear in the plan.
  10. Successor checks: when `QUARANTINED` and the compensation failed, **exactly** one support successor is opened
      (`workflow-support-after-<W>`, with steps `FREEZE_EVIDENCE →
      MARK_UNSCHEDULABLE → QUARANTINE → ESCALATE_SUPPORT`,
      `official_action=ESCALATE_OPERATOR`, no `predecessor_workflow_id`,
      sharing `lifetime_deadline_at` with the original workflow); `reboot`/`replace`/`drain`
      successors must not exist in either outcome. When `RECOVERED`, a separate support successor is not mandatory, but there must be a
      successful recovery successor whose `predecessor_workflow_id` points at the fenced workflow; it must not preempt the original workflow,
      must not execute a reset or any other forbidden node action, and must not involve another node. A bare
      `incident.state=RECOVERED` does not constitute proof of passing.
  11. Data-plane checks: the ledger has no `RESET_GPU` success row for this round (baseline rows are excluded by
      `command_id`, and the Node Agent's 7-day replay must not leak in); the kernel journal
      has no reset row of this round for the target BDF; `boot_id` changed exactly once -- confirmed simultaneously by four mutually independent
      pieces of evidence: the baseline/final values of the Kubernetes Node status, exactly two entries of
      `observed_boot_ids` in the probe's persistent state, the `boot_id_before_reboot` in the marker file,
      and the Agent record with `generation == N+1` and exactly one new entry in `retired_incarnation_ids`.
      The `fire_requested_at` in the marker file must be **later** than the moment the runner observed the barrier in the store,
      and the workflow, incident and boot id matched on the host must agree with the store observation
      (`fired_after_barrier_errors`); all these host reads happen after the node has returned to Ready.
  12. **Disproof assertion**: the set of provider mutation verbs related to this node in CloudTrail is **empty**
      (none of `BatchRebootClusterNodes`, `BatchReplaceClusterNodes`,
      `BatchDeleteClusterNodes`) -- an OS reboot is not a provider
      action, and that is exactly the boundary this case proves.
  13. Run the retired-generation view of workflow-reconcile once in **plan mode** and
      record the plan verbatim into the evidence; **do not apply**; the evidence records
      `retired-generation-plan` + `NOT_APPLIED`. Whether to reap is an operations decision.
  14. Plan, pre-injection, post-reboot and post-cleanup bind the same release-state and key Deployment
      template digests; any drift fails closed.
- Verdict: steps 5–14 are all satisfied. Any of the following is a blocking item: any
  `RESET_GPU` execution or ledger success row appears on the new boot; the old generation's command is recorded as `SUCCEEDED`; the terminal records
  contain no `agent generation changed from N to N+1`; the workflow stays in a non-terminal state until the observation
  budget is exhausted (meaning the fence did not fail closed but renewed indefinitely); any provider
  mutation verb appears; a `reboot`/`replace`/`drain` successor appears; the number of `boot_id` changes is not
  exactly one; the reboot in the marker file is earlier than the runner's barrier observation, or matched a different workflow/incident/
  boot id; the barrier condition never held before the pre-authorization expired (the reboot cancelled itself; recorded as FAIL, not as a defect);
  the node is still quarantined or still unschedulable after cleanup. If the remaining window is already insufficient before the reboot is armed, record
  `INCOMPLETE` rather than a defect.

**Additional data-plane verdict** (observed additionally when run on a real cluster): on the new boot the Node Agent's
`allowed_operations` should equal the baseline (a generation change does not change the authorization surface); in the ledger the rows of the old
`command_id` must not flip from failed to succeeded; the quiesce fail-safe timer
necessarily disappears after the reboot, while the quiesce state file **survives** -- the asymmetry between the two is the
real residue this case must record, and the cleanup steps must handle it explicitly.

- Cleanup (`finally`, fixed order; any failing step makes the case FAIL):
  1. First wait for the node to be Ready -- after the quiesce only a restore or this case's reboot brings kubelet
     back, and never exec into the node while it is unreachable; once the node is back, recreate the probe Pod. If the node never
     comes back, the reboot timer and the holder are considered released only if the boot id has changed (transient units die with the boot) or the holder's bounded lifetime has elapsed;
     the host-side quiet proofs (steps 5 and 6) cannot be assumed,
     and a cleanup failure is still recorded.
  2. If the reboot was armed but has not fired, `cancel-reboot` first; then `disarm-holder` (idempotent;
     run it even when the reboot has already killed the transient unit, to confirm that neither the unit nor the device occupation remains).
  3. Wait for the Node Agent to be ACTIVE, and `wait_incident_idle()` for all incidents and remote commands
     to go quiet.
  4. If the node still carries an ownership annotation or a `gpu-fault.io/` taint: first restore scheduling through the validated-restore workflow on the **successor** support
     incident (the successor took over the annotation); afterwards the original
     incident no longer quarantines any node but is still `QUARANTINED` -- its quiesce was never restored by the product
     (the compensation was refused by the generation fence and the out-of-band reboot voided it), validated-restore would be refused here by the
     quiesce guard, and it is not the exit the product prepared for it -- so the runner uses the same service call as
     `workflow-reconcile --close-quarantined`, with the node isolation evidence it has just read
     (no cordon, no quarantine taint of this incident, no isolation annotation), to close it as
     `RECOVERED`; if the evidence is rejected, record a cleanup failure.
     **Under no circumstances may taints or annotations be deleted by hand to lift the quarantine.**
  5. Explicitly clean up the quiesce residue (GPU services are not restored by the workflow after an out-of-band reboot, see "Known
     limitations"), and verify that every service active at baseline is back to active.
  6. Delete both probe Pods/ConfigMaps and the probe state file on the node, and verify zero residue.
  7. Recompute the release-state and Deployment template digests and check they agree with the plan.
- Known limitations:
  - What this case proves is an out-of-band reboot **inside the maintenance window**. When the window has already expired, or the reboot happens before
    `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES` (generation not yet pinned), two other paths are taken: the former
    hits the window expiry first, the latter has no fence to compare against at all. Neither timing has a live case yet.
  - The generation fence makes the `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES` compensation fail **necessarily**, so the combination "out-of-band reboot +
    maintenance window" always leaves "GPU services not restored" in the control-plane records and escalates to a human. This is
    fail-closed by design, not a defect; but it also means the control plane has no automatic path to bring this
    node's GPU services back, and the validated-restore workflow has no
    `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES` step either. The node side needs no help from the control plane: the reboot takes the quiesce's
    fail-safe timer with it, but the Node Agent, when starting on the new boot, replays the leftover
    QUIESCED state file
    (`src/gpu_fault/node_agent/quiesce.py::GpuServiceQuiesceManager.reconcile_after_boot`:
    if the `boot_id` recorded in the state file differs from the current one, it restores and deletes it); this case asserts on the host snapshot taken after the reboot and before cleanup
    that `quiesce_states` is empty; the `restore-quiesce` in the cleanup is only an
    idempotent safety net.
  - The re-dispatch/INTERRUPTED semantics of `docs/en/detailed-design-v2.md` §7.4 hold only on the `RESTART_NODE`
     path, where the reboot is initiated by the system itself; on the path where the maintenance window pins the generation there is no automatic re-signing:
     the fence failure fails closed and opens a support successor. §7.4 now records both paths, and
     this section is consistent with it.

### GF-REGIONAL-DESTR-018

**Live acceptance of the workflow lifetime hard deadline: RESET_GPU keeps WAITING until the lifetime expires, the whole workflow goes
FAILED, in-flight commands go workflow-timeout, escalation goes only to a human, and the node-side ledger adds no new
RESET rows after the cancellation**

- Level: `live-service-action`. One real XID 46 injection and one real
  `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES`/`RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES` on an idle GPU node,
  **no reboot, no replace, no provider API call**; the real `RESET_GPU`
  never succeeds (cancelled by the lifetime). The case opens a temporary environment window on the CPU-plane
  `gpu-fault-control-worker`, **and therefore must not run in the same window as any other regional
  case**.
- The reusable formal entry point is
  `scripts/e2e/regional/run_destr018_lifetime_deadline.py`. By default it only produces the plan;
  before execute it must read `DESTR-010=PASS` (chain: `010 → 018`; this case only needs the single piece of evidence
  "fabric manager restart established on live hardware", not `001/002/009/012`), and it requires the administrator
  to name the node explicitly:

  ```bash
  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/run_destr018_lifetime_deadline.py \
    --run-dir "${RUN_DIR}" --attempt 1 --plan \
    --site-profile "${SITE_PROFILE}" \
    --cpu-kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-kubeconfig "${GPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-context "${GPU_EKS_CONTEXT}" \
    --namespace "${NAMESPACE}" --cluster-id "${CLUSTER_ID}" \
    --region "${AWS_REGION}" \
    --host-probe-image "${NODE_INSTALLER_IMAGE}" \
    --predecessor-evidence "${PREDECESSOR_EVIDENCE_DIR}" \
    --node "${NODE}"

  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/run_destr018_lifetime_deadline.py \
    --run-dir "${RUN_DIR}" --attempt 1 --execute \
    --confirm DESTR018_LIFETIME_DEADLINE \
    --maintenance-window-end "${MAINTENANCE_WINDOW_END}" \
    --site-profile "${SITE_PROFILE}" \
    --cpu-kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-kubeconfig "${GPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-context "${GPU_EKS_CONTEXT}" \
    --namespace "${NAMESPACE}" --cluster-id "${CLUSTER_ID}" \
    --region "${AWS_REGION}" \
    --host-probe-image "${NODE_INSTALLER_IMAGE}" \
    --predecessor-evidence "${PREDECESSOR_EVIDENCE_DIR}" \
    --node "${NODE}"
  ```

  The runner opens and closes the environment window itself. For manual checking or post-incident wrap-up, the same helper can also be
  run on its own (read-only when neither `--open` nor `--close` is given):

  ```bash
  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/control_plane_env_window.py \
    --site-profile "${SITE_PROFILE}" \
    --cpu-kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" --namespace "${NAMESPACE}" \
    --cluster-id "${CLUSTER_ID}" --region "${AWS_REGION}" \
    --baseline "${RUN_DIR}/cases/GF-REGIONAL-DESTR-018/env-window-baseline.json"

  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/control_plane_env_window.py \
    ... --open --confirm OPEN_CONTROL_PLANE_ENV_WINDOW \
    --set GPU_FAULT_NODE_WORKFLOW_MAX_LIFETIME_SECONDS=180 \
    --set GPU_FAULT_WORKFLOW_EXECUTION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=180

  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/control_plane_env_window.py \
    ... --close --confirm CLOSE_CONTROL_PLANE_ENV_WINDOW
  ```

  The administrator only needs to `--set` these two variables (lifetime L and execution timeout E, 60–3600 s, E ≥ L;
  E > L is also rejected, because the control plane refuses at startup an execution timeout longer than the node lifetime). The helper
  fills in the **whole set of eight** timing variables together following the control plane's startup validation (`complete_assignments`);
  any derived variable explicitly set above its shipped default is rejected at parse time; the completed set first passes
  `validate_timing_relationships`, and any combination the control plane would refuse at startup makes the helper refuse to open the window as well.
  Derivation rules (none goes above the shipped default; with L=3600 the rendered values are the defaults themselves):

  | Variable | Rule | L=E=180 |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `GPU_FAULT_NODE_WORKFLOW_MAX_LIFETIME_SECONDS` | L | 180 |
  | `GPU_FAULT_WORKFLOW_EXECUTION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | E; `min(1800, L)` when not given | 180 |
  | `GPU_FAULT_WORKFLOW_STEP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `min(600, L)` | 180 |
  | `GPU_FAULT_WORKFLOW_STEP_WARNING_SECONDS` | `min(300, step // 2)` | 90 |
  | `GPU_FAULT_HYPERPOD_MANAGED_RECOVERY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `min(1800, L)` | 180 |
  | `GPU_FAULT_WORKFLOW_INSTALL_STEP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `min(1900, L)` | 180 |
  | `GPU_FAULT_WORKFLOW_INSTALL_CONTAINMENT_SECONDS` | `min(600, L − install)` | 0 |
  | `GPU_FAULT_WORKFLOW_LEASE_DURATION_SECONDS` | `min(180, E // 2)` | 90 |

  The per-step ceiling equals the lifetime rather than being below it: above the lifetime the control plane refuses to start, below the lifetime
  the per-step ceiling would end the VERIFY wait before the lifetime this case measures; when both expire on the same tick
  `_execute_step` judges `workflow_deadline_failure` before the per-step ceiling, so the lifetime
  verdict wins. The helper only changes the `control-worker` container of the CPU-plane `gpu-fault-control-worker`,
  and writes the pre-window env of the eight variables plus the Deployment template digest into `--baseline`;
  closing the window restores all eight **exactly** from the baseline (variables that were unset before the window are deleted, not written as
  shipped defaults).
  The administrator may also run only this case in the selective mode of §2.3; in that case `DESTR-010` is recorded as
  `SKIPPED_BY_OPERATOR`, this case's verdict is still judged against every assertion in this section, but it cannot serve as the predecessor of a later
  formal case.
- Purpose: the hard lifetime (`claim_deadlines` in `src/gpu_fault/execution/restart_budget_preflight.py`,
  `workflow_deadline_failure` and `DEADLINE_EXEMPT_COMPENSATION` in `src/gpu_fault/execution/step_bounds.py`)
  is the only guarantee that "one node
  workflow does not occupy a GPU node indefinitely". Until now it had only unit evidence, and
  `PREEMPT-032` only proved it with synthetic ingest, a 1 s lifetime and a node that never returns results. What live acceptance
  adds are the four things a unit test cannot prove:
  1. the lifetime compressed to 180 s is stamped onto the workflow at the **first claim**
     (`lifetime_deadline_at`, never re-stamped afterwards), and at expiry it is judged by
     `_execute_step` in `src/gpu_fault/execution/executor.py` **before** `_dispatch_step`,
     so the whole workflow goes FAILED instead of waiting another WAITING round;
  2. the remote commands **in flight** at expiry are really cancelled: PENDING/WAITING commands go straight to
     `FAILED` + `status_source=workflow-timeout`; already LEASED commands record
     `cancellation_requested_at`, and their late results are forced to `FAILED` +
     `status_source=completed-after-cancellation`;
  3. the only compensation allowed through, `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES`, really still executes and succeeds after the deadline,
     bringing the node's GPU services back to baseline;
  4. after the cancellation the node side really no longer **starts** any mutating action. The Node Agent has no cancellation channel,
     so this can only be proven with the ledger's `started_at` (written only by
     `mark_in_progress` in `src/gpu_fault/node_agent/executor.py`) and the kernel
     reset log.
  Drift in any one of them means a reset is still running on an abandoned node, or an overdue workflow is climbing to
  reboot/replace.
- Preconditions:
  1. `DESTR-010` PASS.
  2. One idle GPU node: Ready, schedulable, no `gpu-fault.io/` taint or
     ownership annotation, no active NVIDIA compute client, no leftover quiesce state,
     `/dev/kmsg` writable; Node Agent ACTIVE with `allowed_operations` containing
     `QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES`, `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS`, `RESET_GPU`,
     `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES`; the node hosts neither controller nor executor arbiter replicas.
  3. In the Runtime Profile `gpuReset` is `OWN` (owner `gpu-fault-node-agent`).
  4. The environment window is currently **closed**: every ready replica of `gpu-fault-control-worker` runs
     the same set of values; if preflight reads a mismatch between replicas (rollout not converged) it refuses to execute.
  5. The timing margins must hold (preflight computes them and writes them into the plan, refusing if unmet; lowering
     `GPU_FAULT_GPU_CLIENT_VERIFY_MAX_ATTEMPTS` is **not allowed**):
     - the site's `GPU_FAULT_WORKFLOW_POLL_INTERVAL_SECONDS` (default 5 s), i.e.
       the re-dispatch cadence of `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS`, must be at least 5 s;
     - the worst-case verify count `ceil((lifetime − 90) / cadence)`, where 90 s is the measured reserve for isolation,
       stopping workloads and quiesce; 180 s / 5 s gives 18, plus a margin of 15 gives 33,
       which must be `≤ 60` (`GPU_FAULT_GPU_CLIENT_VERIFY_MAX_ATTEMPTS`), i.e.
       `lifetime < attempts × cadence` with ample margin;
     - `lifetime` must be strictly less than the site's `GPU_FAULT_WORKFLOW_STEP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` measured **before the window opens**
       (default 600 s). After the window opens the helper compresses
       the per-step ceiling to equal the lifetime, and then the check order in `_execute_step` -- lifetime first, per-step
       ceiling second -- guarantees that the verdict is still the lifetime; preflight reads the pre-window value;
     - `GPU_FAULT_WORKFLOW_EXECUTION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` must not be lower than `lifetime`
       (`claim_deadlines` takes the smaller of the two), and the window values must fall within 60–3600 s.
  6. The cluster has no other GPU workload, and the processor queue and the remote command queue are empty.
- Steps:
  1. Record the baseline: Kubernetes UID, `boot_id`, labels/taints/`unschedulable`,
     every `command_id` in the Node Agent ledger (to tell historical rows apart), quiesce state,
     gpu-fault timer, active service list, host GPU inventory; the plan binds the
     release-state and all Deployment template digests of both planes, recomputed before execute, refusing
     on any mismatch.
  2. **Open the environment window first**: open it with L=E=180 s (the helper fills in the other six variables automatically, see the table above),
     and wait until every ready replica of `gpu-fault-control-worker` runs the new values. Immediately after opening, recompute the runtime identity: apart from
     the control-worker's `generation`/`observed_generation`/`template_sha256`,
     any field change is judged as drift and aborts. **The order is not interchangeable**: this rollout
     moves the single-instance scheduling lease, and swapping the lease holder in the middle of an already opened workflow would leave the timestamps this case measures
     with more than one interpretation.
  3. **Then arm the device holder** (still before injection): the host probe
     `scripts/e2e/regional/probes/destr018_node_probe.py` opens the target card's `/dev/nvidiaN` as a bounded systemd transient
     unit and holds it, so that the Agent's device-client check
     sees the same pid occupying the same card every time. `RESET_GPU` itself has no WAITING branch;
     a late holder would only make the reset **fail** and escalate to reboot -- that is a different case.
  4. **Inject last**: the other host probe
     (`scripts/e2e/regional/probes/destructive_node_probe.py`) writes one XID 46 with a marker into the real
     `/dev/kmsg` and records the injection time.
  5. Observe the control plane: the incident opens a node-scoped RESET_GPU workflow with official steps
     `FREEZE_EVIDENCE → MARK_UNSCHEDULABLE → QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES →
     VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS → RESET_GPU → RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES → VALIDATE_GPU →
     RESTORE_SCHEDULING` (the node is idle, so there is no `STOP_WORKLOADS`); the workflow carries
     `lifetime_deadline_at`;
     `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS` repeatedly enters WAITING with "clients are still active",
     and every re-dispatch leaves one row in the node ledger.
  6. Poll to the terminal state: workflow `FAILED`; the failed step execution lands on
     `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS`, with `details.workflow_lifetime_exceeded=true`
     and containing `workflow_execution_deadline`, `workflow_deadline_overdue_seconds`,
     `workflow_deadline_remote_command_cancellation`; the step execution of `RESET_GPU`
     **never** SUCCEEDED; `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES` SUCCEEDED exactly once; the step executions contain
     no `RESTART_NODE`, `REPLACE_NODE`, `RESET_ALL_GPUS_NVSWITCHES`,
     `VALIDATE_GPU`, `VALIDATE_NODE_HEALTH`, `RESTORE_SCHEDULING`,
     `RESTART_WORKLOAD`; the incident is `ESCALATED` or `QUARANTINED` and covers only that
     node.
  7. The cancellation moment `T_cancel` is the earliest cancellation stamp across all remote commands (for WAITING/PENDING commands that were cancelled
     use their `updated_at`, for LEASED ones use `cancellation_requested_at`). The terminal state of every
     in-flight command must be `FAILED`, with `status_source` either `workflow-timeout` or
     `completed-after-cancellation`; after `T_cancel` the only command allowed to succeed is
     `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES`.
  8. Recompute the margin with the measured cadence: sample the `started_at` differences of the consecutive `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS` rows
     of this round in the ledger (at least two intervals) and re-assert
     `lifetime < attempts × cadence` by the formula of step 5; if no sample can be taken, judge FAIL rather than passing.
  9. Escalation chain: `classify` in `src/gpu_fault/orchestration/escalation.py` must classify
     this failure as the `lifetime_exceeded` stage with `effective_action`
     `ESCALATE_OPERATOR`, and generate the deterministic `inc-support-after-<workflow>` /
     `workflow-support-after-<workflow>`. That support-ticket workflow must be reachable, its steps exactly
     `FREEZE_EVIDENCE → MARK_UNSCHEDULABLE → QUARANTINE → ESCALATE_SUPPORT`
     (an idle node has no `STOP_WORKLOADS`), covering only that node, terminal state SUCCEEDED or still
     PENDING/RUNNING, and **no second escalation** (no next-generation support
     incident/workflow with it as source exists). It also **must not** fail because of an inherited lifetime -- see the known limitations.
  10. Late same-node fault: write one XID 79 to the same node. It must land on the **same**
      incident/workflow as a record-only absorption
      (`lifetime_exceeded → ABSORB_RECORD_ONLY` in
      `src/gpu_fault/orchestration/workflow_merge.py`): the count of official steps is unchanged,
      the already FAILED workflow is not revived, and no new PENDING/RUNNING workflow appears in the cluster
      (apart from the two known request ids).
  11. Disproof assertions: `BatchRebootClusterNodes`,
      `BatchReplaceClusterNodes` and `BatchDeleteClusterNodes` are all empty in CloudTrail; the node's
      `boot_id` is unchanged.
  12. Plan, post-window-open, terminal state and post-cleanup bind the same release-state; apart from the control-worker's
      two writes (open, close), all Deployment template digests of both planes are unchanged,
      and the control-worker's `template_sha256` after closing the window must return to the pre-window value.
- Verdict: steps 5–12 are all satisfied. Any of the following is a blocking item: the workflow is not FAILED because of the lifetime;
  the in-flight commands were not cancelled (`T_cancel` cannot be determined); any in-flight command ends
  SUCCEEDED (except `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES`); `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES` did not succeed
  exactly once; reboot/replace/validate/restore-scheduling appears after the deadline;
  the escalation is not `ESCALATE_SUPPORT` or a second escalation appears; XID 79 opened a new workflow or changed
  existing steps; no margin can be computed from the measured cadence; the control-worker template digest did not return to baseline after closing the window.

**Additional data-plane verdict** (observed additionally when run on a real cluster, with `T_cancel` as the boundary, three checks judged in order):

1. **Strict**: among the ledger rows added in this round, there is no mutating operation
   (`QUIESCE_GPU_SERVICES`, `VERIFY_NO_GPU_CLIENTS`, `RESET_GPU`,
   `RESET_ALL_GPUS_NVSWITCHES`, `VALIDATE_GPU`) whose `started_at` is later than
   `T_cancel`; the node must not **start** any attempt after the control plane has given up. If a row of these operations
   has **no** `started_at` (`save()` only writes
   `completed_at/attempt/state/operation`; `started_at` is written only by `mark_in_progress`),
   that row cannot be positioned relative to `T_cancel` and is judged **undecidable, hence FAIL**, not a pass.
2. **At most one row** straddling the boundary (`started_at < T_cancel < completed_at`) is allowed: a command the node had already claimed before
   the cancellation may finish after the cancellation. That row must be self-consistent:
   - consistent with `kernel_reset_journal` -- when the `RESET_GPU` row is `SUCCEEDED` there is exactly one kernel-sourced reset for the target BDF,
     when it is `FAILED` exactly zero;
   - the control plane must not have turned this late result into a success: the corresponding remote command's terminal state is `FAILED`,
     its `status_source` is `workflow-timeout` or `completed-after-cancellation`,
     and for the latter `result_details.post_cancellation_status` must equal the ledger row's
     own state;
   - the workflow's `RESET_GPU` step execution is never SUCCEEDED;
   - in this case the device holder suppresses every attempt, so the straddling row should only be `FAILED` with an empty kernel log;
     a `SUCCEEDED` straddling row is a blocking item (meaning the reset really ran on the abandoned node).
3. After `T_cancel` there is exactly **one** successful `RESTORE_GPU_SERVICES` row (the only compensation allowed through),
   and it has a `started_at`.

`gpu_fault_workflow_lifetime_exceeded_total` and
`gpu_fault_workflow_merge_record_only_total{reason="lifetime_exceeded"}` each +1
serve as optional evidence: when unreadable, record "unreadable"; when readable but not increased, judge FAIL.

- Cleanup (`finally`, fixed order; any failing step makes the case FAIL):
  1. Release the device holder (`disarm-holder`), confirming the transient unit has vanished and the target card has no leftover occupation.
  2. `wait_incident_idle()`: wait until the workflow, the support-ticket workflow and all remote commands are terminal and
     quiet.
  3. If the node is still cordoned/carries an ownership annotation/carries a `gpu-fault.io/quarantined` taint,
     restore scheduling through the validation-first workflow following `restore_validated_quarantine.py`;
     the taint belongs to the incident that quarantined it (the support-ticket incident first, then the reset incident).
     **Under no circumstances may taints or annotations be deleted by hand to lift the quarantine.**
  4. Close the environment window, restoring exactly from `--baseline` and waiting for the rollout to converge.
  5. Delete both probe Pods/ConfigMaps and verify zero residue.
  6. Recompute the runtime identity and release-state: compare against the **pre-window** baseline; only the
     control-worker's `generation` may have advanced twice (open, close), and
     `template_sha256`, images, replica counts and the other Deployments must be fully identical.
  7. Re-take the node snapshot: Ready, schedulable, no `gpu-fault.io/` taint, `boot_id`
     unchanged.
- Known limitations:
  - **Known defect (this case currently goes red)**: the escalated support-ticket workflow inherits the already expired
    `lifetime_deadline_at` (`src/gpu_fault/orchestration/escalation.py::HardwareEscalationService.emit`
    passes `workflow.lifetime_deadline_at` straight through to the new workflow), while
    `claim_deadlines` in `restart_budget_preflight.py:98-131` does not re-stamp a workflow that already has a
    `lifetime_deadline_at`, so this human-handover workflow is already overdue at its first
    claim. This case judges by "the support-ticket workflow is reachable and does not carry the inherited overdue lifetime",
    so it will FAIL until both places are fixed -- that is the reason the case exists, not a defect of the case.
  - The verdict depends on the node-side ledger's `started_at`. The Node Agent has no cancellation channel,
    and `save()` does not write `started_at`, so a mutating row with only `completed_at` can never
    prove that it started before the cancellation; such rows are treated as undecidable and make the round FAIL rather than
    passing silently.
  - The environment window compresses the lifetime to 180 s. If the site sets
    `GPU_FAULT_WORKFLOW_STEP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` to 180 s or lower, or
    `GPU_FAULT_WORKFLOW_POLL_INTERVAL_SECONDS` below 5 s, preflight refuses to execute
    outright -- this is a configuration fact, not a defect, and must be noted in the report.
  - This case is the live counterpart of `PREEMPT-032`: 032 proves the same terminal-state contract locally with synthetic ingest, a 1 s lifetime and a node
    that never returns results; this case proves it on a real node with a real device
    holder. The additional data-plane verdicts of the two sections must stay consistent.
  - Running in the same window as `COLLECT-004` / `COLLECT-015` or any case that asserts an empty CloudTrail set
     contaminates both; no other regional case may run in parallel during the environment window either.


### GF-REGIONAL-DESTR-019

**Node Agent idle restart keeps the same generation, `/healthz` is writable with counters,
the ledger migrates in place, and the next real command leaves a complete audit trail**

- Level: `live-service-action`. Restart `gpu-fault-node-agent.service` once on an idle
  GPU node (arm a fail-safe start first), then run the two-step XID 45 →
  `RESTART_FABRIC_MANAGER` workflow already proven by `DESTR-010`;
  **no reset, no reboot, no isolation, no provider API call of any kind**.
- The reusable formal entry point is
  `scripts/e2e/regional/run_destr019_agent_restart_ledger.py`. By default it only generates the plan;
  before execute it must read `DESTR-010=PASS` (chain: `010 → 019`) and requires the administrator
  to name the node explicitly:

  ```bash
  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/run_destr019_agent_restart_ledger.py \
    --run-dir "${RUN_DIR}" --attempt 1 --plan \
    --site-profile "${SITE_PROFILE}" \
    --cpu-kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-kubeconfig "${GPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-context "${GPU_EKS_CONTEXT}" \
    --namespace "${NAMESPACE}" --cluster-id "${CLUSTER_ID}" \
    --region "${AWS_REGION}" \
    --host-probe-image "${NODE_INSTALLER_IMAGE}" \
    --predecessor-evidence "${PREDECESSOR_EVIDENCE_DIR}" \
    --node "${NODE}"

  python3 scripts/e2e/regional/run_destr019_agent_restart_ledger.py \
    --run-dir "${RUN_DIR}" --attempt 1 --execute \
    --confirm DESTR019_RESTART_NODE_AGENT_LEDGER_AUDIT \
    --maintenance-window-end "${MAINTENANCE_WINDOW_END}" \
    --site-profile "${SITE_PROFILE}" \
    --cpu-kubeconfig "${CPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-kubeconfig "${GPU_KUBECONFIG}" \
    --gpu-context "${GPU_EKS_CONTEXT}" \
    --namespace "${NAMESPACE}" --cluster-id "${CLUSTER_ID}" \
    --region "${AWS_REGION}" \
    --host-probe-image "${NODE_INSTALLER_IMAGE}" \
    --predecessor-evidence "${PREDECESSOR_EVIDENCE_DIR}" \
    --node "${NODE}"
  ```

- Purpose: ARCH-C3/C4/C5 added three things to the Node Agent that so far have only unit evidence --
  `src/gpu_fault/node_agent/executor.py` emits INFO lines containing only identifier fields at the
  four points accepted/started/completed/failed; the `results` table in
  `src/gpu_fault/node_agent/ledger.py` moved to a `(command_id, attempt)` primary key, gained audit
  columns, and migrates in place when `PRAGMA user_version` goes 0→2 (v3 adds the nullable audit
  column `agent_generation`, the Agent's own live generation at accept time; v2→v3 is only
  `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN`, no table copy); `/healthz` in `src/gpu_fault/node_agent/app.py`
  returns 503 with a heartbeat/counters payload when the ledger is not writable. What the live run
  has to add is: the deployed wheel really migrates an old-schema ledger; one Agent restart does not
  regress incarnation/generation; the first real command after the restart leaves a consistent
  trail in all three places -- journald, the ledger and `/healthz`.
- Preconditions:
  1. `DESTR-010` PASS.
  2. One idle GPU node: Ready, schedulable, no `gpu-fault.io/` taint or ownership annotation,
     no non-system Pods, no active NVIDIA compute client; Node Agent ACTIVE with
     `allowed_operations` containing `RESTART_FABRIC_MANAGER`; Fabric Manager active.
  3. The real ledger on the host has `PRAGMA user_version` equal to the deployed release's
     `gpu_fault.node_agent.ledger.LEDGER_SCHEMA_VERSION` (currently 3; the verdict imports the
     constant from the installed release instead of hard-coding it, so what it refuses is a node
     whose Agent lags the release; otherwise it refuses -- that is the deployment fact "the node did
     not roll with the control plane", not a case defect).
  4. Before the restart `/healthz` is 200: `ledger.writable=true`, a heartbeat has succeeded,
     `counters` contains exactly `accepted/completed/failed/rejected`.
  5. **No remote command in flight and the processor queue is empty** (checked once at preflight
     and once right before the restart); no fail-safe timer left over from a previous round.
- Steps:
  1. Baseline: node snapshot, Agent record (generation, incarnation, boot_id), host
     `snapshot` (Agent `MainPID`/`InvocationID`, ledger schema and INTERRUPTED row count,
     gpu-fault timer list), `/healthz`.
  2. Migration drill: under `/var/lib/gpu-fault-acceptance` the probe builds an old-schema ledger
     using the pre-ARCH-C4 `CREATE`/`ALTER` statements (3 SUCCEEDED rows, one fencing row), opens it
     with the deployed venv's `NodeActionLedger`, reads back `PRAGMA user_version`, primary key,
     columns, row count, `attempt_history`, `get()`, `accept_fencing`, then appends once with
     `mark_in_progress(attempt=2)`+`save(exit_code=7)`, and finally deletes the temporary file.
     **The real ledger is not touched.**
  3. Restart: the probe first runs `systemd-run --on-active=<restore>s systemctl start
     gpu-fault-node-agent.service` (fail-safe), then
     `systemctl restart gpu-fault-node-agent.service`, waits for active, records
     `MainPID`/`InvocationID` before and after; waits until the control-plane Agent record's
     `last_seen_at` is later than the restart instant.
  4. `/healthz` after the restart: 200, all `counters` 0, heartbeat age ≤ 120 s.
  5. Injection: another probe (`probes/node_host_probe.py`) writes one solo XID 45 with a marker to
     `/dev/kmsg`; wait for the workflow terminal state.
  6. Audit: with `<idempotency_key>/<node>/agent-<generation>` as the command_id, read journald
     (`journalctl -t gpu-fault-node-agent`), the ledger audit columns and `/healthz`.
- Verdict:
  - Restart: `MainPID` and `InvocationID` changed, `boot_id` unchanged; the control-plane Agent has
    `lifecycle_state=ACTIVE`, `generation` and `agent_incarnation_id` equal to the baseline;
  - Migration drill: old ledger `user_version=0`, primary key only `command_id` → after opening
    `user_version=3`, primary key `(command_id, attempt)`, all audit columns present (including
    `agent_generation`, NULL for old rows, an integer for new rows), row count unchanged,
    no `results_legacy` left behind; an old row's `attempt_history` reads back one entry with a
    readable payload; fencing preserved, the old token rejected; after the append the history is
    `[1, 2]`, `get()` returns attempt 2 with `exit_code=7`;
  - The workflow is exactly `FREEZE_EVIDENCE → RESTART_FABRIC_MANAGER`, owners
    `gpu-fault-control-plane`/`gpu-fault-node-agent`, SUCCEEDED, with no isolation,
    quiesce, reset or reboot;
  - journald has exactly three lines accepted/started/completed for that command_id, each containing
    `command_id incident_id workflow_request_id operation node_id fencing_token
    agent_generation gpu_count attempt`, with values matching the control plane, the completed line
    has `status=SUCCEEDED` and an integer `duration_ms`; no parameters, GPU UUID list,
    signature or secret;
  - The real ledger has exactly one row for the command with `attempt=1`, `state=SUCCEEDED`,
    `incident_id/workflow_request_id/fencing_token` matching the control plane,
    `started_at < completed_at`, `parameters_digest`/`signature_digest` are 64-character
    sha256, the `gpu_uuids` column is non-empty, `exit_code` is null; the INTERRUPTED row count equals the baseline;
  - After the command `/healthz` `counters` are `accepted=1 completed=1 failed=0 rejected=0`;
  - The CloudTrail set of provider mutation verbs is empty; the node's Kubernetes state is field-by-field identical to the baseline.
- Cleanup (`finally`): `ensure-agent-active`; `disarm-restore` and confirm no newly added
  gpu-fault timer remains; `ensure-fabric-manager-active`; node snapshot identical to the baseline with no non-system
  workload; zero residue from the two probe Pods/ConfigMaps; runtime identity equal to preflight.
  Any failing step makes the case FAIL.
- Known limitations:
  - **The Agent is not restarted while a command is in flight.** `NodeActionLedger._interrupt_in_progress`
    marks in-flight rows INTERRUPTED (`retryable=false`),
    `adapters/node_action/step_execution.py::_fold_result` folds INTERRUPTED straight to
    FAILED (`manual_confirmation_required`); on a RESET_GPU workflow this escalates at the
    `reset` rung to `RESTART_NODE`, i.e. a real provider reboot, with no hard stop on the node
    side. Therefore the ARCH-C2 behaviour "a pinned command during the restart is judged
    WAITING TRANSPORT_RETRY via 409 `AGENT_GENERATION_UNKNOWN`" has unit evidence only
    (`tests/execution/test_node_action_transport_retry.py`) and is not reproduced by this case.
  - The 503 branch of `/healthz` (ledger not writable) cannot be safely constructed on live hardware
    and is covered only by `tests/node_agent/test_agent_observability.py`.
  - The ARCH-C1 resubmission (FAILED retryable → same envelope submitted again → attempt 2) needs a
    deterministic retryable failure (OSError/timeout); there is no harmless way to inject one on live hardware, so it has unit evidence only.


### GF-REGIONAL-DESTR-020

- The reusable formal entry point is
